World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Sheinbaum delivers her second-year report as trade tensions simmer
World.content:
Listen to this article

The week of Aug. 31, President Claudia Sheinbaum delivered her second annual government report, reflecting on the state of the nation as her second year in office draws to a close. She touted falling homicides and a stable economy, only to face a pointed rebuttal from opposition leaders who accused her administration of manipulating crime statistics and shielding officials tied to drug trafficking.

Mexico continues to grapple with security challenges on a variety of fronts, a fact underscored by a car bomb in Zacatecas Sunday night — the state’s third such attack in four days. But Mexico’s security forces remain active and on Monday claimed a high-profile target: Soldiers and marines killed Luis Enrique Barragán, alias “R5,” the accused leader of extortion against Michoacán’s avocado growers, in a shootout in Tocumbo.

Trade friction with Washington ran through much of the week. A dispute over cheese naming rights is complicating already-strained talks over the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). Mexico continues to push back against the threat of U.S. tariffs, and Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on the sidelines of a G20 gathering Wednesday to press Mexico’s case against tariffs on steel, aluminum and cars.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Sheinbaum’s second-year report meets a sharp opposition response

President Sheinbaum delivered her second annual government report Tuesday, a 67-minute address touting a 51% reduction in homicides since taking office, record foreign direct investment and a stable economy. She said her administration’s relationship with Washington “has had its challenges” but reiterated that “sovereignty isn’t negotiated, handed over or shared.”

Opposition senators offered a starkly different account. PAN’s Ricardo Anaya disputed the government’s homicide figures, arguing that reclassified deaths obscure a rising toll, while PRI’s Alejandro Moreno accused the administration of an unspoken “pact” with organized crime, pointing to the unresolved U.S. extradition request for Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya. Sheinbaum has said her administration won’t shield anyone who has committed a crime.

The president also used Wednesday’s press conference to accuse the Trump administration of trying to “create divisions” within her cabinet ahead of November’s U.S. midterms, calling it part of a long-standing U.S. pattern of pressuring “independent governments.” Her approval rating stood at 68% heading into the report, among the highest of any Mexican president at this point in a term, according to polling firm El Financiero. Along with the high approval rating, the newest results of the MND Sheinbaum Index™ found an almost 10-point increase in the president’s performance.

Security: Zacatecas car bomb and a cartel leader’s death

Eleven people, including a policewoman, were injured Sunday night when a car bomb exploded outside a municipal police station in Ojocaliente — the third explosives attack in Zacatecas in four days. Authorities are investigating whether the blast was retaliation for the Saturday capture of an alleged Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) sicario. The explosion damaged 30 properties and 13 vehicles; classes were suspended and army troops deployed to the municipality.

The next day, Mexican Army and Navy forces killed Luis Enrique Barragán Chávez, known as “El Güicho” or “R5,” in a shootout in Tocumbo, Michoacán. Federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch identified Barragán as the leader of the Cártel de Los Reyes and the main coordinator of extortion against avocado producers in the state; the U.S. had offered a $3 million reward for his arrest on drug and firearms charges.

At her Friday mañanera in Zacatecas, Sheinbaum’s Security Cabinet reported the state’s daily homicide rate fell 85% in August compared to September 2024, and that more than 3,800 people have been arrested there since she took office. Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla Trejo, responding to a Fox News report on U.S. anti-drone operations at the border, said the drones are mainly used by migrant smugglers and declined to confirm Mexican military involvement in the U.S. takedowns.

Mexico-U.S. trade relations: Tariffs, cheese and an uncertain USMCA

Mexico-U.S. trade talks hit a snag over cheese this week, with U.S. officials pressuring Mexico to amend a May agreement with the European Union that grants regional-name protections to products like Parmigiano Reggiano and manchego. The U.S. government’s position is that these names are generic; the European Commission says the deal isn’t open to amendment, leaving Mexico caught between two trading partners.

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on the sidelines of a G20 Innovation Ministerial in North Carolina on Wednesday, pressing the U.S. to lift tariffs on Mexican cars, steel and aluminum, which Mexico calls unjustified. Sheinbaum said Thursday her government is working to secure a better tariff agreement, noting that most Mexican exports still enter the U.S. duty-free under the USMCA.

The tariff dispute traces back to Washington’s decision not to renew USMCA in its current form for a further 16 years, leaving the pact’s future — and Mexico’s manufacturing-heavy states — in limbo pending ongoing bilateral talks.

Economy: The peso strengthens as growth forecasts improve

The peso hit a 28-month high against the dollar on Friday, trading at 16.863, reviving talk of a “super peso.” Analysts attribute the gains partly to peso strength and partly to the dollar’s weakness. A stronger peso cuts import costs and inflation but squeezes exporters’ margins and remittance values, with agricultural states like Michoacán most exposed.

Earlier in the week, Banxico raised its 2026 GDP growth forecast to 1.5%, up from 1.1%, citing stronger-than-expected second-quarter growth, while flagging USMCA uncertainty and geopolitical tensions as downside risks.

Mexico’s tourism sector added a bright note: The World Travel & Tourism Council ranked Mexico fourth globally in tourism-generated GDP, behind only the U.S., China and Germany, with Quintana Roo cited as the main driver.

Looking ahead

Trade talks with Washington remain unresolved on both cheese labeling and industrial tariffs, with no clear timeline for a new USMCA agreement as bilateral dialogue continues. Meanwhile, Hurricane Marie, a Category 2 storm off Baja California Sur, is expected to weaken to a Category 1 by Saturday as it moves out to sea, though Conagua warned that atmospheric instability could keep bringing rain to the country’s interior into next week. Zacatecas remains under heightened security following last week’s car bomb attack, with federal, state and municipal forces reinforcing operations in Ojocaliente.

Some good news to end the week

Mexico News Daily

World.title: The singing frog that came to symbolize midcentury Mexico
World.content:
While it may be a fine place to avoid New Orleans’ sweltering heat, Tulane University’s Doris Z. Stone Latin American Library serves a much larger purpose as a repository of Mexico travel and tourism ephemera, including magazines, hotel brochures and highway maps.

Together, the collection offers a unique look at how the United States’ southern neighbors were constructed as attractive vacation destinations throughout the midcentury.

Mexico especially loomed large in the imagination of U.S. tourists. It was a period when, as historian Mauricio Tenorio notes, Mexico was understood as a “Brown Atlantis” — where revolutionary thought fermented, and the Pan-American Highway promised access to exotic adventures. Everyone wanted to meet Frida Kahlo and visit Teotihuacán, all while dreaming up global politics anew.

Two brochures found in the Mexican ephemera collection tell how Mexico feted itself for an international community, including the crooning amphibian that would become the country’s unofficial mascot during the time.

The singing frogs of Taxco

First is a trifold brochure from arguably Mexico’s most famous nightclub during the second half of the 20th century — Cantarranas. However, the site didn’t always host the international glitterati.

Located in the silver-mining town of Taxco, roughly 2.5 hours outside of Mexico City, the estate was initially conceived in 1538 by Hernán Cortés, who ordered its construction so that he could extract the region’s precious materials.

Dubbed Hacienda Cantarranas, – literally “singing frogs” due to the loud chorus of frogs living in the nearby area – Cortés’ son Martín de Cortés oversaw its construction, which featured large stones along a hillside. Over the years, the infrastructure took its toll on the unstable land it was built on and was ultimately abandoned in favor of a new locale.

For the next four centuries, the site was nothing more than a derelict ghost of Mexico’s colonial past. That is, until one entrepreneur saw an opportunity.

Antonio “Tony” Reyes Ramírez, who would later become Taxco’s minister of tourism, officially opened Cantarranas in 1957. Eager to capitalize on its history, Reyes Ramírez kept the name and leaned on its playful imagery in his marketing materials.

Cantarranas quickly developed a global reputation as a lively hangout throughout the 1960s and 70s, and even featured prominently in a popular television show of the time.

The brochure for Catarranas promises tourists a night of “flamenco dancing by Estela Calderón,” “Carl Brice directly from Nassau, Bahamas,” “Primitive African Drums by the owner and Manager of Cantarranas Tony Reyes,” and “The Latin American Rhythms of the great pianist Juan García Esquivel.”

The nightclub also housed several distinct spaces, including the “Twilight Room,” the “Patio,” the “Flamenco Room” and the “Mulata Room.” Newspapers of the time reported that, inside Cantarranas, “the audience moves en masse from room to room as each show finishes.”

During that same decade, the brochure from Tulane notes that Cantarranas was chosen as the backdrop for an episode of the NBC series, “I Spy,” entitled “Return to Glory,” which aired Feb. 23, 1966.

In it, Alexander Scott – played by Bill Cosby – is tipped off by U.S. intelligence to visit Cantarranas, where he rendezvouses with the wife of a deposed president of an unnamed Latin American country. Famed Mexican actress Dolores del Río plays the part of the wife, as Cosby and costar Robert Culp try to negotiate the democratic leader’s return to his home nation.

Cantarranas’ popularity continued to grow throughout the early- to mid-1970s.

A newspaper article from 1974 lists several of the club’s attractions, including “Flying Indian Men,” a discotheque called “The Psychedelic Cave,” bullfighting lessons, a piñata party, and calypso songs by Carl Brice.

However, as a new decade dawned, Cantarranas was beginning to lose its luster.

An article from 1978 reported that “Cantarranas is a little rough around the edges.” Two years later, the club was described as “the kind of place that you wouldn’t miss if you missed it. But worth it if you’re utterly bored.”

Unable to sustain itself any longer, in 1983, the Mexican state of Guerrero acquired the property and converted it into a culinary school and arts center. In 1992, it changed hands once again, this time to the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México as a school for foreign nationals.

Despite its short life, Cantarranas heralded Mexico’s midcentury miracle as its nascent legacy was beginning to be forged.

The birth of Señor Frogs

Twelve years after Cantarranas opened, another Mexican restaurateur, Carlos Anderson, was cooking up a similar concept that would come to define the Mexican resort experience well into the 21st century – Señor Frog’s.

First opened in Mazatlan in 1969, Señor Frog’s capitalized on that same midcentury swagger, with waiters slinging tequila shots and cajoling spontaneous conga lines in a neon cave. It’s unclear why Señor Frog’s succeeded where Cantarranas ultimately failed, but it did.

It wasn’t just the nightclub scene, either. The Tulane collection includes another brochure with a singing frog on it — this one from Pemex or Petróleos Mexicanos, the company formed in 1938 by the Mexican government to sell the nation’s significant oil supply.

The brochure includes maps of Mexican highways and invites travelers to explore the best routes. There is no mention of Cantarranas, or Taxco, or even nightclubs. However, at this point the singing frog had become emblematic of Mexico’s exotic sights, electric nights and cultural spectacle.

From Hacienda Cantarranas to Tony Reyes’ “Singing Frogs” bar, through a national oil company and today’s Señor Frog’s franchises, the brochure in Tulane University’s Doris Z. Stone Latin American Library chronicles the birth of a national symbol, while documenting how tourists were meant to imagine the delights of midcentury Mexico – strange, inviting and culturally savvy, not unlike a crooning amphibian.

Kevin M. Anzzolin earned a PhD in Romance Languages and Literatures from the University of Chicago. He is the author of “Guardians of Discourse: Literature and Journalism in Porfirian Mexico,” published by the University of Nebraska Press (2024), which received an Honorable Mention from LASA-Mexico for Best Book in the Humanities in 2025. He currently teaches language and literature courses at Christopher Newport University (Virginia, USA). He also publishes in more public fora.

World.title: Is Mexican-made kombucha underrated?
World.content:
There are few drinks in history with an eccentrically bubbly origin story like kombucha.

The fermented probiotic can be traced back to China around 221 B.C. during the Qin Dynasty, when it was consumed as a “remedy for immortality” by those who considered the yeasty, naturally carbonated black tea a source of long-lasting health and vitality.

The long history of kombucha

In 414 B.C., the Smithsonian reports, the cloudy beverage was imported to Japan by a Korean doctor named Kombu, in order to treat Emperor Inkyo. To further complicate its history, Japan already had its own form of kombucha, made from kombu (brown seaweed) and cha (tea).

According to Forbes, kombucha began to spread during the global trade expansion of the 20th century, when the fermented Chinese tea variety migrated into Europe, with Russia and Germany having adopted it as “kambucha” and “kombuchaschwamm,” respectively.

In 1955, Italian piano prodigy Renato Carosone delivered a hit single, “Stu Fungo Cinese!” (translated as “The Chinese Fungus!”), which was rooted in a Chinese mushroom infusion similar to kombucha.

The drink gained mainstream popularity in China during the 1960s, ’70s and ’80s, with homebrews known as “Stomach Treasure” touted as digestive tonics.

Finally, in the 1990s, kombucha entered the North American market, largely thanks to major U.S. brands like GT’s Kombucha.

In the past decade, kombucha’s ubiquity — and value — has skyrocketed as one of the fastest-growing beverage markets on the continent. Now a mainstream supermarket item, North American kombucha sales generated revenue of US $2.1 billion in 2025, with revenues expected to top US $4 billion by 2033.

Of course, the United States accounts for much of the lion’s share. But a market study revealed that Mexico is predicted to have the continent’s largest compound annual growth rate for kombucha in the coming years.

So what has taken kombucha so long to work its magic in Mexico?

Mexico as a country of many beverages — except kombucha, until recently

In my personal recollection, the Eurasian style of kombucha was never plentiful in Mexico. As a child, I could get all sorts of aguas frescas, carbonated sodas and any flavored drinks imaginable. As I grew older, that evolved into other forms of consumption (micheladas, carajillos, etc.). But I have no memory of ever seeing kombucha on a restaurant menu, at a cafe or in mercados.

Here’s my theory: With all of the other beverages that are made in, and often native to, Mexico — including tepache, a naturally fermented pineapple drink — the craft of Asian and Western kombuchas couldn’t get a foothold. In a country where you can easily get tequila, mezcal, pulque, sugar cane aguardiente, rum, atole, arroz con leche and so much more on practically every corner in any pueblo (often made by someone in the neighborhood with generations of family knowledge, ancestral practices and native ingredients at their disposal), kombucha didn’t necessarily have much demand. I’ve watched señoras prepare natural tea remedies from flowers they’ve handpicked from their gardens. But getting offered kombucha inside someone’s home? Never.

It wasn’t until the mid-to-late 2010s that I started to notice kombucha — commercially and independently bottled — as a relatively more common option around Mexico.

Kombucha in Veracruz and other states in Mexico

Near my home in downtown Xalapa (a region known for its rich and deeply rooted coffee history), all of the new-school cafes now offer kombucha, with a noticeable amount of homebrewed and locally made brands available. While recently enjoying my neighborhood on foot, I popped into a few nearby cafes — touted for their espressos, flat whites and other caffeinated brews — and was excited to see artisanal kombucha on nearly every menu. I asked the owner of Marcelo whether she has noticed a rise in kombucha’s popularity and consumption; she confirmed that within the past five years (by her estimation) kombucha has exploded with trendiness across Mexico. She even started to experiment with brewing her own batches, but after failed attempts, opted to get her supply from LindaSol Fermentería, a micro-kombuchería located a few miles from her cafe in Xalapa.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by the pickle (@thepickleofbrighton)

My personal go-to is Agua Brava, made by the chef at Bravo Pizza, a small pizzeria that opened in Xalapa two years ago. Their kombucha flavors rotate weekly and are made in-house and bottled on-site. Among other favorites that I’ve found in Veracruz are Komboocha Puerto (from the port city of Veracruz), Dominga Kombucha (from Cholula, Puebla) and Naran Fermentos (from Xalapa). Mexico City, Guadalajara, San José del Cabo and other cities are no different, offering their own unique brands like Cali Kombucha in Baja California Sur. Data and testimonials suggest that kombucha first infiltrated Mexico’s market roughly a decade ago, when Mexican-owned brands like the aforementioned Cali Kombucha and Brew Lab from Oaxaca launched their brands around 2015 and 2016, respectively.

To highlight the Mexicanization of kombucha since then, “kombucherías” are now a thing in Mexico — as evidenced in the social media reel above, made by a British tourist tasting Oaxacan kombucha in Mazunte. Spoiler: It’s “banging.”

Kombucha a la mexicana: Basil jamaica, pineapple coconut, and more

Though you won’t casually walk past a kombuchería on every corner, you’re likely to encounter a local kombucha brewer in your neighborhood, who might directly sell unmarked jugs or labeled microbatches of their SCOBY-made (Symbiotic Culture Of Bacteria and Yeast) concoctions. You’ll also find it in most grocery markets with a cosmopolitan clientele, or in small businesses that are dedicated to holistic living and organic products.

Often, the flavors have a tropical Mexican vibe: maracuyá, tamarindo, coconut, mango. Some brands add additional ingredients like ancho chile peppers, jalapeño, honey or kiwi for an extra kick of spice, sweetness or tang. Puebla’s Domingo Kombucha has a killer guayaba option — subtly effervescent, fruity and mellow. Mexico City’s Umani offers canned options including orange turmeric, Mexican pepperleaf and fig. Bruja Sana from Yucatán emphasizes herbally minty options with green, earthy additions like romero and hierba buena.

Many of Mexico’s leading kombucha brands are independent, and offer or encourage other lifestyle supplements like yoga and Pilates classes, SCOBY workshops and more. It’s far from commercial profit and mass-made consumer-targeted sales; instead, kombucha offers a doorway into a wider range of health-centered practices and mindful consumption with regional flavor.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: New episode: ‘Confidently Wrong’ podcast tackles expat money habits and mistakes

Money affects everyone living in or traveling to Mexico. It is with that in mind that Mexico News Daily has launched a new weekly series called “Mexico and My Money.” You can read about the thinking behind the series here: Mexico and My Money: A new series MND on personal finance.

Our team recently conducted a survey of over 700 expats living in 25 states throughout Mexico about how they handle money while living in the country. The results were striking: Despite wariness of Mexican banks, 71% of respondents own a home in Mexico and nearly eight in 10 have made some kind of investment here — in real estate, a business, stocks or bonds. Nearly one in five respondents said they’d been victimized by a financial crime, with stories ranging from a landlord who kept a deposit “without cause” to a household employee who stole from a family over eight years. You can see the full results here: Mexico and My Money: What you told us about your personal finance habits and hang-ups.

In this week’s episode of “Confidently Wrong,” George and I dig into those results. We talk about banking in Mexico, cash and credit cards, the money mistakes expats wish they’d avoided. You will learn what are others doing differently and about best practices for money in Mexico. Check it out!

World.title: Why isn’t the peso at 37 to the US dollar? A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Here is a mindblowing number to think about: If the peso had performed similarly from 2020 to the present as it did in the previous 25 years (from 1995 to 2020), the current exchange rate would be near 37 pesos to the US dollar!

That statistic puts into perspective how incredible the current exchange rate of 16.86 (as of Friday) really is. With the peso back near record highs in what seems like an unbreakable trend, I thought it would be a good time to do a refresher on the topic of the MXN:USD exchange rate.

For decades, the peso reliably lost about 10% of its value against the dollar every year. Although that devaluation was bad for some and good for others, its consistency and predictability allowed businesses, governments and families to plan around it. The fact that the past five-plus years have been so dramatically different — so unpredictable — has had some real impacts on Mexico.

With that in mind, I thought I would share some of the top columns I have written about the peso over these past several years to help us understand why its its happening, if it might continue, and what we can do about it. Each one tackles a different angle of the story. Please enjoy.

When will the Mexican peso begin to behave rationally again? — Why the peso stopped following its old, predictable rules — and what “rational” behavior would even look like now.

Is the peso punching above its weight? The results of our latest MND Peso Index™ — Our MND Peso Index™ compares real prices in Mexico and the U.S. to understand the real value of the peso.

Mexico in Numbers: The peso’s wildest swings since 2000 — A numbers-driven look back at 25 years of exchange rate history.

What’s next for the peso? — A forward-looking read on where the exchange rate could realistically head next.

Is the peso about to peak? — The signs that suggest the peso’s historic run might be nearing its limit.

How to stop a speeding super peso — What tools the government and Banco de México actually have to slow the peso down, and whether they’re likely to use them.

How can we predict what will happen next with the Mexican peso? — A practical framework for reading the signals, so you’re not just guessing.

Pros and cons of the superpeso — Who wins and who loses when the peso gets this strong, and why it’s not all good news.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: An Attack on a Hunting Camp Moves Mozambique’s Insurgency West
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

MOZAMBIQUE · SECURITY

Key Facts —The attack: Suspected insurgents attacked a hunting camp in Niassa province on Thursday morning, killing two people. —The evacuation: Three American hunters were rescued by helicopter after being out of the camp when the attack began. —The damage: Staff fled into the bush and the camp was burned; there were no confirmed fatalities among the Americans. —The response: Mozambican military forces intervened after the attack. —The ownership: The camp was partly owned by the football coach Carlos Queiroz, according to reporting on the incident. —The warning: The US State Department had told citizens not to travel to the Niassa Special Reserve for any reason. —The pattern: It warned that armed groups had targeted upscale hunting lodges in and near the reserve and had taken hostages. —The catch: The attack moved the insurgency west of the province where it began, which is the part that is new.

A Niassa attack on a hunting camp killed two people this week and forced the helicopter evacuation of three American hunters, in the clearest sign yet that Mozambique’s insurgency has moved west of the province where it began. The camp was burned and its staff fled into the bush.

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

What happened

Suspected insurgents attacked a hunting camp in Niassa province on Thursday morning. Zitamar reported two people killed, Portuguese-language outlets one, and 13 camp workers are still missing. No group has claimed the attack.

Three American hunters were away from the camp on a hunting trip when the attack began, and were later rescued by helicopter. There were no confirmed fatalities among them.

Mozambican military forces intervened, and the camp was reported burned. Reuters and the Mozambique-focused outlet Zitamar both carried accounts of the incident.

Why the Niassa attack matters geographically

Mozambique’s insurgency has been concentrated in Cabo Delgado since 2017, the province that hosts the country’s liquefied natural gas developments. Niassa lies inland and to the west.

Attacks in Niassa are not new, and their frequency has been the clearest indicator that the conflict is spreading rather than being contained. Each westward incident lengthens the front the army has to hold.

The Niassa Special Reserve is one of Africa’s largest protected areas and is very thinly policed. Its size is precisely what makes it useful to armed groups.

The warning that already existed

The US State Department had advised its citizens not to travel to the Niassa Special Reserve for any reason. It specifically warned that terrorists had targeted upscale hunting lodges in and near the area and had taken hostages.

That advisory is now a matter of record rather than a precaution. It was issued before this attack, not after it.

Any commercial operator working in the reserve was therefore operating against an explicit published warning.

The economics of hunting concessions

Large parts of the Niassa reserve are managed through hunting and photographic concessions, which fund anti-poaching patrols and provide most of the employment in an area with almost no other formal economy. Conservation there is paid for by tourism revenue.

The camp attacked was partly owned by the football coach Carlos Queiroz, whose involvement gives the story an international profile it would not otherwise have. It also illustrates who invests in these concessions.

When a camp closes, the anti-poaching capacity it financed closes with it. That is the second-order effect of an attack like this.

What it does to Mozambique’s risk profile

Mozambique is trying to restart the largest energy investment in its history in Cabo Delgado, and the security narrative around the north is central to that. An attack on foreign tourists in a neighbouring province complicates it.

Insurers price this kind of incident quickly. Coverage for operations in northern Mozambique has already been expensive and difficult to obtain.

The government’s position is that the security situation is improving. Incidents in new provinces are the strongest argument against that position.

The people who cannot be airlifted

Three foreign hunters were evacuated by helicopter within hours. The camp staff who fled into the bush had no such option.

That asymmetry is the routine reality of insecurity in remote concession areas, and it rarely features in coverage. Local employees carry the residual risk.

Reporting from Zitamar has separately described the front line in Niassa as effectively outsourced, with private operators and community scouts filling gaps the state cannot cover.

The regional read

Insurgencies that expand into protected areas are difficult to dislodge, because the terrain that makes conservation valuable also makes military operations expensive. The same problem exists in the Sahel and in eastern DR Congo.

Wildlife economies are therefore among the first casualties of spreading conflict, and among the last things to recover. Tourists return slowly.

For investors weighing frontier exposure, the useful signal is not the number of attacks but their geography. Movement into new provinces is the change worth pricing.

What to watch

The first marker is whether other concessions in Niassa suspend operations for the season. A general suspension would cost the reserve most of its patrol funding.

The second is the Mozambican army’s posture in the province, and whether forces are redeployed from Cabo Delgado to cover it.

The third is travel advisories from other governments. If they follow Washington, the concession economy in Niassa becomes very hard to run.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in Niassa? Suspected insurgents attacked a hunting camp in Mozambique’s Niassa province on Thursday morning, killing two people and burning the camp. Staff fled into the bush. Were the American hunters harmed? Three American hunters were out of the camp on a hunting trip when the attack began and were later rescued by helicopter. There were no confirmed fatalities among them. Had there been any warning? Yes. The US State Department had advised citizens not to travel to the Niassa Special Reserve for any reason, warning that armed groups had targeted upscale hunting lodges and taken hostages. Why does this matter beyond the camp? Mozambique’s insurgency has been concentrated in Cabo Delgado since 2017. Attacks in Niassa indicate westward spread, which lengthens the front and complicates the security narrative around northern energy projects. What is the economic effect? Hunting and photographic concessions fund anti-poaching patrols and provide most of the formal employment in the reserve. When camps close, the conservation capacity they finance closes with them.

World.title: Zambia’s Bemba Royal Council Has Called Off Its Biggest Ceremony
World.content:

ZAMBIA · CULTURE

Key Facts —The decision: The Bemba Royal Establishment has cancelled this year’s Ukusefya Pa Ng’wena ceremony. —The dates lost: It had been planned for 17 to 19 September 2026. —The reason given: Paramount Chief Chitimukulu’s royal council said the prevailing mood in Ulubemba was not conducive to festivities. —What happens to the money: Sponsorships and donations already made will be carried over and accounted for at next year’s ceremony. —The postponement: The council has pushed the 2026 edition to next year rather than abandoning it. —The political line: The royal establishment says its policy is to work with whichever government is in power, without aligning with a party. —What the ceremony is: Ukusefya Pa Ng’wena commemorates the Bemba people’s migration and settlement, and is among Zambia’s largest traditional gatherings. —The catch: The ceremony is postponed rather than cancelled, and the sponsorship money carries over to next year.

The largest Bemba ceremony in Zambia’s calendar, Ukusefya Pa Ng’wena, will not be held this year. Paramount Chief Chitimukulu’s royal council cancelled the 17 to 19 September event, saying the prevailing mood in Ulubemba does not allow for celebration of that kind.

What was announced

The Bemba Royal Establishment cancelled this year’s Ukusefya Pa Ng’wena, which had been scheduled for 17 to 19 September. News Diggers and Zambia Monitor both reported the decision.

The royal council said the prevailing mood in Ulubemba, the Bemba heartland, was not conducive to holding festivities. The ceremony has been pushed to next year rather than abandoned.

Sponsorships and donations already received will be transferred to and accounted for at the 2027 edition. That is an unusually specific commitment for a cancellation notice.

What the Bemba ceremony commemorates

The ceremony commemorates the migration of the Bemba people from the Luba-Lunda kingdoms and their settlement in what is now northern Zambia. Its name refers to the crocodile, the clan symbol of the ruling house.

It is one of the largest traditional gatherings in a country that has dozens of them, drawing tens of thousands of people to Mungwi in Northern Province. Chiefs, government ministers and diaspora visitors attend.

Zambia’s traditional ceremonies are also a genuine tourism product, and several are promoted internationally as cultural events.

The phrase doing the work

The royal council’s language was careful. It cited the prevailing mood rather than naming any cause, and gave no further explanation.

That phrasing is not accidental in a country that has just held a general election. The ceremony would have fallen weeks after the vote.

It is worth stating plainly that the council did not give a political reason. That inferring one would be inference rather than reporting.

The royal establishment’s own position

The Bemba Royal Establishment has separately said its policy is to work with whichever government is in power, without aligning itself with a particular political party. That statement was issued in the context of Zambia’s political developments.

Traditional authorities in Zambia occupy a delicate constitutional space. They hold real influence over land and local legitimacy, and are formally expected to stay out of partisan politics.

A cancellation that avoids explanation is one way of protecting that position. It is also a signal in itself.

Who loses money when a ceremony is called off

Large traditional ceremonies generate real local economic activity: transport, accommodation, catering, traders and craft sellers. For Mungwi and the surrounding district, three days of visitors matter.

Corporate sponsorship is the other side of that economy. Zambian banks, brewers and telecoms companies sponsor ceremonies as a marketing channel with genuine reach.

Carrying sponsorships forward protects those relationships and pushes the spending into next year. The district still loses this year’s trade.

Cultural calendars as economic infrastructure

Across the region, traditional ceremonies have quietly become part of the tourism offer, alongside wildlife and landscape. They are among the few products that draw visitors into rural districts rather than into parks and capitals.

That gives them an economic weight their organisers rarely claim. It also makes cancellations more consequential than they look.

For readers who follow Latin America, the parallel with regional festivals is close. They are cultural events that function as annual income for places with few alternatives.

What it says about the moment

A royal council choosing not to celebrate is making a statement about the temper of its constituency. Institutions with long time horizons tend to be cautious about appearing tone-deaf.

Zambia has had a politically intense year, and the Bemba-speaking north is one of its most significant political blocs. That context is real whether or not it is cited.

The honest summary is that a major cultural institution has decided this is not a year for a festival, and has declined to say more.

What to watch

The first marker is whether next year’s ceremony is confirmed with dates, which would settle the question of postponement versus quiet lapse.

The second is whether sponsors accept the carry-over or seek refunds. That will indicate how the corporate side reads the situation.

The third is whether other Zambian ceremonies scheduled for the coming months proceed as planned. If they do, this decision was specific to Ulubemba.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Ukusefya Pa Ng’wena? It is the main ceremony of Zambia’s Bemba people, commemorating their migration and settlement in what is now northern Zambia. It is among the largest traditional gatherings in the country. Why was it cancelled? Paramount Chief Chitimukulu’s royal council said the prevailing mood in Ulubemba was not conducive to holding festivities. No further explanation was given. When was it due to be held? It had been scheduled for 17 to 19 September 2026. The council has pushed the edition to next year. What happens to sponsorship money? Sponsorships and donations already made will be carried over to next year’s ceremony and accounted for then. Is the Bemba Royal Establishment taking a political side? It has said its policy is to work with whichever government is in power without aligning itself with a particular party.

World.title: Namibia’s Reserves Rose While Its Banks Got Tighter
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

NAMIBIA · MARKETS

Key Facts —The level: Official international reserves reached N$58.04 billion at the end of July, about US$3.6 billion. —The move: That is a rise of N$1.62 billion, or 2.9%, from N$56.42 billion in June. —What drove it: Higher receipts from the Southern African Customs Union and large foreign-currency placements by commercial banks with the central bank. —Import cover: Estimated import cover rose to about 3.6 months, or 4.0 months excluding oil and gas related imports. —Composition: Foreign currency holdings were N$53.74bn, SDRs N$3.72bn, gold N$573.4m and the IMF reserve position N$3.4m. —The peg: Reserves covered 10.1 times the value of currency in circulation, supporting the one-to-one link to the South African rand. —The counterpoint: Average commercial bank liquidity fell 31.5% in a month, from N$9.77 billion in June to N$6.69 billion in July. —The catch: Reserves rose while bank liquidity fell 31.5%, so the money moved out of the domestic system, not into it.

Namibia reserves rose 2.9% in July to N$58.04 billion, lifting estimated import cover to about 3.6 months and comfortably supporting the currency’s one-to-one link with the rand. The same month, average liquidity in the commercial banking system fell by almost a third.

What the central bank reported

Official international reserves reached N$58.04 billion at the end of July, up N$1.62 billion or 2.9% from N$56.42 billion in June. In dollar terms that is roughly US$3.6 billion.

The Bank of Namibia attributes the increase mainly to receipts from the Southern African Customs Union, traditionally the largest single contributor to foreign currency inflows. Large placements of clients’ foreign currency by commercial banks with the central bank added to the total.

The Bank of Namibia credits a weaker Namibia dollar against the US dollar and further purchases of gold during the month.

Import cover, and the oil and gas asterisk

Estimated import cover rose to about 3.6 months at the end of July. Excluding imports related to oil and gas activity, it reaches 4.0 months.

That distinction is not cosmetic. Namibia is in the middle of an offshore exploration and appraisal cycle that pulls in capital equipment and services from abroad.

Those imports are investment rather than consumption, and they will eventually be matched by export revenue. Reporting both numbers is the honest way to present the position.

What Namibia reserves are actually for

The Namibia dollar is pegged one-to-one to the South African rand, and the peg is what makes the reserve level a policy variable rather than a statistic. Reserves covered 10.1 times the value of currency in circulation at the end of July.

That ratio is the technical foundation of monetary credibility in a small open economy inside a currency arrangement it does not control. It also covers short-term external obligations.

A country in this position does not choose its interest rates freely. It defends a peg and manages liquidity around it.

The composition tells its own story

Of the N$58.04 billion, N$53.74 billion was held in foreign currency, N$3.72 billion in Special Drawing Rights, N$573.4 million in gold and N$3.4 million in the IMF reserve position.

Gold is therefore about 0.99% of official reserves, some 8,574 fine troy ounces. The N$573.4 million holding is worth about US$35.9 million at N$15.96 to the dollar on 5 September 2026. Its role is symbolic rather than structural.

The overwhelming weight of foreign currency is what a peg requires. Gold is not a defence against a run on a fixed exchange rate.

The number that complicates the good news

Average commercial bank liquidity fell 31.5% in a single month, from N$9.77 billion in June to N$6.69 billion in July. That is a sharp contraction in the money available inside the banking system.

The central bank puts the liquidity drop down mainly to large investment-related outflows.

The effect on borrowers is nonetheless real. Tighter bank liquidity generally means dearer and scarcer domestic credit.

Why SACU receipts are a vulnerability as well as a support

The customs union pool is the largest single source of Namibia’s foreign currency inflows and one of its largest budget lines. Its size depends on imports into South Africa and on a formula negotiated between members.

That makes a substantial share of Namibia’s external position a function of decisions taken elsewhere. Eswatini and Lesotho face the same exposure in sharper form.

Any renegotiation of the SACU revenue-sharing formula is therefore a first-order risk for Namibian reserves, not a technical footnote.

What the oil cycle changes

Namibia’s offshore discoveries have made it one of the more closely watched frontier hydrocarbon stories, and appraisal spending has been running for several years. First production would transform the external accounts.

Until then the country carries the import cost of exploration without the export revenue. That is exactly what the 3.6 versus 4.0 month distinction is measuring.

Investors should read the reserve series with that timing in mind. The position looks tighter than the underlying prospect.

What to watch

The first marker is whether bank liquidity recovers in August, or whether July was the start of a tightening trend. One month is not a trend.

The second is the next SACU distribution and any commentary on the pool’s size. That is the largest single swing factor.

The third is import cover through the rest of the appraisal cycle. If cover holds above three months while oil-related imports continue, the external position is stronger than the headline suggests.

Frequently Asked Questions

How large are Namibia’s reserves? Official international reserves reached N$58.04 billion, about US$3.6 billion, at the end of July 2026. That was a rise of 2.9% from N$56.42 billion in June. What caused the increase? Higher receipts from the Southern African Customs Union and large foreign-currency placements by commercial banks with the central bank. A weaker Namibia dollar and higher gold prices also helped in local-currency terms. How many months of imports do the reserves cover? About 3.6 months at the end of July, or 4.0 months excluding imports related to oil and gas activity. Why does the reserve level matter? The Namibia dollar is pegged one-to-one to the South African rand, and reserves covered 10.1 times the value of currency in circulation. That ratio underpins the peg and short-term external obligations. What is the concern? Average commercial bank liquidity fell 31.5% in a month, from N$9.77 billion to N$6.69 billion. Stronger reserves alongside tighter domestic liquidity is a combination worth watching.

World.title: One Civil Servant Chairs Three Malawian Power Companies That Must Negotiate With Each Other
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

MALAWI · ENERGY

Key Facts —The arrangement: The Secretary to the President and Cabinet chairs the boards of Escom, Egenco and Power Market Limited. —Why that matters: The three companies must negotiate power purchase agreements, tariffs and debt settlements with one another. —The finding: Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee says the structure creates an obvious conflict of interest. —The quote: Good governance is not about who may legally sit on a board, its chairperson said, but whether the arrangement inspires confidence. —The precedent: Former secretaries Zanga-Zanga Chikhosi and Colleen Zamba chaired boards at Egenco, PML and the national oil company. —The regulator problem: A former energy regulator chairman warned in 2022 that a regulator cannot easily discipline a body chaired by the head of the civil service. —Government response: The information ministry says it has received no formal communication from Parliament and will not comment until it does. —The catch: One official chairs all three companies, so the negotiations between them happen on one side of the table.

Malawi power sector governance now has a specific problem with a specific name. The Secretary to the President and Cabinet chairs the boards of all three state power companies, which means the agreements they strike with one another are negotiated, approved and signed off by the same office.

The structure, described plainly

Malawi’s electricity industry was unbundled into separate companies. Egenco generates, Escom supplies, and Power Market Limited operates as the single buyer between them.

The Secretary to the President and Cabinet, who heads the civil service, chairs the boards of all three. That is the arrangement Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee has now formally questioned.

Power Market Limited was reinstated as the single buyer in April 2026, after the High Court cleared it to resume operations following an earlier dissolution.

What the committee actually said

PAC chairperson Steven Malondera told The Nation that the setup creates an obvious conflict when the utilities must negotiate power purchase agreements, tariffs and debt settlements among themselves. Nyasa Times reported the same finding.

His formulation deserves quoting once: good corporate governance is not about who is legally allowed to sit on a board, but about whether the arrangement inspires confidence that decisions are independent.

He added that if three interconnected utilities are controlled through overlapping board leadership, transparency must be exceptionally high, or accountability becomes blurred.

Why the Malawi power sector case is not merely technical

Inter-company balances between generator, single buyer and supplier are where money hides in every unbundled electricity market. They are settled through negotiation, and negotiation requires two sides.

When one office chairs all three boards, there is no independent counterparty to test a number. Malondera warned specifically about public funds lost in unverified inter-company balances.

Corporate governance specialist Dicks Mfune added that the secretary also acts for the state as owner under the Companies Act. The office ends up judging its own decisions.

The regulator cannot regulate upwards

Leonnard Chikadya, a former chairman of the Malawi Energy Regulatory Authority, warned as far back as 2022 that the arrangement made independent regulation close to impossible. A regulator cannot easily discipline a body chaired by the head of the civil service who oversees it.

That is a structural point rather than a personal one. It would apply whoever held the office.

It also explains why the problem has persisted across successive holders, including Zanga-Zanga Chikhosi and Colleen Zamba.

The evidence that it already causes problems

Mfune noted that previous debt-collection disputes between Escom and Egenco had to be taken to the Office of the Ombudsman because internal structures could not resolve them. Two subsidiaries of the same shareholder could not settle a bill between themselves.

That is the practical cost of the arrangement, and it is already on the record. It is not a hypothetical risk.

Disputes escalated to an ombudsman are slower and more expensive than disputes settled by boards that can actually take opposing positions.

Why investors care

Independent power producers sign long-term agreements with the single buyer. The value of those agreements depends on the buyer’s independence and creditworthiness. Both are in question when the buyer, the generator and the supplier share a chairman.

Malawi needs generation investment badly, and its ability to attract it rests on contractual credibility rather than on tariffs alone. Investors price governance directly into their required return.

Malondera made this point himself: the setup undermines investor confidence. That is the argument most likely to move policy.

The government has not engaged

Harold Msusa, secretary for information and communications technology, said the government had received no formal communication or submission from Parliament or its Public Accounts Committee on the issues raised through the media. It would not comment until the matter came through institutional channels.

That is a procedurally correct answer and a substantively empty one. Parliament says it has already raised the concerns with the executive without evident response.

Malondera has indicated that Parliament may pursue legislative changes if the executive continues not to act.

The fix is not complicated

The state can remain the shareholder in all three companies without installing its own chief bureaucrat as chairman of each. Independent, commercially minded directors exist.

Separating ownership from board leadership is standard practice in every well-run state-enterprise system. It is also the cheapest reform available here, because it costs nothing but discretion.

The obstacle is that convenient arrangements are rarely surrendered voluntarily. That is what makes the parliamentary route relevant.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the governance problem in Malawi’s power sector? The Secretary to the President and Cabinet chairs the boards of Escom, Egenco and Power Market Limited, three state companies that must negotiate power purchase agreements, tariffs and debt settlements with each other. Who raised the concern? Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee, whose chairperson Steven Malondera said the structure creates an obvious conflict of interest and undermines investor confidence. Has this happened before? Yes. Former secretaries Zanga-Zanga Chikhosi and Colleen Zamba chaired boards at Egenco, Power Market Limited and the national oil company. A former energy regulator chairman warned about the practice in 2022. What has the government said? The secretary for information and communications technology said the government had received no formal communication from Parliament and would not comment until the matter came through institutional channels. Why does it matter to investors? Independent power producers contract with the single buyer, and the value of those contracts depends on the buyer’s independence. Governance risk raises the return investors require.

World.title: Mauritius Gains Two More Years of Duty-Free US Access
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

MAURITIUS · TRADE

Key Facts —The law: The United States extended the African Growth and Opportunity Act to 31 December 2028. —The votes: The House of Representatives approved the extension on 1 September by 370 votes to 48, after Senate approval in August. —The signature: President Donald Trump signed the legislation on 2 September 2026, inside a stopgap federal funding bill rather than a standalone AGOA act. —What Mauritius keeps: The extension secures American market access for the roughly US$70 million of manufactured exports that depend on the preference. —The gap before it: AGOA expired on 30 September 2025 and preferences lapsed for four months before being restored on 3 February 2026, retroactively, to 31 December 2026. —Why 12 months was not enough: A one-year horizon gives exporters too little visibility to negotiate contracts, plan orders or invest in capacity. —Who did the work: Foreign Minister Ritish Ramful and Industry Minister Aadil Ameer Meea led months of representations in Washington. —The catch: Two years is long enough to keep an order book, and short enough that the lobbying starts again next year.

The AGOA extension carrying African trade preferences to the end of 2028 was signed into law on 2 September, and Mauritius has put a number on what it saved: the manufactured exports that depend on it. The difference between a one-year and a two-year horizon is the difference between surviving and planning.

What was signed, and when

The House of Representatives approved the extension of the African Growth and Opportunity Act on 1 September by 370 votes to 48, following approval in the Senate in August. President Donald Trump signed the legislation on 2 September 2026, inside a stopgap federal funding bill rather than a standalone AGOA act.

The preference regime now runs to 31 December 2028. Eligible African countries retain duty-free access to the United States for a defined list of products.

That resolves a question that had hung over African exporters for more than a year.

The gap that preceded it

AGOA expired on 30 September 2025, and preferences were suspended for four months. They were restored on 3 February 2026, retroactively, but only to 31 December 2026.

A twelve-month reauthorisation solved the immediate problem and created a new one. No manufacturer can negotiate a contract, plan an order book or invest in a production line on a year of visibility.

Buyers price that uncertainty. An exporter who cannot promise duty-free delivery in eighteen months loses the order to one who can.

What the AGOA extension is worth to Mauritius

Mauritius sent about Rs 8 billion (US$174 million) of goods to the United States in 2025, roughly 11% of its goods exports. The manufactured share that depends on AGOA is put at about US$70 million and around 1,000 jobs. Textiles and apparel are the largest component.

Mauritius is a small, relatively wealthy economy that has spent decades moving up the manufacturing value chain. Its apparel sector competes on quality and compliance rather than on the lowest unit cost.

That positioning makes preference margins particularly valuable. A duty differential is decisive when your labour cost is not the cheapest available.

Diplomacy that actually produced something

Foreign Minister Ritish Ramful and Industry Minister Aadil Ameer Meea led months of representations in Washington. The government has been lobbying on AGOA since 2025 rather than waiting for a decision.

Small states rarely change American trade legislation on their own. They can, however, make sure their case is in the file when a decision is taken.

That is what economic diplomacy looks like when it works: unglamorous, repetitive and measurable afterwards.

What it means for the rest of the continent

Lesotho, Kenya, Madagascar, Ghana and several other economies have apparel sectors built substantially around AGOA access. For some of them the preference is the industry rather than an advantage within it.

Our earlier reporting on Lesotho noted that the extension had passed the Senate but not completed the legislative process. That process is now complete, and the position has changed.

Any assessment of those garment sectors written before 2 September needs updating on that point.

The caveat that still applies

A two-year extension is not permanence. The same cliff arrives at the end of 2028, and the political conditions attached to eligibility can be reviewed annually.

Country eligibility has been suspended before on governance and human-rights grounds, which means the preference is conditional as well as temporary. Exporters carry that risk.

The sensible planning assumption is that AGOA buys time to diversify rather than removing the need to.

Where the diversification would go

For Mauritius the obvious hedges are the European market, regional African demand under the continental free trade area, and higher-value services. All three are being pursued.

The island has also spent years building a financial-services and blue-economy offer precisely to reduce dependence on preference-driven manufacturing. That strategy looks better every time AGOA wobbles.

Diversification is slow and unglamorous, and it is the only durable answer to a preference cliff.

What to watch

The first marker is order books for the 2027 season, which is the first full year the extension covers. If orders lengthen, the extension has done its job.

The second is the annual eligibility review, which is where political risk actually sits.

The third is whether African governments use the window to negotiate a successor arrangement rather than waiting for another expiry. The lesson of the past year is that expiry dates arrive.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does the AGOA extension run? The African Growth and Opportunity Act has been extended to 31 December 2028. President Trump signed the legislation on 2 September 2026. How was it passed? The Senate approved the extension in August, and the House of Representatives followed on 1 September by 370 votes to 48. What is it worth to Mauritius? It secures American market access for the manufactured exports that rely on the preference, put at about US$70 million a year and roughly 1,000 jobs, with textiles and apparel the largest component. What happened before the extension? AGOA expired on 30 September 2025 and preferences lapsed for four months. They were restored retroactively on 3 February 2026, but only until 31 December 2026. Is African access to the US market now secure? Only until the end of 2028, and eligibility is reviewed annually on governance and human-rights grounds. The extension buys time rather than removing the risk.

World.title: Rwanda Named 22 Baby Gorillas, and Sold a Conservation Model
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

RWANDA · CULTURE

Key Facts —The ceremony: Twenty-two baby mountain gorillas born over the past year were named at Kinigi at the 21st Kwita Izina. —The running total: More than 438 mountain gorillas have been named since the event became annual in 2005. —The theme: This year’s theme was “Conservation is Life: Sustaining the Future”. —The namers: They included Patrice Evra, Mamadou Sakho, Olympic high-jump champion Mutaz Essa Barshim and cycling federation president David Lappartient. —Institutional weight: Shaikha Al Nuwais, Secretary-General of UN Tourism, named Ishakwe; Rio Tinto chairman Dominic Barton named Umukondo. —Rwandans on the list: Namers also included Jeanette Uwimbabazi, a Nyungwe National Park ranger working against wildlife crime. —The origin: The ceremony adapts a Rwandan tradition of naming newborn children in front of family and community. —The catch: Naming gorillas is the shop window; the revenue-sharing that keeps the model working returns 10% of park income.

Kwita Izina named 22 baby mountain gorillas at Kinigi this year, taking the total past 438 since the ceremony became annual in 2005. It is a naming ritual, a conservation record and, quite deliberately, a tourism sales pitch.

What happened at Kinigi

Twenty-two mountain gorillas born over the past year were named one by one at Rwanda’s annual ceremony. Among the names given were Ishakwe, Umukondo, Shikama, Inkera, Rugamba, Umucyo and Muganura.

Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva represented President Paul Kagame and placed the celebration in the context of Rwanda’s wider conservation ambitions. The theme was Conservation is Life: Sustaining the Future.

The event is now in its 21st year, and more than 438 gorillas have been named since 2005.

Where the ritual comes from

The ceremony adapts an old Rwandan practice of naming newborn children in the presence of family and community. Rwanda applied that form to its mountain gorillas.

The effect is to move each animal from a scientific record into a public one. A gorilla that would otherwise exist in a conservation database is named in front of thousands of people.

The names carry meaning. Some mark strength, leadership or resilience; others point at values Rwanda wants attached to its conservation story.

Kwita Izina as an economic instrument

The argument Rwanda has spent two decades making is that protecting nature and developing economically are not opposed. Conservation generates tourism, tourism supports communities, and communities then have a reason to protect the forest.

Gorilla permits in Rwanda are among the most expensive wildlife experiences in the world, and a share of tourism revenue is directed to communities around the parks. That revenue-sharing is the mechanism the whole model rests on.

It is a real policy rather than a slogan, and it is also fragile. High-price, low-volume tourism is exposed to any shock that stops long-haul travel.

The guest list is the strategy

This year’s namers included the former Manchester United and France captain Patrice Evra, the former Paris Saint-Germain captain Mamadou Sakho, the Olympic high jumper Mutaz Essa Barshim and David Lappartient, president of the international cycling federation.

They were joined by Shaikha Al Nuwais, Secretary-General of UN Tourism and the first woman to lead the organisation, and by Dominic Barton, chairman of Rio Tinto. Alastair Fothergill, the filmmaker behind Planet Earth, named Mpinga.

That is a carefully assembled list covering sport, tourism governance, mining capital and natural-history broadcasting. Each guest carries a different audience home.

The Rwandans who were also named

Alongside the international guests were Rwandans whose work happens away from any spotlight, including Jeanette Uwimbabazi, a ranger at Nyungwe National Park who works against wildlife crime. Including her is a deliberate corrective.

Conservation in the region is delivered by rangers, trackers and community scouts, often at physical risk. The naming ceremony is one of the few moments that fact becomes visible.

It also matters for recruitment. A job that is publicly honoured is easier to fill.

The recovery behind the celebration

The mountain gorilla is one of the few large mammals whose numbers have risen in recent decades, after decades of decline. That recovery is the reason the ceremony exists at all.

It was achieved through sustained anti-poaching work, veterinary intervention and cross-border cooperation between Rwanda, Uganda and DR Congo. None of those is cheap or quick.

The population remains small and concentrated, which means it is still vulnerable to disease and to instability in the wider region.

The risk nobody names at the ceremony

The gorillas live in a landscape that crosses into eastern DR Congo, where armed conflict has continued for years. Conservation work there has been repeatedly interrupted, and rangers have been killed.

Rwanda’s own role in that conflict is disputed and politically charged, and it is not the subject of this ceremony. It is nonetheless part of the environment the animals live in.

A conservation model that depends on regional stability has an exposure that no permit price can hedge.

Why this is a business story too

Tourism is one of Rwanda’s largest foreign-exchange earners, and the gorillas are its single most identifiable asset. Brand-building of this kind is a national export strategy carried out through an animal.

For readers who follow Latin America, the comparison is with Costa Rica, which built a similar reputation and monetised it over decades. Both cases show that a conservation brand takes twenty years to construct and one bad season to damage.

That is why Rwanda spends money on a ceremony rather than only on rangers. The ceremony is the marketing budget.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Kwita Izina? It is Rwanda’s annual gorilla naming ceremony, adapted from a Rwandan tradition of naming newborn children before family and community. It has been held annually since 2005. How many gorillas were named this year? Twenty-two baby mountain gorillas born over the past year were named at Kinigi. More than 438 have been named since the ceremony became annual. Who took part? Namers included Patrice Evra, Mamadou Sakho, Mutaz Essa Barshim, David Lappartient, UN Tourism’s Secretary-General Shaikha Al Nuwais, Rio Tinto chairman Dominic Barton and filmmaker Alastair Fothergill. Why does Rwanda hold the ceremony? It supports an argument that conservation and economic development reinforce each other, with tourism revenue funding protection and community benefit. The event is also a marketing instrument for Rwandan tourism. What are the risks to the model? High-price, low-volume tourism is exposed to any shock that halts long-haul travel. The gorilla landscape also crosses into eastern DR Congo, where conflict has repeatedly interrupted conservation work.

World.title: South Sudan Has Removed the Legal Obstacles to Voting in December
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

SOUTH SUDAN · POLITICS

Key Facts —The signature: President Salva Kiir assented on 2 September to constitutional amendments intended to remove legal obstacles to elections. —The instrument: It is the Transitional Constitution of the Republic of South Sudan, 2011 (Amendment No. 13) Act, 2026. —The route: The bill was passed by the Transitional National Legislature and presented for assent under Article 85 of the Transitional Constitution. —What it changes: It delinks the permanent constitution-making process and the National Population and Housing Census from the conduct of national elections. —The date: Elections are intended to take place in December 2026. —The official line: Presidential Affairs Minister Africano Mande Gedima called it a historic milestone and said it removes obstacles to citizens electing their leaders. —The history: Elections have been postponed repeatedly since independence in 2011, amid difficulties implementing the 2018 Revitalised Peace Agreement. —The catch: Removing the legal obstacles is not the same as holding the vote: the December date has slipped twice before.

South Sudan elections in December are now legally possible, after President Salva Kiir signed a constitutional amendment that cuts the vote free from two processes that had been holding it hostage. The permanent constitution and the national census no longer have to be finished first.

What the amendment does

The Transitional Constitution of the Republic of South Sudan, 2011 (Amendment No. 13) Act, 2026 was passed by the Transitional National Legislature and presented for presidential assent under Article 85. Kiir signed it in Juba on 2 September.

Its central effect is to delink the permanent constitution-making process and the National Population and Housing Census from the conduct of national elections. Both had previously been treated as prerequisites.

Africano Mande Gedima, the minister of presidential affairs, told reporters the changes remove key obstacles that could delay the electoral process. He described the moment as a historic milestone.

Why those two processes were blocking everything

A permanent constitution defines who may stand, how power is divided and what the state actually is. Writing one in a country still implementing a peace agreement has proved impossible on any timetable.

A census determines constituencies. Without one, seats cannot be apportioned by population, and any apportionment becomes contestable.

Delinking both is pragmatic and creates a real problem. An election held without either will produce a legislature whose boundaries and mandate rest on older, weaker foundations.

What the South Sudan elections would settle

The country has never held a national election since independence in 2011. The current arrangement rests on the 2018 Revitalised Peace Agreement and a series of extensions.

A vote would, in principle, replace a negotiated distribution of offices with a mandated one. That is a meaningful change in a system where positions have been allocated between signatories.

It would also test whether opposition parties can organise and campaign, which is a different question from whether ballots are counted correctly.

The political weather is not calm

The main opposition movement is in the middle of a leadership dispute, with reporting from Juba describing the suspension of a senior figure and questions about who authorised it. Its armed wing has publicly ruled out internal fighting.

Violence continues in several states, including an attack on an army barracks in Warrap reported this week. Security conditions vary sharply by region.

None of this is disqualifying on its own. All of it affects whether a December vote can be conducted uniformly across the country.

The oil question sitting underneath

South Sudan’s public finances rest almost entirely on crude exported through Sudan, which means its budget is hostage to a neighbour’s war. Pipeline disruptions have repeatedly cut revenue.

Elections cost money, and an election commission cannot function on arrears. The financing of the process is a live constraint that has already drawn public comment in Juba.

Any investor reading this file should treat the electoral timetable and the oil export timetable as one question rather than two.

What outside actors are doing

United Nations human rights experts are travelling to South Sudan as the government pushes ahead with the electoral timetable. Their assessments will shape international recognition of any result.

Regional bodies have generally pressed for elections to be held rather than extended again. Fatigue with transitional arrangements is real.

Recognition matters commercially as well as politically. It determines access to concessional finance.

The honest reading

Removing a legal obstacle is not the same as being ready. The amendment makes a December vote lawful; it does not make it administratively feasible.

Voter registration, constituency delimitation, security arrangements and funding all remain to be demonstrated. Each has failed to materialise before.

The most likely outcomes remain a delayed election or a partial one. The amendment simply removes the excuse that the constitution made it impossible.

What to watch

The first marker is the publication of an electoral calendar with registration dates. Without registration there is no vote.

The second is the funding of the National Elections Commission, and whether the budget line is released.

The third is whether opposition parties accept the amended framework or challenge it. A boycott would change the meaning of any result.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did President Kiir sign? He assented on 2 September 2026 to the Transitional Constitution of the Republic of South Sudan, 2011 (Amendment No. 13) Act, 2026, passed by the Transitional National Legislature. What does the amendment change? It delinks the permanent constitution-making process and the National Population and Housing Census from the conduct of national elections. Both had previously been treated as prerequisites. When are elections due? They are intended to take place in December 2026. South Sudan has not held a national election since independence in 2011. Does this mean the vote will happen? Not necessarily. The amendment removes a legal obstacle, but voter registration, constituency delimitation, security and funding all still have to be delivered. Why is funding a problem? South Sudan’s revenue depends almost entirely on crude exported through Sudan, and pipeline disruptions have repeatedly cut income. Election financing has already drawn public comment in Juba.

World.title: Djibouti Wants to Turn Its Cables Into a Computing Business
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

DJIBOUTI · TECHNOLOGY

Key Facts —The event: Djibouti held its first national forum on artificial intelligence at the Palais du Peuple, under the patronage of President Ismail Omar Guelleh. —The organisers: It was run by the ministry for the digital economy and innovation with the Secretariat General of the Government, supported by UNESCO and ESCWA. —The starting point: The national AI readiness index is put at about 24.5 out of 100. —Other scores: Cybersecurity is rated at 31.5, while the ICT development index reaches 61.6. —The asset: Several subsea fibre-optic cables, data centres and a position on the Bab el-Mandeb approaches put the country on the region’s digital routes. —The ambition: The government wants a sovereign cloud and national computing capacity, not only transit. —The framing: A country that does not control its data cannot control its digital future, the government’s secretary general told the forum. —The catch: Djibouti scores 24.5 out of 100 on artificial-intelligence readiness, so the cables are ahead of the skills.

Djibouti artificial intelligence policy now has a starting number. It is a modest one: a readiness index of about 24.5 out of 100. The country’s first national AI forum opened this week with an argument that its cables and data centres should be turned into computing capacity rather than left as transit infrastructure.
