What was held, and by whom

The forum opened at the Palais du Peuple under the patronage of President Ismail Omar Guelleh, who toured public and private exhibition stands before the ceremony. Prime Minister Abdoulkader Kamil Mohamed received him.

It was organised by the ministry delegate for the digital economy and innovation, led by Safia Mohamed Ali Gadileh, together with the Secretariat General of the Government. UNESCO and the UN Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia provided support.

The opening day was built around vision, governance and the launch of the national UNESCO readiness assessment report. That report is the source of the numbers below.

The numbers the government published

The minister described the national position without flattery. The AI readiness index stands at about 24.5 out of 100 and the cybersecurity index at 31.5.

The ICT development index is considerably higher at 61.6, which reflects connectivity rather than capability. Djibouti is well connected and not yet well equipped.

Publishing an unflattering baseline is itself a policy choice. Governments that begin with a real number are easier to hold to a target later.

Why Djibouti artificial intelligence policy is a geography story

Djibouti sits where several subsea fibre-optic cables come ashore, linking Europe, the Gulf, South Asia and East Africa. It also hosts data centres and the region’s densest concentration of foreign military bases.

That position has made the country a transit point for data in the same way it is a transit point for containers. Transit generates fees and very little else.

The stated ambition is to convert geographic advantage into technological advantage, which means keeping computation onshore rather than only routing packets through it.

Sovereign cloud, and what it would take

The government wants to consolidate Djibouti as the digital convergence point of the Horn of Africa and to develop national sovereign cloud and computing capacity. That is a serious infrastructure commitment.

Computing capacity needs reliable power, cooling and skills in roughly that order. Djibouti’s electricity supply and water constraints are the obvious limits.

The country has been building renewable capacity, including geothermal and wind, partly for this reason. Whether it is enough to run training workloads is a separate question.

The governance argument

Almis Mohamed Abdillahi, the government’s secretary general, framed the issue beyond technology. He argued that a country which does not master its data cannot durably master its digital future or artificial intelligence.

He also listed the domains that must be integrated into national thinking: governance, ethics, law, economics, society, diplomacy and security. That is a broader remit than most national AI strategies begin with.

The framing is deliberate. Small states that treat AI purely as procurement end up buying systems they cannot audit.

The gaps the assessment identified

The UNESCO-supported diagnostic describes the country’s preparation as emerging, with institutional and strategic foundations in place. It identifies significant challenges in data, regulation, training, research, digital inclusion and computing infrastructure.

That list is honest and unremarkable. It is roughly the same list most middle-income countries would produce.

The difference is scale. A country of about a million people can move faster on regulation and slower on skills, because both constraints are smaller in absolute terms.

Who else is competing for the same role

Kenya, Rwanda, Morocco and South Africa are all positioning as African digital hubs, and each has more domestic demand than Djibouti. Competition for regional cloud investment is real.

Djibouti’s counter-argument is the cables and the neutrality of a small state with no domestic market to protect. That is the same argument it has used successfully in ports.

It is a plausible pitch, and it has worked before in a different industry.

What to watch

The first marker is whether a national AI strategy document is actually published, with dates and a budget. Forums produce reports; strategies produce procurement.

The second is any announcement of computing capacity landing in Djibouti, whether commercial or sovereign. That is the difference between transit and industry.

The third is data-protection legislation. Sovereign cloud without a data law is a marketing term.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Djibouti’s AI readiness score? The national artificial intelligence readiness index is put at about 24.5 out of 100. Cybersecurity is rated at 31.5 and the ICT development index at 61.6. What happened at the forum? Djibouti held its first national forum on artificial intelligence at the Palais du Peuple under the patronage of President Ismail Omar Guelleh. It was organised by the ministry for the digital economy with UNESCO and ESCWA support. Why is Djibouti relevant to digital infrastructure? Several subsea fibre-optic cables come ashore there. The country hosts data centres on the routes linking Europe, the Gulf, South Asia and East Africa. It wants to convert that transit position into computing capacity. What does the government want to build? It wants to consolidate Djibouti as the digital convergence point of the Horn of Africa and to develop sovereign cloud and national computing capability. What are the main obstacles? The national assessment cites data, regulation, training, research, digital inclusion and computing infrastructure. Power and water constraints are the practical limits on hosting large computing loads.

World.title: Motorcycle slams into SUV doors, leaving teen with fractured foot
World.content:
Motorcycle slams into SUV doors, leaving teen with fractured foot

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): An 18 year old labourer sustained two fractures to his left foot after his motorcycle collided with an SUV in Independence Village on Saturday.

Police say the rider was travelling along Fadden Avenue from the direction of Triangular Park toward Big Creek Road on a black motorcycle.

On reaching a tire shop along the route, a black 2013 Ford Edge SUV drove onto Fadden Avenue. The motorcycle collided with the driver and passenger doors of the vehicle.

The rider, Melvin Rene Arteaga of the Newsite Area, received two fractures to his left foot. The motorcycle sustained a broken left handle.

The SUV driver, 35 year old Barry Wayne Zuniga, complained of pain to his left upper ribs. His vehicle received dents to the left driver and passenger doors.

All parties were issued with medico legal forms.

Arteaga was transported to Belize Health Care Partners for further medical attention.

Investigations continue.

World.title: Guatemalan man dies after motorcycle and pickup collide at Red Bank junction
World.content:
Guatemalan man dies after motorcycle and pickup collide at Red Bank junction

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 59 year old Guatemalan labourer of Red Bank Village died Saturday following a collision at the junction of Red Bank Village and the T.V. Ramos Highway.

Police visited the scene around 10:45am and found a grey Toyota Tundra pickup parked at the junction, driven by 30 year old Deidra Jackson of Polak Road, Silk Grass Village.

A black Meilun motorcycle without licence plates lay at the edge of the junction, with the injured man beside it.

Nerry Campbell had sustained injuries to his right leg and right arm, complained of pain all over his body and was spitting blood.

Initial investigation revealed he was travelling along the T.V. Ramos Highway in a north to south direction when he made a right turn into Red Bank Road, colliding with the right front portion of the pickup.

He was rushed to the Southern Regional Hospital where he succumbed to his injuries while undergoing surgery. He was pronounced dead at 1:01pm.

The scene was visited and processed and a sketch plan drawn. A urine specimen was obtained.

The pickup driver is detained pending investigation.

World.title: Belizean Cacao makes its way to Chocolate makers around the world
World.content:
Belizean Cacao makes its way to Chocolate makers around the world

By Zoila Palma: Maya Mountain Cacao (MMC) has announced that its final container of Belizean cacao for the 2026 U.S. market is now on its way, marking another milestone for Belize’s growing fine-flavor cacao industry.

The company said it will also ship its final container to the European Union market next week, officially bringing the 2026 export season to a close.

MMC sources premium Belizean cacao for fine chocolate makers while supporting farmers and creating social impact in cacao-growing communities.

The company said the end of the 2026 export season also signals a new chapter, as beginning in 2027, international exports will be managed by the Maya Mountain Cacao Co-operative Society Limited, placing farmers at the center of the business and its future growth.

World.title: Teach them to plant! Why Agriculture could transform Belize’s schools and future
World.content:
Teach them to plant! Why Agriculture could transform Belize’s schools and future

By Zoila Palma: As Belize looks toward a future of greater food security, entrepreneurship and economic resilience, agriculture should be given a much stronger place in the secondary school system.

Every high school student should have the opportunity to learn how to plant, cultivate, harvest and care for crops—not simply as a school subject, but as a practical life and business skill.

Teaching agriculture can help young Belizeans understand where their food comes from while developing skills that can become sources of income.

Students can learn vegetable production, livestock rearing, soil management, composting, irrigation, greenhouse farming, aquaculture and even the business side of agriculture.

Such knowledge can encourage young people to see farming not as an outdated occupation, but as a modern industry with opportunities in food production, agribusiness, technology and entrepreneurship. Belize’s education planning has previously identified the reintroduction of gardening and agriculture into primary and secondary education as a way to better connect education with the country’s needs.

An excellent example of this demonstrating what is possible is Mopan Technical High School in Benque Viejo del Carmen.

Its agriculture program provides students with hands-on experience in areas including soil and organic-matter management, planting, crop care, harvesting, greenhouse production and animal husbandry.

Mopan’s model demonstrates that agriculture education can extend far beyond a classroom.

The school has historically utilized its campus for agricultural activities, including crop fields, greenhouses, poultry and pig production and aquaculture.

Students have also participated in community activities such as World Food Day, giving tours and providing plant seedlings. The school’s own history notes that it was among the first high schools in Belize to enter students in CXC Agriculture examinations.

Imagine if more high schools across Belize had productive school farms.

Students could grow vegetables used in their school feeding programs, raise chickens or fish, learn to propagate fruit trees and sell surplus produce to help finance school projects.

Every Belizean eats, and every Belizean benefits when the country can produce more of its own food.

If Belize wants a generation that is more self-sufficient, entrepreneurial and prepared for the challenges of food security and climate change, our high schools should be teaching young people not only how to pass exams, but also how to grow something, produce something and build something of their own.

World.title: Belize Coast Guard Commandant completes strategic leadership Seminar in South Korea
World.content:
Belize Coast Guard Commandant completes strategic leadership Seminar in South Korea

By Zoila Palma: Coast Guard Commandant Rear Admiral Gregory Soberanis has completed a Senior Leadership Seminar in Strategic Studies in South Korea, focusing on lawfare and the evolving geopolitical environment.

The engagement provided senior military leadership with greater insight into the legal, geopolitical and security dynamics shaping today’s operating environment.

The Belize Coast Guard said participation in strategic engagements of this nature strengthens leadership awareness and helps prepare commanders to anticipate emerging challenges.

As Belize’s maritime security environment continues to evolve, the Coast Guard remains committed to developing strategic leaders capable of safeguarding Belize’s national and maritime interests.

World.title: Minister of Home Affairs seek to expand BPD’s K-9 unit
World.content:
Minister of Home Affairs seek to expand BPD’s K-9 unit

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Home Affairs Julius Espat has indicated that the Ministry is seeking the expand the Belize Police Department’s K-9 unit.

“ And right now I’m looking at the K-9 Unit, and we only have two dogs nationally, and I believe we should have at least 20, so we will work on that. I’ve been looking at other things within the force. We’ve been looking at the infrastructure, which is for us the easiest part of it. So, we did a national analysis of all the substations that we have, and we did an evaluation as to what is needed to bring them up to an acceptable level. That report has been sent to Ministry of Finance already, sent to the Prime Minister. And then we’re looking at vehicles,” Espat said.

Espat says that the Ministry is also looking at acquiring ATV so that the police are able to reach urban areas.

“We just signed the contract to roof the Raccoon Street station, and we’ll be doing another part to do the cladding of it. That’s by MIDH. We just had a bid out for purchasing of weapons; we are awaiting that bid to come in. So, the transfer of personnel is just a part of what the Police Department needs.

There’s a lot of work that has to be put in, and I think we have very good police officers who are frustrated,” Espat added.

Espat says that the Ministry continues to seek ways to improve the Belize Police Department.

World.title: International News: Deported to a country they’ve never called home: The 8 top ICE destinations
World.content:
International News: Deported to a country they’ve never called home: The 8 top ICE destinations

By Zoila Palma: The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has been deporting thousands of people to their countries of origin, but an increasing number are being sent instead to third countries—nations where they are not citizens. The practice has raised concerns about deportees being left in unfamiliar countries where they may not speak the language or understand local customs.

Mexico has emerged as the largest destination for third-country deportations, with about 20,000 people without Mexican heritage reportedly sent there during the second Trump administration, according to Refugees International’s Third Country Deportation Watch. Mexican authorities reportedly give many third-country nationals only 10 days to remain, leaving asylum systems under significant pressure.

Other Central American countries have also become destinations. Guatemala has received several thousand deportees, including 2,284 Mexican nationals between April and August 2026, while approximately 360 non-Panamanians have been deported to Panama.

Costa Rica has received about 331 people, while approximately 250 non-Salvadorans have been sent to El Salvador since ICE transfers to that country began in July 2026.

Honduras has also received about 170 non-Honduran deportees under a transfer agreement with the United States. Officials have indicated that sending some Mexican nationals farther south could serve as a deterrent to irregular migration, while Mexico has objected to its citizens being deported to other countries.

The policy extends beyond Central America, with more than 130 people sent to Uzbekistan and over 100 people without Ghanaian heritage deported to Ghana, according to the Third Country Deportation Watch.

Human rights organizations have raised concerns about the treatment and legal protections of people transferred to countries where they have no established ties.

World.title: Tracy Panton, saddened by murder of young Brianna Myvett, calls for action against gun violence
World.content:
Tracy Panton, saddened by murder of young Brianna Myvett, calls for action against gun violence

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Leader of the Opposition Tracy Panton has extended condolences to the family and friends of young Brianna Myvett.

“I heard every word you shared, and I felt the words you could not bring yourself to say. The shock, disbelief and pain of it all are simply too much, not only for you, but for every parent who has lost a child to senseless acts of violence.

By all accounts, Brianna was a beautiful, intelligent, talented and ambitious young woman with plans for her life. She kept herself out of harm’s way, yet harm still found her. Her life mattered. Her contributions to our Belizean society mattered.

We may never understand why bad things happen to good people,” Panton said.

“We MUST find solutions to gun violence that is robbing the lives, potential and future productivity of our young people. Belize’s very survival depends on how well we protect them and create opportunities for them not merely to survive, but to thrive and to triumph,” Panton added.

Myvett was a recent graduate of Wesley Junior College. In June, Anglican Cathedral College congratulated her on graduating from the institution, noting that she was a distinguished alumna of ACC’s Class of 2023.

Myvett was laid to rest on September 2, 2026.

World.title: 10 months in pain
World.content:
Ten months and 21 days. That is how long Ralston Thomas has been awaiting surgery at Spanish Town Hospital to fix a fractured femur in his right leg, which was broken in a car accident on October 16, 2025.

The 52-year-old said that despite already paying for the tools needed for the operation, his surgery was postponed twice. He said last December he had a surgery scheduled but doctors told him that the machine needed for the procedure was out of service. On another occasion he said he was informed that although the machine was back in operation, his case was not considered an emergency and other patients were ahead of him.

At the same time, he said doctors continue to refer to his case as complicated and in need of attention; conflicting stories, he said, are leaving him spiralling.

Thomas said his frustration has reached breaking point. Confined to a bed and enduring constant pain at the Spanish Town Infirmary, he is left wondering when, if ever, his turn will come.

He told the Jamaica Observer that following the postponement of his surgery in December, he was moved to the infirmary as he had no one at home to care for him as his relatives are all overseas, and the hospital needed to make the bed available to other patients.

“From that time them have me and a gwaan put me off. Every month I go to the clinic they keep putting me off and say I have to wait. The last time, they said July 3, 2026 I should come back and them a guh give me a surgery date, and dem a go make mi talk to the ward clerk to prepare my admission. When I went back they said they can’t admit me because the hospital beds are full, and it’s one machine working, and whole heap of emergency a come in, so I asked them if my case is not an emergency,” said Thomas.

“They said it’s an emergency but they have some other cases ahead of me that are more urgent because those people [were] in the hospital before me, so they have to run through those cases,” Thomas shared.

“I went back on August 28 to the clinic and they gave me another six-week date. Every time I go I see a different doctor and dem a tell mi seh my foot a go take a long time to heal,” Thomas said, his voice laced with frustration.

He said what has been even more frustrating is that he already paid $187,000 to have the surgery, money his family rushed to raise through a GoFundMe account because they were informed that he urgently needed the procedure. However, now he is forced to wait and watch as others get the medical assistance they need.

“They just have me all around the corner, and I don’t know why. From the time I was in hospital, a patient come in after me, and the other day I went to the clinic and he told me that he got his surgery. It’s about two months after [me when] he came in, and another youth too; the two of them came in after me and get them surgery so I want to know why my surgery can’t be done,” said Thomas.

“It’s terrifying and stressful. I have to just go through a lot of [clinic appointments], and medication, and all of them things there. It’s not a normal thing, for almost one year now… I just want my foot to do so I can come out. More time when mi mind run on certain things I kinda shed a little tear because of depression and sadness, but me a tough youth. Me a 52-year-old and me born struggling, so me a hold it,” he told the Sunday Observer.

Spanish Town Hospital CEO Jacqueline Ellis said that while she could not speak to the specifics of Thomas’s case, she will have the matter investigated to provide the family with answers.

Thomas’s cousin, Beverly Armstrong, said the family is sick with worry and is left with more questions than answers. The United States resident said that on a recent visit to Jamaica she accompanied Thomas to a doctor to seek answers, but they left with more questions. She said she also reached out to many individuals in the health sector for assistance, only for her cries to fall on deaf ears.

Armstrong said the situation has caused her to seriously question if she wants to return to Jamaica.

“It’s very heartbreaking. His mother cries every day. It’s frustrating and very disappointing, because while we’re living here in the United States — because we come to get a better life — we always want to come back home. We come back home all the time because home is where our heart is, and now that I think about if I happen to be in Jamaica, God forbid, you’re going to tell me that this is what it is like and that the health-care system down here is so horrible that you cannot even come home?” she said.

“It’s very disturbing and I’m very disappointed. I go to bed at night wondering, ‘Okay, is he going to be infected? What if infection sets in?’ And then it’s traumatising for me as well,” she said.

Armstrong also alleged that the medical professionals at the hospital exhibit a lack of respect and empathy as they are not quick to provide updates and are dismissive when pressed for information.

She said the family requested a transfer for Thomas to Kingston Public Hospital (KPH), but they faced challenges with Spanish Town Hospital not wanting to cooperate despite KPH stating its willingness to take him as a patient.

She added that the family also faced difficulties getting the full money paid to a third-party facility for devices needed for the surgery. She said she was told by the company that 10 per cent would be deducted from the money paid, a move she said she finds unfair, given that the delay was outside of their control.

Armstrong said the family decided not to pursue the refund, and simply wants the surgery done.

“All I want at the end of the day is to get Ralston his surgery so we can leave them alone. Just give him surgery so he can get the proper care and the healing process can start properly — because right now I’m sure he has healed somewhat, but not properly, and to me, that is detrimental to his health. Whether it’s from the Spanish Town Hospital or any other facility that accommodates him, I believe that someone in authority can make it happen,” she said.

“I just want him to get the surgery so he can get on with his life. We don’t want to be fighting with these people all this time. I’m not out to attack anybody…because I don’t like that, but at the end of the day they push you to the limit, and you’ve got to do what you got to do. At the end of the day, the goal is to fix him,” said Armstrong.

World.title: Hurricane Melissa a blessing in disguise
World.content:
Newly installed roofs shine bright blue at Edwin Allen High School in Clarendon, last Wednesday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

“I think am one of the happiest principals in Jamaica!”

Those were the words of Edwin Allen High School Principal Jermaine Harris as he marvelled at the work done to transform the institution after it was extensively damaged during the passage of Hurricane Melissa. Though the storm left widespread destruction in its wake, Harris considers the disaster a blessing in disguise — delivering the infrastructure upgrade the 62-year-old institution had sought from the Ministry of Education for years.

The Category 5 hurricane had destroyed the roofs of nine classrooms, many of which the principal said were deteriorating from a termite infestation. The school’s canteen, tuckshop, and a few administration offices were also impacted. Now, fresh paint and new roofs have revived the institution, a welcome move for the school’s principal.

“The grade 10 block consists of nine classrooms, and those roofs were removed as a result of Hurricane Melissa. The offices of the guidance counsellors and dean of discipline were also removed, totally. The canteen and the storeroom adjoining the canteen, those roofs were also affected, not totally, but we had leaking roofs. The entire grade seven block was also affected. And all of those areas that I mentioned are now back in immaculate condition,” said Harris.

He added that the roof of the agriculture block was also repaired, the bathrooms upgraded, and the tuckshops are being retrofitted. The school is fit to reopen on September 7, with non-emergency repairs to continue into October.

“I am ecstatic and over the moon because when I took up leadership in 2021 and I looked at the campus, that was one of my major pet peeves. I was not pleased with the campus, because I believe that when you enter a campus it speaks to the performance, the ethos, and the culture of a school. I wanted to start improving the aesthetic so that we can have a campus that is befitting of the high-performance culture that we have at Edwin Allen High School. To see the campus looking this immaculate, I am really satisfied and I know that this will translate into the students’ behaviour and performance,” he told the

Jamaica Observer on a visit to the school last Wednesday.

He thanked the team at the Ministry of Education and the National Education Trust for the work done, making special mention of the contractors who worked tirelessly to restore the school before the start of the new school year on September 7.

Harris said the team officially began work in January, ramping up operations during the summer break. He said the contractors worked on shifts, and even on weekends, to get the job done.

“I wanted to make sure that we got back our buildings, because when we went on the rotation schedule it created havoc for our parents and students. Some of them even transferred as a result because we had to schedule them: three days of school for some students, two days for others, and even online. It was just not working out. I said to the contractors, ‘Hey, I need my school back for the new school year so whatever needs to be done, let’s get it done.’ They listened, and I’m really happy for what would have been achieved,” he said.

According to the principal, mainly cosmetic work remains, including installing rain gutters and windows as well as some electrical work. Sourcing issues have, however, stalled the installation of windows.

While massive repairs are nearing completion, Harris said the school is yet to replace computers damaged by the storm. The principal pleaded for past students and Jamaicans overall to provide assistance to replace the computer monitors, noting that the school heavily relies on them for teaching information technology.

“The computers were damaged, and other equipment was damaged as well. We have the space but we don’t have the equipment, so that will be an issue for our Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) information technology students because they have to do their school-based assessments and their practicals…The teachers were very creative last year, and we got about a 97 per cent pass mark for information technology [previously],” said Harris.

“Students brought their tablets and their laptops, and they worked miracles with the little that they had, but it really stretched the teachers and the students. We are asking for support in getting back our computers — approximately 60 computers and printers. We also had a smart board that was damaged, and other accessories within the computer department that will aid in the teaching of information technology,” he added.

In the meantime, he said the school will continue to strive for excellence, making use of their new and improved upgrades.

“Our objective is not simply to reopen the school; we want to reopen with a safe, clean, organised and conducive environment that will allow all of our students to focus on learning and our teachers to focus on teaching. We usually use a theme to drive our operation each year, and this year we are focusing on high performance driven by innovation.

“We want to encourage our staff members to innovate so that we can continue the trajectory in terms of our improvement in performance, and we can maintain our high performance in sports. We are fully committed to the school improvement plan, and with the support from all stakeholders I believe that we will achieve that high performance and we will innovate so that our children can certainly benefit from these exploits,” said Harris.

World.title: Going major still matters
World.content:
HARDING...if that artiste’s ambition is to be on top of the Billboard charts consistently...then that...requires being signed to a major label.

OVER the past few weeks there have been discussions on social media platforms about the relationship between Jamaican artistes and major US record companies.

Some persons have argued that major labels offer nothing to the careers of Jamaican artistes, whom they claim achieve greater success by remaining independent, while others have reasoned that the labels provide opportunities that artistes would not have been able to achieve independently.

The Jamaica Observer spoke to industry professionals who shared their experiences working with major labels and reggae and dancehall artistes.

Jeremy Harding, a respected music producer and artiste manager, has worked with major labels on the production side. He produced Kevin Lyttle and Spragga Benz’s Turn Me On for Atlantic Records, remixed Body Party by Ciara for Epic Records, and mixed and engineered songs on Kardinal Offishal’s Not 4 Sale album for KonLive/Geffen.

Harding is also the former manager of international dancehall artiste Sean Paul.

Asked if he believed that, in today’s music environment, Jamaican artistes do not need the support of a major label, Harding said, “ ‘Do not need’ is too definitive of a statement to place on the requirements of a successful career. Jamaican artistes have had mixed success being signed to major labels over the years, with some achieving multi-platinum successes and many more, unfortunately, being released from deals without being able to chart, sell or stream enough for the major label to continue its investment in them or without being able to recoup [on investment] or [to make a] profit. There have been many successful artistes from Jamaica that have had lucrative and celebratory careers without a major label, for sure. We have a very supportive Diaspora market which keeps them touring and doing shows, and their social media base can also be very supportive in keeping their fan base energised and keeping them relevant. But that’s doesn’t say artistes ‘do not need’ a major label.”

Harding continued, “If that artiste’s ambition is to be on top of the Billboard charts consistently and to line their walls with gold and platinum plaques, to be on late night network TV shows, appear on top-rated Spotify playlists and top 40 radio across the world, then that 100 per cent requires being signed to a major label for their resources, relationships and budgets that make all those things happen. That’s not going to happen with only YouTube views and TikTok content.

“A major label is more designed to grow the career of the artiste one single at a time through repetition and exposure to the largest audience possible. To create big hit records rather than flood the market with continuous content potentially overexposing the artiste and having too many songs in the same space, by the same artiste, competing for listeners’ attention. If the playing field was level, then the thought of owning 100 per cent of your own masters sounds appealing. But in reality, your 20 per cent royalty from the label owning the master and what they can do with it far outweighs what you can achieve with your own DSP distribution and your followers on

Instagram,” Harding shared.

Cristy Barber, president of the Tuff Gong Collective and former chair of the Grammys’ Reggae Committee, has worked at several major labels throughout her career, where she signed a number of Jamaican acts.

Barber concurred with Harding about the benefits and support that an artiste can access once signed to a major label.

“It can be beneficial if you understand the benefits you get from them and capitalise off of it. The biggest mistake an artiste can make by going into a major label relationship is thinking they will do all the work for you. Usually, the artiste will have better financial support and access to a wider reach of promotion and exposure to opportunities worldwide. However, it depends on your career goals and talent whether or not you need a major label, no matter the genre,” said Barber. “Major labels and artistes can co-exist once there is a clear understanding of what each of them brings to the table.”

Barber has worked with a long list of acts during her tenure at major labels, including Spragga Benz (Capitol Records), Super Cat (Columbia Records), Beenie Man, Buju Banton, Jimmy Cliff (Island Records), Sly and Robbie (Elektra Records), and Stephen and Damian “Jr Gong” Marley (Tuff Gong International /Republic/Universal Music).

Clyde McKenzie, cultural commentator and former music executive at Shocking Vibes Productions, interacted with major labels including Sony Music and Virgin Records on behalf of his artistes at Shocking Vibes.

McKenzie doesn’t believe that the current generation of artistes are as welcoming to the idea of being signed to a major label as many of the acts were in the 1990s and early to mid-2000s.

“I am not sure many Jamaicans are as wedded to the idea of becoming signed to a record label as they were in the last century. Many Jamaican acts have accentuated a trend which has been a feature of our music for some time now. They are more reliant on earning money from shows and tours than they are from record sales. This means that what they want is to get as much publicity as they can — officially and underground. Record labels still matter, though, because they still have promotional platforms, which can provide considerable reach for upcoming artistes. VP Records has been important to reggae and dancehall more than the major labels like Universal, Sony and Warner, or their affiliates. However, it seems that while the labels can still be helpful in the digital and traditional distribution of their music, a number of these artistes are trying to blow up first without the intervention of the labels,” McKenzie reasoned. “My experience with large labels is that they have the financial resources but they were not sufficiently close to the streets to allow Jamaican acts to maximise their impact. Management had to make sure that they were integrally involved in the forging of strategy because many of the record company executives were often not familiar with how to promote and market Jamaican acts which did not have dedicated media outlets like some of the mainstream American acts.”

Brian Greenspoon worked in the International Department at Elektra Records in New York and represented the likes of Missy Elliott, Busta Rhymes, Fabolous and Mark Ronson. He is also a former head of marketing at VP Records, former general manager at Lizard King Records, and he also did a stint at EMI Music Publishing shortly after he finished college in the late 1990s.

Greenspoon, who today works as an independent publicist representing acts signed to independent and major labels, believes that major labels know the potential of reggae and dancehall acts but that not every artiste is suited for the major label system.

“Reggae and dancehall music have permeated every facet of popular culture, so majors already know the potential. Majors can continue to acquire catalogues and work with reggae acts through their independent distribution arms like ADA at Warner, The Orchard or AWAL at Sony, and Virgin Music Group at Universal. They continue to support and sign acts directly like Masicka at Def Jam Records or Shenseea at Since ‘93/Columbia Records. Of course, not every act is suited for the major label system. It’s a matter of pairing a culturally aware label with a globally appealing act who has a catalogue of music that can speak to the masses and generate income, via various revenue streams, over time. Jamaican acts and major labels have more opportunities to coexist now than ever before, but it’s up to the artiste and manager to create an undeniable story and an unbreakable base upon which a label can build. Once a Jamaican artiste has maximised their audience at home and in the Diaspora, a major label’s job is to provide the resources, ideas, and global network to amplify that story to the world beyond,” said Greenspoon.

World.title: Shrinking numbers, growing fears at Bustamante High
World.content:
Bustamante High School in Clarendon (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

BUSTAMANTE High School is fighting to keep its gates open as the institution grapples with a dramatic decline in its student population, falling from an average of 1,000 pupils five years ago to around 400 in recent days.

School Principal Wayne Evans said the sharp decline is due to a combination of factors such as low admission rates and socio-economic challenges that see students leaving school before completing their educational requirements because of financial issues at home, with some opting to seek employment to help support their families.

He said approximately 60 per cent of the school’s population are from single-parent households headed by mothers, and so in many instances the students drop out or are not consistent with class attendance because they have to become providers.

“If we start off with 100 children — particularly in upper school, our grades 10 and 11 — the economic pull for them to earn to support the family is very strong. So unless they’re doing well in school academically or they feel that they’re going to probably be able to pass the Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) exams, you’re not going to see them still in school because their mind is now on surviving, so they don’t finish school. We will lose approximately 20 per cent of them by the time they reach grades 10 and 11,” said Evans.

“[And] it’s not just that the children are thinking that [way], the parents are also pushing that on them. So by the time they complete their first term and do the exam in December, by January you start to have a significant fallout in population,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

The principal said the reality is frustrating because he knows that quite a number of the students have the potential to succeed.

“Many of them come in as completely low-performing students who were well behind but you see where they are getting there. If we could keep them around long enough, for another year or two, you can get them to where they can advance academically. But what you find is that when you call the parents, they are going to [say] right to your face, ‘Look here, I just can’t afford to send my child to school,’ and you’ll see where these children are missing out on not being able to achieve what the potential is for them because they have to move to survival mode,” said Evans.

To add to the problem, he said the school has low admission rates from the Primary Exit Profile (PEP) exams. He said Bustamante High School only received 28 new students following the release of exam results, a decline from last year when the school got 47 students.

“Our numbers were normally in the 100 and something [range]. Pre-COVID-19 pandemic we had maybe 180 new students coming in, so that tells you where the population is going if we don’t see a change…The last two cohorts were significantly below what it used to be. The present grades eight and nine are the smallest cohorts, which represent a significant drop in strength.

“If we don’t get an increase next year then the school will definitely see up to, maybe, a 60 per cent drop in [the] population. We still have a bigger cohort in grades 10, 9, and 11, but if next year we don’t get a good cohort to replace those leaving, that would be a significant drop,” explained Evans.

He said Hurricane Melissa, though it was a disaster, is somewhat helping the school to boost its population as families relocate from hard-hit areas such as St Elizabeth and Westmoreland. He shared that, so far this year, the school has received 10 to 15 transfer requests and are hopeful they can get more requests to increase the population.

While the future of the institution is not looking too bright, Evans said administrators are not rolling over and calling it a loss.

“We cannot just sit back and allow the school to close. We are going all out to rebrand our school and to get our name up there to see if we can pull some of the traffic to make Bustamante High School a school that persons will want to send their children and that children will want to attend. We are definitely seeking and developing all of our programmes, the whole ambience of the school, and trying to get our name up there.

“At the end of the day — even though we know that the population has dropped — some schools are very full, and that means that we can still get a few from there to make it a little bit more equitable. But we have to make our name, because the children have to choose a school and nobody can force them to come to us,” he told the Sunday Observer.

He added: “We are developing our brand. And we are making sure that our children get the best opportunity in terms of the product that we offer as educators; and the expectations that they have in meeting their goals, and their interests, and developing their potential to become the kind of person that they can be in Jamaica and around the world. We definitely are not going to play dead, and we are going to make sure that Bustamante High School comes out on top,” he declared.

World.title: MR BIG SHOT
World.content:
Jamaica’s Rajindra Campbell celebrates after winning the men’s shot put during the World Athletics Diamond League athletics meeting at King Baudouin Stadium in Brussels, Belgium, on Saturday. (Photo: AFP)

RAJINDRA Campbell became only the fifth man in history to throw beyond 23.00m when he won the men’s shot put with a Jamaican record 23.08m during the Wanda Diamond League final of the Allianz Memorial Van Damme at King Baudouin Stadium in Brussels, Belgium, on Saturday.

Campbell rewrote Jamaica’s history in the throwing events, joining discus thrower Fedrick Dacres as the only Jamaicans to win a Diamond Trophy in a throwing event. His 23.08m is the farthest throw in the world this season and moved him to fourth on the all-time list.

Tina Clayton was also a winner, taking the women’s 100m in 10.93 seconds (0.3m/s) to become the fifth Jamaican woman to win the Diamond Trophy in the event.

Campbell produced his winning throw in the final round after setting a Jamaican record of 22.62m in the second round. Only three Americans have gone farther — Ryan Crouser with 23.56m in May 2023, Joe Kovacs with 23.23m in September 2022, and Randy Barnes with 23.12m in May 1990.

The Olympic Games bronze medallist, who declared his wish to switch national allegiance to Türkiye, said after the contest, “There have been signs in practice of a throw like this being on the way, but to put it together today feels incredible. The 23.00m line is a badge of honour for every shot putter so I’m extremely grateful to have crossed it.”

Campbell believes he can go even farther, and has his sights set on the world record.

“There are still a lot of things that I can improve on, but every time I come closer to perfection, the throw will be further. That is an exciting challenge.”

“There are still marks to hit,” he said. “A lot of shot putters are extremely strong. They bench press 500 pounds and squat 700 pounds [but] I’m nowhere close to that yet. The world record is definitely an ambition. If I can be more consistent next year then the outlier will be at an even higher level.”

Campbell is not fazed by World Athletics’s rejection of his application to switch allegiance to Türkiye in time for the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.

“There are two more years left until the Olympics, which gives me time to become even better. Over there I want to represent Türkiye. The Turkish federation has given me all the support that I was missing, and it pays off immediately. I’m in my best shape ever.”

Campbell broke his Jamaican national record for the fifth time this year. His first-round 22.25m would have been enough to win, with American Jordan Geist second with 22.23m and Kovacs third with 22.09m.

He improved the Jamaican record to 22.34m in China in May, then threw 22.44m in June in Zagreb, Croatia, and 22.59m in Brescia, Italy, last weekend.

Clayton, who joined Veronica Campbell Brown, four-time winner Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce, three-time winner Elaine Thompson-Herah, and Shericka Jackson as Jamaican winners of the women’s 100m Diamond Trophy, dedicated her victory to the late Stephen Francis.

“I guess it’s kind of a perfect night, because winning the Diamond League final is something special. We all want to go home with the trophy and, to be honest, there were a lot of candidates for the title. Tonight I was the most determined athlete, and that made the difference,” she said.

She said she was not bothered by the time she ran.

“I’m satisfied with the time of 10.93, especially because it was a little bit too cold for sprinting. I would like to dedicate this victory to my coach, Stephen Francis, who passed away early this year. It’s very emotional but I have my family, the team around me that gives me all the support I need.”

Great Britain’s Amy Hunt was second in 11.06 seconds, followed by American Sha’Carri Richardson in 11.07 seconds, with Jonielle Smith placing fifth in 11.08 seconds.

Nickisha Pryce was third in the women’s 400m, running 49.36 seconds as Marileidy Paulino of the Dominican Republic ran a meeting record 48.64 seconds to win her fourth Diamond Trophy in the past five years.

She lowered Sanya Richards-Ross’s 48.83 seconds record set in 2009, with Norway’s Henriette Jæger finishing second in 49.20 seconds.

Megan Simmonds ran a season’s best 12.43 seconds (1.0m/s) for third in the 100m hurdles, which was won by world record holder Masai Russell in a meeting record 12.20 seconds — under the 12.27 seconds set in 2022 by Jasmine Camacho-Quinn.

Devynne Charlton broke her own Bahamian national record with 12.33 seconds to take second.

Jordan Scott was third in the men’s triple jump, with 17.18m (0.2m/s) in the first round, as Italy’s Andy Diaz Hernandez jumped 17.74m (0.6m/s) to win and break Christian Taylor’s 17.66m mark set in 2019. Portugal’s Pedro Pichardo was second with 17.51m (0.0m/s).

Lamara Distin was sixth in the women’s high jump final with 1.88m, while Sabrina Dockery won the invitational women’s 100m final in 11.17 seconds (0.1m/s), beating Australia’s Torrie Lewis, who ran 11.24 seconds, and Spain’s Jael Bestue who clocked 11.28 seconds.

Kadrian Goldson was second in the men’s invitational 100m in 10.05 seconds (-0.2m/s), behind Ghana’s Abdul-Rasheed Saminu who ran 10.04 seconds. Max Thomas of the United States was third in 10.23 seconds.

World.title: Jamaican defender Brown’s Macedonia transfer hinges on late FedEx package
World.content:
Richard Brown

JAMAICAN centre-back Richard Brown’s chances of playing professional football with Macedonian top-flight outfit FK Skopje has taken a dramatic turn, his signing stalled by a FedEx package sitting in a closed office with a transfer deadline of midnight Sunday, September 6, looming.

Jason McKay, owner of the McKay Security Football Group, which includes McKay New Raiders, said on Saturday that Brown’s signing has been left in a precarious position, held up by a FedEx package sent from Jamaica on August 26.

“It has been nine days,” McKay bemoaned. “I have no idea why it has taken so long. The package is now verified to be in Macedonia. However, FedEx isn’t open on weekends.

“All it takes is for some store owner to open his door for a few minutes so the federation there can get the documents. These are important documents such as police and school records, which the federation requires to be original copies,” McKay added.

“The package was sent on August 26 via FedEX after being verified by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to meet the transfer window of midnight, September 6,” he emphasised.

Reports out of newly promoted FK Skopje, who lost their third match of the new season Saturday, 1-2 to Bashkimi, indicated that Brown was on the verge of signing for the club now sitting at the bottom of the 10-club First Football League on three points from six games.

FK Skopje, who won promotion to the First League, June 1, after finishing as runners-up in the

Second League, are bolstering their squad for a third stint in nine years among North Macedonia’s top-tier teams.

Meanwhile, Brown, raring for a shot at his first international break, said he has been giving his

best with his family back home in mind.

“A lot of sacrifice has been put into this. I am here trying to make myself, McKay Raiders and

my family proud,” he said during a break from training.

Brown has been a feature player in Jamaica’s Premier League since age 18, first representing Cavaliers. The 25-year-old has also donned the colours of Tivoli Gardens, Dunbeholden, Racing and St Catherine Police.

World.title: Tina Clayton joins list of Jamaican 100m Diamond trophy winners
World.content:
Jamaica's Tina Clayton celebrates winning the women's 100m final during the World Athletics Diamond League athletics meeting at the King Baudouin Stadium in Brussels, on September 5, 2026. (Photo by NICOLAS TUCAT / AFP)

KINGSTON, Jamaica—Tina Clayton joined an impressive list of Jamaicans to win the women’s 100m Diamond League trophy after she sped to 10.93 seconds on Saturday’s second and final day of the Wanda Diamond League Final in Brussels, Belgium.

Clayton became the fifth Jamaican woman to take the trophy, joining four-time champion Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce, three-time champion Elaine Thompson-Herah, Shericka Jackson and Veronica Campbell-Brown.

She was also the fourth Jamaican to win Diamond trophies at this year’s meet after Rajindra Campbell threw a national record 23.08m to win the men’s shot put, Oblique Seville won the men’s 100m and Tajay Gayle the men’s long jump on Friday.

Great Britain’s Amy Hunt was second in the women’s 100m in 11.06 seconds, American Sha’Carrie Richardson was third in 11.07 seconds, and Jamaica’s Jonielle Smith was fifth in 11.08 seconds.

Three Jamaicans placed third in their respective events: Nickisha Pryce in the women’s 400m, Megan Simmonds in the 100m hurdles and Jordan Scott in the men’s triple jump.

Pryce ran 49.36 seconds for her podium finish as Marileidy Paulino of the Dominican Republic set a meet record of 48.64 seconds to win her fourth Diamond trophy in five years and complete an unblemished Diamond League season. Henriette Jaeger of Norway was second with 49.20 seconds.

Simmonds ran a season’s best 12.43 seconds (1.0m/s), for third in the 100m hurdles, which was won by world record holder Masai Russell in a meet record 12.20 seconds, under the 12.27 seconds set in 2022 by Jasmine Camacho-Quinn.

Devynne Charlton broke her own Bahamian national record with 12.33 seconds to take second place.

Scott jumped 17.18m (0.2m/s) in the first round to finish behind Italy’s Andy Diaz Hernandez, who had a meet record of 17.74m (-0.6m/s), bettering Christian Taylor’s 17.66m set in 2019, with Pedro Pichardo of Portugal second with 17.51m (0.0m/s).

Lamara Distin was sixth in the women’s high jump with a best clearance of 1.88m.

Sabrina Dockery won the women’s invitational 100m in 11.17 seconds (0.1m/s), beating Australia’s Torrie Lewis- 11.24 seconds with Jael Bestue of Spain placing third with 11.28 seconds.

Kadrian Goldson was second in the men’s invitational 100m in 10.05 seconds (-0.2m/s), just beaten by Ghana’s Abdul-Rasheed Saminu with 10.04 seconds, with American Max Thomas third with 10.23 seconds.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: German startup makes European space history with first successful orbital launch
World.content:
We made history. On just our second flight, we became the first commercial space company from Europe to deliver satellites into orbit. Mission 'Onward and Upward' successfully lifted off and deployed payloads into orbit. A new chapter for European spaceflight. More:… pic.twitter.com/AWvqG2l8Mn — Isar Aerospace (@isaraerospace) September 5, 2026

Germany’s Ministry for Research, Technology and Space hailed the launch as a “milestone that impressively demonstrates our country's innovative strength and technical expertise.”

Europe is trying to reduce its reliance on non-European launch providers, particularly Elon Musk’s SpaceX. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the Norwegian launch site in March and warned Europe has been “dependent on other supply chains and other countries in the world for far too long.”

The two-day International Space Summit will be held in Paris on Wednesday and Thursday with delegations from more than 120 countries. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is set to give her first speech solely about space policy, as the Commission prepares to unveil its European Space Shield, an action plan aimed at protecting the bloc's satellites.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration is discouraging American companies from attending the conference.

Isar’s first launch, in March last year, ended with the rocket crashing into the sea shortly after liftoff.

Calling Saturday night’s successful launch “historic,” European Space Agency Director General Josef Aschbacher said it was “yet another step towards a more diverse autonomous European launch service sector.”

Isar is one of several European startups seeking to break into the orbital launch market, alongside Spain’s PLD Space and France’s MaiaSpace. Arianespace, a Paris-headquartered company, has long operated from France’s overseas territory of French Guiana.

Based near Munich, Isar plans to move toward serial production of its Spectrum rocket, with a target of manufacturing over 30 a year, and is developing a second launch site in Canada.

World.title: Nigel Farage wants to be a global statesman. First he needs distance from Trump.
World.content:
The pair signed a “memorandum of understanding” pledging to stop the flow of small boats trafficking migrants across the English Channel to British shores. For Farage, it was a chance to prove he can cut a deal with a foreign political leader even before he’s elected to office.

The surprise was that the leader wasn’t Donald Trump.

Showing off a French connection — and even suggesting he would speak in French when he repays the visit — might just help dilute the impression that Farage is a disciple of the world’s most divisive and disruptive head of state.

Farage has long made a point of his ideological kinship with the American president, but these connections to the “Make America Great Again” universe now pose perhaps the most serious threat to his campaign to win power in the U.K.

Goodbye to the ‘British sherpa’

Farage’s set-piece Friday press conference alongside Bardella was overshadowed by a storm of controversy over an alleged funding scandal that hours earlier had claimed the scalps of two of his most senior aides.

One of them, policy chief James Orr, is almost as well plugged into Trump’s world as the Reform leader himself. Orr has nurtured a friendship with U.S. Vice President JD Vance, whom he has described as a kind of “mentor.” For his part, the vice president has called Orr his “British sherpa.”

World.title: Farage would use military to ‘crush’ Argentina in any Falklands dispute, senior ally says
World.content:
But last week, U.S. President Donald Trump suggested he was reconsidering Washington’s support for Britain’s sovereignty over the islands. “I always review every position — that’s just one of many,” he told reporters.

Days later, on Friday, right-wing Argentinian President Javier Milei, a Trump ally, escalated the rhetoric over his country’s enduring claim to the islands, pledging to levy sanctions against companies drilling for oil nearby without approval from Buenos Aires.

Britain’s center-left Labour government immediately rejected Milei’s threat. A Downing Street spokesperson said the islanders have a right to self-determination and that the U.K. supports their right “to develop their natural resources for their own economic benefit.”

Jenrick told journalists at the Reform UK conference in Birmingham: “If Nigel Farage was our prime minister, Milei would not be doing what he’s doing. This is happening because Milei is weak, and he senses that we have a weak government too.”

He added: “If Nigel Farage was our prime minister, we would use every lever of the British state — our armed forces, our economic sanctions, everything — to defend the Falklands, and we would crush Argentina.”

Reform UK’s decision to turn on Milei over the issue contrasts with Farage’s previous praise for the Argentinian leader for his right-wing, small state ideology. In 2024, Farage described Milei’s agenda as “amazing,” “incredible” and “like Thatcherism on steroids,” adding: “I’m beginning to think about buying Argentinian bonds.”

World.title: Putin signs off on 72-hour ceasefire with Kyiv as US envoys visit
World.content:
“This is due to the preparation and conduct of American contacts in Kyiv,” Peskov said. Witkoff and Kushner are expected to travel to the Ukrainian capital on Sunday.

Russian drone attacks on Ukrainian cities have intensified in recent weeks. Ukraine, meanwhile, has stepped up its hits on Russia’s oil infrastructure, in August reaching a monthly record for strikes since the start of the war in 2022.

Saturday’s pause order followed a broad Russian overnight attack across Ukraine that killed at least five people and injured six others, according to the Kyiv Independent.

“They were deliberate, for the first time in a long while,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram of the strikes targeting airports in Kyiv and Boryspil. “Clearly, Russia’s strikes on the airports are a reaction to discussions and preparations concerning the possibility of the American side using an aircraft to arrive in Ukraine.”

The U.S. emissaries are scheduled to meet with Putin later on Saturday.

World.title: UN backs effort to depict Africa correctly on maps despite US opposition
World.content:
Mercator, the world’s most commonly used map projection, was devised by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate using compass bearings. | iStock

The American delegation dismissed the resolution as part of a “much larger and more radical ideological project.”

The United Nations on Friday largely endorsed a resolution to promote maps that reflect the true scale of continents after an African-led campaign to move away from the ubiquitous 16th-century Mercator projection.

The United States was the only country to vote against the initiative, denouncing it as part of a “much larger and more radical ideological project” and urging “countries to instill common sense to this body.” Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine abstained.

Mercator, the world’s most commonly used map projection, was devised by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate using compass bearings.

World.title: Ein Spaziergang mit Sahra Wagenknecht
World.content:
Endspurt im Wahlkampf in Sachsen-Anhalt: Zwischen Plattenbauten in Halle-Neustadt steht für das Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW) weit mehr auf dem Spiel als nur der Einzug in den Landtag. Sahra Wagenknecht skizziert ein Klima der extremen Polarisierung, in dem ihre Partei von zwei Seiten unter Beschuss gerät. Fällt die Brandmauer, oder zwingt das BSW die etablierten Parteien in völlig neue Bündnisse?

Im Spannungsfeld zwischen der AfD um Ulrich Siegmund und den Altparteien kämpft das BSW um Sichtbarkeit und beklagt eine mediale Blockade. Wagenknecht zieht scharfe rote Linien zu Björn Höcke, fordert eine leistungsgerechte Aufstiegsgesellschaft und rechnet mit der Agenda-Politik von Gerhard Schröder ab. Was bedeutet der Begriff „links“ heute überhaupt noch, wenn die einstige Linkspartei ihr traditionelles Milieu verliert?

Neben landespolitischen Fragen geht es um die große geopolitische Linie, von der Kritik an teurem US-Gas bis zur Forderung nach mehr Diplomatie. Ein Spaziergang, der die strategischen Ziele des BSW offenlegt und in der Gordon Repinski mit Wagenknecht auch ihre persönliche Prägung zwischen DDR-Vergangenheit und dem Bruch mit ihrer alten Partei beleuchtet.

Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.
