World.title: The lonely crusader against Gianni Infantino
World.content:
That being said, it’s impossible now to bring back the Russian teams. Because of the way they are used, the national teams, it’s so hard to separate from the propaganda. But that is a failure, I’m not happy to say that it’s impossible; it’s sadly so, even though we are in 100 percent solidarity with Ukraine. It’s never good to make kids never play with each other. That is the aim, that they could play with each other and not be affected by the war. But that’s not possible now, football would stop and Ukraine would not play. So then we are there, and that’s a sad situation, but happening because of war.

When it comes to the Israel situation, we have always said, and we will always say, when you have a breach of FIFA statutes, it needs to be treated. It was delayed, delayed, delayed for many years, that they play with teams from [settlements in] Palestinian territories, which is not allowed by FIFA statutes. And then it’s politically very difficult, but legally not so difficult. So then you need sanctions, and then what the sanctions should be. You’ve got to look at precedents. Do you have any similar cases where you play in other people’s territories? What about Crimea? What about former Yugoslavia? Maybe you have some precedent. What’s the sanction? If it’s not changed, you increase the sanctions, because you need a rules-based system. And you need territory lines.

Klaveness at a press conference in Oslo on August 7, 2026. | Terje Bendiksby/NTB via Getty Images

When we played Israel, we gave the money to the victims of Gaza, not because we did not want to give to the victims of October 7th, but because there were ongoing attacks on the kids in Gaza, and they were poor, they needed the money.

In the end, it’s all about having bridges that are actually working when this is over, when people come to terms, you need to be effective bridges that speak to both sides. For us, we have had projects in Palestine for very many years, decades, educating girls and women there to be coaches; also in Jordan, in this area. So it’s an area [where] we know how difficult it is, how many good people live there on both sides. You know, in Israel, Jordan, everywhere. So we feel very connected to the region because of these projects.

Daria Zakharova contributed to this report.

World.title: Why Macron’s space summit risks blowing up on the launchpad
World.content:
Six participants with first-hand knowledge of the summit's organization described it to POLITICO as a poorly coordinated event with an unclear outcome. They were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.

“It’s falling behind schedule, it hasn’t really been coordinated with the major players in the European space sector, and it’s not entirely clear what its purpose is,” said a senior space expert involved in the summit’s preparation.

“And now that the White House has effectively decided to use it against Emmanuel Macron, it’s becoming even more awkward — it shows that, from a diplomatic standpoint, they didn’t do what they should have done,” they added.

Next week’s event aims to gather the international community — including leaders, large corporations, startups and researchers — to discuss issues including the regulation of space activities, competitiveness, security and defense, and space exploration.

Macron is keen to ensure that France and Europe remain credible space powers, with an independent launch capability and their own global satellite communications system, in an effort to reduce dependence on U.S. technology.

The French president's office insisted Friday that the absence of SpaceX and Blue Origin — two of the world's leading space companies — will have little impact on the summit.

World.title: Netanyahu calls Qatar ‘hostile state’ as Doha pushes back against Iran
World.content:
In an interview with Israel’s i24NEWS, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected claims that Qatar had influenced Israeli policy during the war in Gaza, calling it a “hostile state” but saying it had not dictated Israeli decisions.

 

“Qatar is a hostile state, but Qatar is not a state that dictated anything here,” Netanyahu said.

He also referred to Israel’s attack on Doha last year, saying: “I attacked Qatar — I also bombed it.”

The September 2025 strike targeted senior Hamas officials who were in Doha as part of negotiations over a US-backed Gaza ceasefire proposal.

Six people were killed, including a member of Qatar’s security forces, while Hamas said its senior negotiating team survived. Qatar condemned the attack as a violation of its sovereignty.

Later that month, Netanyahu apologised to Qatar during a call with US President Donald Trump and the Qatari prime minister, saying Israel would not carry out such an attack again.

Netanyahu made the latest comments while defending his government over the transfer of Qatari money to Gaza before the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel.

He said the funds were intended for humanitarian purposes and that the transfers had been recommended by Israeli security agencies.

Qatar has repeatedly denied financing Hamas, saying its aid went to Palestinians in Gaza through mechanisms known to Israel and the United States.

There was no immediate public response from Doha to Netanyahu’s latest remarks.

Qatar pushes back against Iran over attacks

The comments came as Qatar and Iran disputed accounts of Iranian missile and drone attacks on Qatari territory.

On Friday, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed Al Ansari accused Tehran of selectively using a Qatari security document to support its claim that Iranian attacks had mainly targeted US military facilities.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei had cited a Qatari security assessment prepared for the International Telecommunication Union, saying it showed that Iranian strikes were directed at US military sites and did not target civilian areas.

Baghaei said the document showed that almost all attacks had been aimed at US facilities, with the exception of a strike on gas facilities at Ras Laffan in March. He alleged that the facilities struck there had been supporting US military operations against Iran.

Al Ansari rejected that interpretation, saying Iran was quoting the document out of context.

“If the Iranian side wishes to reference official documentation, we invite it to refer to the record formally submitted by the State of Qatar to the United Nations,” he said.

He pointed to Qatari submissions to the UN that documented Iranian missiles flying over civilian, commercial and residential areas and said previous attacks had caused damage and injuries.

Al Ansari also rejected Iran’s description of the Ras Laffan attack as “alleged," saying the strike had been formally documented by Qatar.

“The State of Qatar is not a party to this conflict,” he said, adding that attacks on Qatari territory and civilian infrastructure could not be justified as legitimate responses.

Qatar also sent letters to the UN Secretary-General and the president of the Security Council on Friday rejecting Iran’s legal justification for attacks that began on 28 February.

Doha said Tehran remained responsible under international law and that Qatar retained the right to defend itself and seek compensation for the damage.

Qatar has said it will continue diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions in the region.

World.title: Germany's satellite rocket marks first successful launch from continental Europe
World.content:
The Spectrum launcher, developed by German company Isar Aerospace, has lifted off from the Andøya spaceport in Norway and placed its payload into low Earth orbit. This was the rocket’s second flight; the first, carried out in 2025, managed only to clear the launch pad for 30 seconds before crashing into the sea.

 

Spectrum is 28 metres tall and 2 metres in diameter. It is powered by ten engines, nine on the first stage and one on the second, and is designed to carry payloads of up to 1,000 kilograms to low Earth orbit (LEO).

Isar Aerospace’s Spectrum rocket being moved to the launch pad, 23 March 2026 ESA

Unlike the first flight, which carried no passengers, this mission, named "Onward and Upward", included six commercial and educational payloads, among them several CubeSats and an experiment designed to test new technologies in space and give European students practical, hands-on experience.

A milestone for the European Launcher Challenge

The Director General of the European Space Agency, Josef Aschbacher, described the launch as historic and hailed it as the first time a European competitor in the launcher sector has reached orbit. He said that Isar Aerospace, founded only eight years ago, has taken an important step towards a more diverse and autonomous European space sector.

The mission was supported by ESA’s Boost! programme, which funds commercial space transport initiatives. Isar Aerospace had already received backing through the agency’s Business Incubation Centre, and also won the first Microlauncher Competition organised by the German Space Agency (DLR), a contest that determined the selection of the payloads carried on this flight.

In 2025, Isar Aerospace was selected, along with other companies, to take part in the European Launcher Challenge, a programme that requires providers to achieve an orbital launch before 2027. With this flight, the company has become the first to reach that initial milestone of the programme.

Géraldine Naja, ESA’s Director of Space Transportation, stressed that this is the first European company to reach orbit with its own launch vehicle and congratulated the teams involved, while pointing to the expectation of seeing more launches from Andøya in the near future.

First successful launch of the Spectrum rocket with satellites from continental Europe, 5 September 2026 ESA

A fast-growing sector

Isar Aerospace’s success comes at a time of strong momentum for Europe’s microlauncher ecosystem, with companies such as Spain’s PLD Space also beginning to secure contracts under the same European Launcher Challenge.

At the end of August, ESA signed a 158.9 million-euro contract with the Alicante-based company to increase the launch rate of its MIURA 5 rocket, in a move designed to serve the same objective: reducing Europe’s dependence on foreign launchers to put satellites into orbit.

World.title: Berlin planning 'protective shield' to defend against sabotage, report says
World.content:
Germany is planning to develop a "protective shield" to combat sabotage attempts following an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport last month, Bild newspaper reported on Sunday.

 

Alexander Dobrindt, Germany's Interior Minister, told the outlet that Russian hybrid attacks had become a "daily reality" and would likely increase, but he said there were ways the country can defend itself.

Bild reported, citing information from the German Interior Ministry, that the new plan would see the creation of a "Cyberdome," a network of digital sensors that would help seek out and intercept hacking attempts.

The plan would also involve the expansion of the German police's mobile drone defence capabilities, with "rapidly deployable units" based in key cities such as Berlin, Munich and Hamburg to protect airspace above major transport centres.

The use of AI technology, such as facial recognition, would also be ramped up to help seek out potential attackers, while companies would be given the rights to detect drones and "actively defend against them," the report added.

The Leipzig/Halle Airport incident

It comes after the German government formally blamed Moscow for an attempted drone attack in Leipzig in August.

On 4 August, a drone carrying explosives was found at Leipzig/Halle Airport - a major cargo hub - forcing runway closures and flight diversions.

In a press conference on Tuesday, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul announced that Berlin would be taking action against Russia "as the perpetrator of the hybrid attack in Leipzig," with Russia's consulate in Bonn and its Berlin cultural centre to be closed.

"The Russian general consulate in Bonn will be closed by 18 September," he said, adding that there would also be tighter border controls for Russian nationals and increased pressure on Russia's shadow fleet.

The Russian embassy in Germany later issued a statement denying Berlin's claims and threatening "consequences" for the sanctions.

Sergey Nechayev, the Russian ambassador to Germany, "categorically rejected the accusations made by Berlin as unsubstantiated, absurd, and contrary to common sense," the statement said.

Referring to the German sanctions, it added: "He noted that the measures announced by the German side represent an unprecedented escalation in Russian-German relations and will not remain without consequences, for which the German government will bear full responsibility."

Speaking earlier this week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen expressed "full solidarity" with Germany over the attempted attack, which she said had used "military-grade material" and had been "carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil."

"If the intention was to make us think twice about supporting Ukraine, I can tell you it has only strengthened my resolve," she added.

World.title: Chainsaw maker STIHL chief calls for longer hours without extra pay
World.content:
The family entrepreneur from Waiblingen in southern Germany does not mince his words: "The German economy has been stuck in crisis mode for years. The prerequisite for overcoming the persistent weakness in growth is better framework conditions," Stihl said.

 

STIHL: €5.48bn in revenue and more than 20,000 employees

In 2025, STIHL generated €5.48 billion in revenue and employed 20,246 people worldwide. Founded by Andreas Stihl in 1926, the company is celebrating its 100th anniversary. Nikolas Stihl is the founder's grandson.

Head office in Waiblingen ANDREAS STIHL AG & Co. KG, Waiblingen

Family businessman Stihl takes a long-term view, and for him one thing is clear: "The situation of the German economy is serious, very serious. In the past eight years we have lost around 15 percent of our industrial output. Month after month Germany is losing around 15,000 industrial jobs."

The industrial base, he warns, is at risk of eroding – and with it prosperity and the welfare state. According to the company, STIHL has been the world's best-selling chainsaw brand since 1971. Nikolas Stihl acknowledges that "the US tariffs, China's aggressive industrial policy and geopolitical tensions" are also weighing on companies like his. But he argues that it is mainly home-grown problems holding firms back: "an overregulated economy, high energy costs, high labour costs, high taxes and a declining level of education and qualifications."

First STIHL one-man chainsaw with electric motor (c) Stihl

The Government's planned reforms fall short

The federal government’s planned reforms – covering statutory health insurance, pensions, taxes and the labour market – are good compromises, but they do not go far enough to pull Germany out of its structural crisis. If these compromises were now to be "unpicked", it would have devastating consequences for business confidence in politics, the entrepreneur warns.

Stihl says: "Now we need to muster all our strength for further reforms that will then generate tangible investment and growth impulses. For that, the governing coalition and the social partners must overcome their own reservations in order to live up to their responsibility towards Germany."

The next steps, he argues, should include cutting red tape, increasing the overall volume of work in the economy, reducing labour costs and creating additional incentives for research and development.

Germans need to work more to preserve prosperity

Stihl is calling for "high-quality public administration" with clear rules, streamlined and swift procedures, reasonable reporting requirements, and processes that are digital and supported by AI. "Accordingly, statutory reporting requirements should generally be abolished and retained only where their necessity is explicitly justified. If public authorities act much more as service providers for citizens and companies, that increases trust in Germany as a business location and in politics."

For Stihl, the key issue is increasing the volume of work – in other words, Germans need to work more again: "If we want to maintain our prosperity and keep social benefits at a high level, the total volume of work in the economy has to increase. A higher volume of work boosts economic output. In that sense, the debate about more work is a debate about preserving our prosperity, and by no means a debate about employees being lazy."

STIHL brand world in Waiblingen, Germany (c) Stihl

40-hour week without pay rises

Germany must use every available option to increase the volume of work: by incentivising overtime, extending working lives with fair exceptions for physically demanding jobs, making better use of the existing labour pool – including unemployed and part-time workers – and attracting skilled workers from abroad.

Stihl also calls for sick pay to be paid only from the second day of sickness and for phone-in sick notes to be abolished. Productivity gains from digitalisation and the growing use of AI will not offset the negative effects of demographic change.

From October 2026, collective bargaining talks in the metalworking and electrical industries are due to begin between trade unions and employers. Stihl warns: "We no longer have the productivity advantage over key competitors that used to justify our high labour costs. That is why I advocate increasing weekly working hours to 40, without any pay compensation.

Promoting AI, robotics, biotech, space and quantum technology

He acknowledges that he is asking a great deal of employees, but says he does not want to take anything away from anyone.

The aim, he insists, is to remain competitive, keep production in Germany and safeguard jobs. STIHL has production companies in eight countries, as well as 40 of its own sales and marketing subsidiaries and more than 50,000 specialist dealers worldwide.

Modern production with robots at STIHL in Waiblingen (c) Stihl

When it comes to non-wage labour costs – including contributions to pension, health, long-term care and unemployment insurance – he says a ceiling of 40% of gross wages is the maximum that can be accepted.

Stihl is also calling for more attractive conditions for innovative companies, including regulatory breathing space, greater tax incentives and wider access to venture capital. "Overall, innovation and the granting of approvals must be given an even higher priority than at present and must not be held back by bureaucracy."

Future-focused fields such as the industrial use of artificial intelligence, robotics, biotechnology, medical technology, space travel and quantum technologies should receive more targeted support.

'Germany has proved many times that it can reinvent itself'

The conclusion reached by the head of the world's leading chainsaw brand and a global technology company is clear: "We must not waste any more time, because only a high-performance and competitive business location can secure prosperity and a strong welfare state. Germany has proved many times that it can reinvent itself."

For the public to embrace the challenges ahead, "a ruthless stocktake of the current situation" is needed, followed by an overall plan setting out the changes people can expect. "The time has come to act with determination," says Nikolas Stihl.

World.title: Iranian forces target US naval drone attempting to enter Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
Iran said on Sunday that its forces had targeted a US naval drone as it attempted to enter the Strait of Hormuz, as tensions in the region escalate once again.

 

In a statement shared by state TV, the Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) said it had launched an attack on an "unmanned surface vessel" off the south coast of Iran as it was about to enter the strategic waterway.

“The aggressor United States must understand that it has no choice but to leave the region and stop its acts of mischief,” the statement read.

It comes after the IRGC said it had also carried out strikes on three oil tankers and three US-linked vessels in the Strait.

The force has also warned ships against attempts to navigate the passage - a crucial oil and gas transit chokepoint - through unapproved routes.

The incidents are the latest flashpoints in renewed confrontation between the two nations.

On Saturday, US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced that its forces had struck three Iranian oil tankers in response to what it said were ballistic missile strikes launched by the IRGC against two navy warships.

"Following Iran’s failed attacks, CENTCOM permanently disabled the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask," it said in a statement. "American forces also completely destroyed the unladen crude oil carrier M/T Kylo (also known as the “Noxen”) in the Gulf of Oman, striking the vessel in multiple critical locations to render it inoperable after the crew was directed to abandon ship".

"A U.S. aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer successfully evaded multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks. No American personnel were harmed," it added.

CENTCOM has also shared video footage on social media appearing to show the strikes.

The conflict reignited last Sunday after US forces targeted Iranian rocket launchers in the Strait of Hormuz.

The IRGC later confirmed strikes had hit Larak Island, before launching retaliatory attacks on US bases across the Middle East.

On Saturday, Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of CENTCOM, issued a warning to Tehran and its oil fleet in the wake of the strikes.

"Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost —taking out three of yours. We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet," he said.

World.title: Polls open in Saxony-Anhalt as AfD predicted to win state election
World.content:
On Sunday, polls opened in the German federal state of Saxony-Anhalt in a key regional vote.

 

More than 1.7 million voters have until 6 pm local time to cast their votes in an election seen as an important test for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's federal coalition.

According to opinion polls, the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, led by its top candidate Ulrich Siegmund, is well ahead of the CDU, polling at more than 40%.

A large AfD victory would pile more pressure onto Merz and his increasingly unpopular coalition.

The political atmosphere is intense. And the outcome is still uncertain: according to the ZDF Politbarometer, 26% of eligible voters surveyed shortly before the state election were still undecided.

AfD candidate Siegmund has announced that he would only govern if his party won an absolute majority. Whether the AfD manages to secure an outright majority of seats in the state parliament in Magdeburg will depend on how the smaller parties perform.

The more parties that cross the 5% threshold and enter the state parliament in Magdeburg, the smaller the AfD’s chances of an absolute majority of MPs become.

That is why various groups have called on voters to vote tactically. The AfD, the CDU, the Left, the SPD, the FDP and the BSW have criticised the tactical voting campaign, with only the Greens backing it.

The CDU has ruled out forming a coalition with the AfD. However, Merz's party could work with other parties. At the same time, the CDU has also ruled out cooperation with the Left party by adopting an incompatibility clause at a party conference.

Polling stations in Saxony-Anhalt are open from 8 am to 6 pm.

World.title: US peace envoys arrive in Kyiv visit after talks with Putin
World.content:
US peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrive in Kyiv on Sunday for their first visit to the Ukrainian capital, a day after holding talks with Russia’s Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin on ending more than four years of war, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

 

A White House official told the AFP news agency that the duo had met with Putin to "advance President Trump's agenda of peace in the Russia-Ukraine War."

"The two sides discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks, and look forward to equally productive meetings tomorrow in Ukraine," they said.

Yuri Ushakov, a Kremlin aide, called the talks "extremely frank" and said that the US side had "put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement."

He added that the Russians had told the Americans that Moscow was "confident" it could seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had also spoken with Witkoff and Kushner on Saturday and reaffirmed Kyiv's commitment to pausing strikes during their visit.

"From the moment of this conversation, we are ready to observe a ceasefire in airstrikes against the cities involved in the negotiation process," he wrote in a post on social media. "From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv".

Putin has ordered his forces to halt strikes on Kyiv for three days while the envoys make their trip, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told the Russian news agency Interfax. The pause was in place from midnight Saturday, he said.

US President Donald Trump told reporters on Friday that Witkoff and Kushner would be bringing a "proposal to end the war" to Kyiv and Moscow.

"I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, two great negotiators. They've done a great job, and we sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done," he said. "And there may be a good chance that we'll do it".

Zelenskyy said on Saturday that the Ukrainian plan for discussions with the envoys had been approved and that Kyiv was ready for a "substantive conversation."

World.title: Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade
World.content:
Turkey is racing to restore safe passage for cargo ships in the Black Sea as attacks on shipping disrupt grain exports and push up prices. Russia and Ukraine are major global wheat exporters, but Black Sea trade has been severely disrupted as both sides step up attacks on shipping and port infrastructure.

Advertising

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan announced this week that Turkey was working on a plan to ensure safe passage in the Black Sea for commercial shipping and said he was in touch with both Ukraine and Russia.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan confirmed that he raised the issue with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, on the sidelines of a gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan.

The Turkish move comes as Ukraine and Russia have ramped up their attacks on shipping and ports in and around the Black Sea. In 2022, Turkey and the United Nations brokered a deal between Ukraine and Russia to ensure safe passage for Ukrainian grain exports through the Black Sea.

The agreement lasted a year.

While Turkey has maintained good ties with both sides, reaching another agreement will be much harder, warned international relations professor Huseyin Bagci of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University.

“The tension is increasing more than ever before,” Bagci said. “It's not enough to have good relations, because the two sides – the Ukrainians and Russians – should sit down and talk about a common solution to this problem. Turkey cannot solve this problem alone.”

What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey

Growing attacks

In August Ukraine offered a ceasefire on commercial shipping, but the offer was rejected by Moscow, which said it wanted a broader deal. Ukrainian drones continue to strike Russian shipping, while Russia has continued missile attacks on Ukrainian ports and ships.

This surge in attacks comes as both nations rush to export their grain harvests.

Grain prices have risen sharply, by as much as 30 percent, international grain broker Can Atbasoglu said, even as both sides scramble to find new routes for their exports.

“Russia will do their best to export as much as they can, both from Russian Baltic ports and EU Baltic ports like Latvia and Lithuania; they're also exporting,” Atbasoglu said.

“Ukraine will also export as much as they can from Romania as well and through the Danube ports. But the export pace will be definitely lower. So it will definitely stay bullish for the markets. Prices are definitely going to stay like this or can have a further increase.”

Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea

Ships staying put

At one of Istanbul's many shipyards, the docks are crowded with ships that once braved the Black Sea. One vessel bears the scars of a drone attack and is under repair. Others undergo routine maintenance as shipowners hesitate to risk new journeys into dangerous waters.

The superintendent of one ship, speaking anonymously, says repairs are nearly finished, but uncertainty clouds the future.

“We wanted to take the ship out to the Black Sea before entering the shipyard, but because of that risk, we didn’t enter the Black Sea and didn’t take on any cargo. We’ve been in the shipyard for 50 days for repairs, but we don’t know what will happen once the repairs are finished,” the superintendent said.

Turkish shipowners warn that many are on the brink of bankruptcy, as idle ships rack up costs of up to 50,000 euros a month in mooring and crew expenses.

Ziya Ustel, CEO of Turkish shipping company VI-ZA STAR, says high freight rates are being offered for Black Sea routes, but the risks are too great.

“They are offering high freight rates, etc,” Ustel said.

Without a diplomatic solution, few shipowners will be prepared to risk their vessels, Ustel warned.

“The main thing is to find out a real solution,” Ustel added. “Otherwise, no one will try anything anymore.”

Turkish diplomacy

Ankara is expected to step up its efforts to find a solution.

Grain brokers say hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough may be one reason prices have so far remained below the record highs seen at the start of the war.

But if Turkish efforts fail and attacks on Black Sea shipping continue, higher grain prices could have a considerable impact, especially on the world’s poorest nations, many of which depend on Russian and Ukrainian grain.

World.title: India news: Rahul Gandhi backs student protests in Maharashtra
World.content:
Published 09/06/2026 Published September 6, 2026 Congress' Rahul Gandhi says Maharashtra student protest reflects 'shattered' trust in system

In recent days, several parts of Maharashtra also witnessed a protest by tribal students — including a hunger strike Image: ANI/IMAGO

India's main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi has voiced support for students protesting in Maharashtra against alleged irregularities in a state-level recruitment examination.

"Thousands of students are on the streets, protesting peacefully — the reason isn't just one exam or recruitment, but a trust that's been shattered by the entire system," Gandhi said in a statement on X as he called on the government to listen to the protesters' demands and act.

"Otherwise, this echo of the students will only grow louder until justice is served," the senior Congress party leader said.

Why are the Maharashtra student demonstrations about?

Gandhi's remarks come as the Maharashtra government initiated a probe into an alleged paper leak of the Maharashtra Public Service Commission's (MPSC) Food and Drug Administration examination for Drug Inspector posts.

The offline exam was held on March 22, following which there were complaints that some candidates had allegedly received the question paper or questions beforehand.

Aspirants said that their complaints were not looked into. The recruitment process was completed and the MPSC published a merit list of 488 candidates.

However, the commission later canceled the recruitment process and in a statement cited a police inquiry which prima facie indicated that a candidate had got hold of the question paper before the exam and benefited from it.

On Saturday, the Maharashtra government also constituted a high-level committee to take full stock of the existing recruitment exam system in the country's second-most populous state.

The committee is tasked with suggesting measures to make the screening process more transparent, secure, reliable and candidate-friendly.

Tribal students' protest

In recent days, several parts of Maharashtra also witnessed a protest by tribal students — including a hunger strike — over poor conditions in student hostels, student safety and recruitment to some 12,500 vacant posts reserved for tribal communities.

The protesters' demands were accepted by the Maharashtra government, leading to the hunger strike being withdrawn.

On Sunday, Rahul Gandhi railed against the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which leads the government in Maharashtra.

"Whether it's the central or state government, every student is tormented by the BJP regime," he alleged.

"Paper leaks, stalled recruitments, the unbearable cost of education, inhumane conditions in hostels, food like poison ...and now, they've seized control of a constitutional body like MPSC and destroyed its credibility," Gandhi, who is the leader of opposition in the lower house of the Indian parliament, said.

Education minister concedes to 'Cockroach' demands, resigns To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The protests in Maharashtra come after a massive Gen Z-led protest demanding an overhaul of India's examination system, rocked the country in July. The demonstrations marked one of the biggest public challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's three-term rule and culminated with the resignation of the then education minister.

World.title: Germany, Kosovo unite against ticks carrying deadly virus
World.content:
Germany has high-security labs while Kosovo has Hyalomma ticks and experience with the deadly Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever. Working together, German and Kosovar scientists are fighting the disease and its vectors.

It can spot its prey from up to 200 meters (about 650 feet) away — but unlike many of its fellow species, it doesn't lurk in the grass waiting for its victim to come closer. Instead it runs after it, chasing animals and humans alike.

The Hyalomma tick, often called "the great hunting tick," was previously found mostly in Africa, Asia, and southern Europe. But climate change means it can now survive further north and it has already been spotted in Germany and various Eastern European countries. Kosovo, in southeastern Europe, has been a hot spot for the tick for some time now.

The Hyalomma tick is also a vector of the highly pathogenic virus for Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a potentially deadly disease with a high fatality rate. Symptoms of the disease are comparable to those of Ebola fever or the Marburg virus. These are capable of destroying blood and lymphatic vessels, which can lead to internal bleeding and death.

Ticks are spreading To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Kurtesh Sherifi first read about Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever in the newspaper in 2005, when he was completing his studies as a veterinarian in Berlin. The article said that 11 people in his homeland, Kosovo, had contracted the disease and five had died. He was already interested in pathogens that can be transmitted between animals and humans, known as zoonoses, and Crimean-Congo fever intrigued him.

Back home, Sherifi started work with the faculty of agriculture and veterinary medicine at the University of Pristina. But the budget for research was tight. Kosovo, a small country with only about 1.6 million citizens, didn't have a high-security laboratory or the equipment necessary for investigating the Crimean-Congo fever virus.

Seeking German cooperation

Sherifi got in touch with Germany's largest institution for study in this area, the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg.

One of the researchers was Petra Emmerich, a virologist and expert on what are known as Risk Group 4 viruses — viruses that cause severe, often fatal, diseases and usually have no widely available treatment. The Crimean-Congo virus is in that risk group.

Emmerich also acts as a reservist in the German military, which is especially interested in viruses that could be used as biological weapons. She was sent to Kosovo in 2009, which is when she met Sherifi.

While the much smaller common longhorn beetle (left) waits for a suitable victim to pass by, the Hyalomma tick prefers to go hunting Image: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

A lively exchange began between the researchers. In Kosovo, a structure was established to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma tick and the virus. In 2013, the researchers' joint work began to receive funding through the German Biosecurity Program, run by the country's Foreign Ministry and "intended to help partner countries tackle biological threats."

"It's give and take," said Emmerich of the scientific partnership. "We have the diagnostic expertise and the necessary resources but we don't have the patients." Doctors from Germany regularly come to Kosovo with Emmerich where they can exchange information with their counterparts there.

Raising public awareness is another important pillar of the Germany-Kosovo cooperation.

Farmers in Kosovo are particularly susceptible to infection — and not solely due to ticks biting them, but because they often use their bare hands to remove ticks from animals. If infected blood from the animals gets into a small wound on the human hand, the virus can be transmitted to the human.

"This is quite likely how a large proportion of the [infected] population in Kosovo got infected," Sherifi explained.

Patients require intensive care, isolation

He and Emmerich have visited schools to educate students about the dangers of the virus and how to protect against it. For example, certain tick repellents help, as do long pants and sturdy shoes.

Not all Hyalomma ticks carry the virus, and most people who are bitten by a Hyalomma tick do not become ill. However, the larger problem is that there is neither a vaccine nor any specific course of treatment for those who do end up suffering from Crimean-Congo fever.

Farmers in Kosovo are at particular risk from the Hyalomma ticks Image: Idro Seferi

"If you do get sick, it's particularly severe," Emmerich explained. The disease begins with nonspecific, flu-like symptoms including fever, chills, aches and headaches. In severe cases, a patient will begin bleeding from the skin, nose and gums and may also experience gastrointestinal bleeding. The worst causes can result in organ failure.

Patients require intensive care and isolation because they are highly contagious.

Much of the treatment in intensive care focuses on maintaining a patient's vital functions, but they are also given the antiviral drug, ribavirin. But, as Emmerich said, "ribavirin is not all that effective in acutely ill patients." That is something the scientists have seen firsthand with cases in Kosovo.

The best answer is prevention, which is why it's also very important for the researchers to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma ticks and for them to recommend avoiding certain areas where the ticks are prevalent, if possible.

Successful tick tactics

Over the years, the researchers have not only collected thousands of the ticks but they have also conducted so-called seroprevalence studies. These use blood tests to find antibodies from past infections. This allows the scientists to determine whether humans or animals have come in contact with the virus.

Farm animals are particularly suitable for this type of study, Sherifi said, as the virus doesn't affect them. And unlike wild animals and humans, they usually remain in a clearly defined area. That means that if antibodies are detected in the blood of these animals, it's clear the virus is circulating in that area.

In Kosovo, the number of serious infections has dropped drastically in the past decade, amounting to just five cases in total. In the previous decade, there were about 100 cases. Sherifi and Emmerich believe this indicates how successful their work has been.

Of course, that doesn't mean the ticks and the virus won't spread further in Europe, and the researchers both expect this to happen.

Hyalomma ticks with the Crimean-Congo virus have just been detected in France although, so far, no humans have been infected there.

"Over the past 13 years, Hyalomma ticks have spread geographically," said Emmerich. "As a virologist, that's something to think about, and it needs to be closely monitored."

This is why it's important for the German and Kosovar scientists to pass on what they've learned to countries that haven't yet had as much experience monitoring the Hyalomma ticks, such as Macedonia and Albania.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Germany plans anti-drone shield after Leipzig attack: report
World.content:
Several German cities will receive rapidly deployable units capable of defending against drone strikes on critical infrastructure, Bild am Sonntag newspaper reported.

Germany is planning a comprehensive protective shield to prevent attacks like the failed assault on Leipzig airport, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Sunday.

On August 4, several small drones targeted Leipzig-Halle Airport in eastern Germany, with one hitting a parked plane, while another is thought to have struck an inbound cargo jet.

German intelligence agencies blamed Russia for the incident, which Moscow has denied.

Leipzig-Halle Airport is a major cargo hub used to fly weapons and supplies toward Ukraine Image: Daniel Kessler/imageBROKER/picture alliance

What did Dobrindt say about the shield?

Dobrindt told Bild am Sonntag newspaper that Russia's hybrid attacks are now a "daily" reality, adding: "These attacks will increase, but we can defend ourselves and protect ourselves."

Bild cited information from the Interior Ministry showing the government plans to expand the federal police's mobile drone-defense units.

The measures include vehicles and helicopters that can be quickly deployed to protect airspace over key cities like Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin to counter drone attacks.

Putin denies Russian involvement in Leipzig drone attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bild said the shield would not only intercept drones, but could also defuse drone bombs and other explosive devices.

The newspaper described how a change in the law would allow critical infrastructure operators — including water, power and defense companies — to detect and defend against drone sabotage.

Jammers flood drones with radio noise, so its pilot can no longer steer it Image: Michael Bihlmayer/Bihlmayerfotografie/IMAGO

New tech planned to boost cyber security

Bild also described how a national protective cyber shield would be set up to detect and intercept hacking attacks.

The measure comes amid hundreds of cyberattacks on government departments, infrastructure and companies each day, many of them blamed on Russia, other states and criminal gangs.

The newspaper said the government ⁠also wants to increase the use of AI, biometric facial recognition ⁠and video surveillance, especially at transport hubs, to identify suspected attackers before they carry out attacks.

Over 1,000 drone sightings in 2025

The head of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), Holger Münch, told Bild in December that more than a thousand suspicious drone flights were recorded over Germany last year.

These incidents mostly targeted military sites, airports, ports and defense firms and were treated as surveillance or harassment, rather than attacks.

Leipzig airport has been targeted by sabotage before. In July 2024, a suspected Russian incendiary parcel caught fire at the airport's DHL hub.

The cargo hub is also utilized by the Ukrainian military and NATO to airlift arms for use in the Ukrainian defense against Russia's invasion.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

World.title: How climate change and food insecurity could fuel future conflicts
World.content:
Climate change, conflict, and trade tensions are putting pressure on the global food system. New research suggests the biggest risk is not food shortages, but whether societies can peacefully adapt to change.

The world's food system is under growing stress, and new research is pointing to areas where this could lead to conflict.

Severe droughts and extreme weather are damaging harvests in many regions. A developing El Niño event is even threatening to worsen food shortages for millions of people next year. At the same time, wars and geopolitical tensions are disrupting supply chains that keep food and farm supplies moving.

The war in Ukraine has repeatedly shaken grain markets, while the Iran war's impact on the Strait of Hormuz has driven up fuel and fertilizer prices, increasing costs for farmers everywhere.

Experts have long warned that rising food insecurity could fuel instability. When people can no longer feed their families, they argue over land, water, and other resources — or they move. In fragile countries, these pressures can contribute to social unrest and even armed conflict.

Now, new research has suggested where some of these risks are greatest. The Climate-Driven Agricultural Decline Index (CADI) , developed by Hannes Mueller and his colleagues, maps how climate change is reshaping agricultural productivity around the world. "The heaviest losses are in the tropical regions," said Mueller, a researcher at the Institute for Economic Analysis and the Barcelona School of Economics.

Climate change is already reducing food production in many parts of the world. Hundreds of millions of people live in areas where harvests are smaller than 30 years ago. Mueller mentioned Cambodia, Bangladesh, Burundi, Nigeria, Paraguayand El Salvador as countries where agricultural losses are already being felt.

"Northern Africa is another region we should pay much more attention to. If you look at the map, it just looks terrible. It really looks horrible," he said.

Burundi's vanishing lakes and the fight to bring them back To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

And climate change is only one part of the story. Wars, trade disruptions, export bans, and rising fertilizer costs can magnify food insecurity.

Within the next 25 years, nearly half of the world's people could be living in areas where farms are producing less food.

New winners, losers, and conflicts

These pressures can undermine governments, help causemigration, and make it easier for armed groups to recruit fighters. In societies that are already unstable, such factors can push them toward crisis.

Yet CADI's research points to a surprising reality: Gains in agricultural productivity also appear to increase the risk of violence. Mueller said the key issue is not just scarcity, but change. The climate crisis and other shocks do not simply make some regions poorer. They also create new opportunities, changing the value of land and resources.

In some places, land that had been marginal becomes more productive and more valuable. And that attracts investors and produces competition for ownership and access.

So countries that appear to benefit overall may face new tensions. Sudan, for example, is projected to produce more food as the climate changes. But while some areas could become more productive, others may suffer losses, creating new winners and losers within the country and increasing the risk of conflict.

This looming instability, Mueller said, also applies to areas where the change in productivity hasn't even happened yet. "If we know that your land is going to become more productive, maybe I want to grab it from you today. That is exactly where negotiations break down and where we will have violence," he said.

Even in stable, wealthy regions, the climate crisis is creating future problems. It may seem trivial, but the change in grape-growing options in Europe is affecting local farmers. Major producers of sparkling wine have started to buy up land in mountainous regions.

"It is not productive yet, but they already know where future grape harvests will be," Mueller said. "Big agricultural companies are buying land. This is happening all over the world. Locals are displaced because large producers come in, land prices rise, and you start having fights about something that is still 20 or 30 years in the future."

How climate change is reshaping the world's wine map To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

One of the CADI team's most striking findings is that agricultural change is more likely to lead to conflict in non-democracies. When climate shocks, food insecurity, and competition over resources hit democracies, they tend to have institutions that force competing interests to negotiate rather than fight.

"Democracies may look annoying and cumbersome. Nothing moves as fast as people want. But this is a great thing because it makes people talk to each other," Mueller said. "There is a platform for negotiation. There are institutions that help people negotiate. That process of constantly finding solutions is at the heart of what prevents conflict."

South Asia as a warning sign

"We do not pay enough attention to the threats to the source of our livelihoods," said Abdullah Fahimi of the think tank German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP). "These threats can trigger major crises and displace millions and millions of people. The regions we should watch most closely are South Asia and the Sahel, where climate vulnerability and rapid population growth mean the number of people affected could rise dramatically."

As India counts its population, researchers warn that climate change could make it harder for parts of the country to produce enough food for a growing number of people Image: Diptendu Dutta/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Fahimi said South Asia stands out because it depends on both vulnerable water supplies and global food markets. Food prices have already risen significantly over the past decades. "South Asia, with a population of around 2 billion, is highly dependent on imports," he added. Those imports include wheat, maize, and palm oil from countries including Russia, Ukraine, Canada, and Malaysia.

At the same time, local agriculture is increasingly threatened by heat waves, floods, declining land productivity, and saltwater intrusion from rising sea levels.

As well as the immediate human toll, events such as the devastating floods that struck Nepal in August 2026 offer a glimpse of the long-term challenges that could become more common in the future. "The Himalayas and the Hindu Kush mountain ranges supply most of the water for agriculture and drinking water in the region," Fahimi said. "Because of climate change, the glaciers and snow are melting very fast."

In the short term, meltwater could increase water availability. But later in the century, he warned, the region could face "a huge humanitarian crisis that could affect around 2 billion people."

Farmland was covered in mud after severe flooding along Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River in late August Image: Ambir Tolang/NurPhoto/picture alliance

As food insecurity deepens, the social and political consequences can multiply. "When resource scarcities or the impacts of climate change force people to look for other livelihood opportunities, sometimes they end up being hired by terrorist groups," said Fahimi, who cited examples from Nigeria and Afghanistan.

In other cases, public frustration is directed at governments if they fail to mitigate the effects on people's livelihoods. Their legitimacy is questioned, and this can escalate into violent conflict.

That echoes Mueller's broader conclusion. Climate change, wars, and trade disruptions do not automatically lead to conflict. But climate adaptation cannot just be about growing different crops or using new technologies. People and societies also need to adapt to changes in who has access to land, water and jobs.

The key question is whether societies have institutions that can manage these changes. Where governments, courts, and local institutions can help communities negotiate new realities, shocks may be absorbed. Where those institutions are weak, the pressure on food systems may become a pressure on peace itself.

Edited by: Hannah Cleaver

Graphics: Olof Pock

World.title: Indonesia: Flights canceled as Anak Krakatau volcano erupts
World.content:
The spread of ash after the volcanic eruption of Anak Krakatau has impacted thousands of passengers, as flights were canceled at Jakarta's international airport.

Hundreds of flights were canceled at Jakarta's international airport after Indonesia's Anak Krakatau volcano erupted early Sunday morning, more than 150 kilometers (93 miles) away.

The volcano produced a fountain of lava and loud sounds heard up to 700 kilometers away, Indonesia's geological agency said in a statement.

The cloud of ash was detected up to a height of 6,000 meters (20,000 feet) on the Java side of the volcano and a plume of up to 15,000 meters on the ‌Sumatra side and some parts of Banten province in Java, the ‌meteorological ​agency BMKG posted on its website.

No incidents of casualties were reported, and no evacuation orders were issued.

Danger remains in Indonesia in the wake of volcano eruptions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The closest township is more than 16 kilometers away, but the authorities warned residents and visitors to stay at least 3 kilometers from the volcano's active crater.

Two new eruptions were recorded on Sunday, the volcanology agency warned.

Indonesia cancels flights

The ash spread across parts of the capital Jakarta and Lampung province on the southern tip of Sumatra island, Indonesia's Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said.

Authorities have suspended operations at six airports following eruptions from Mount Anak Krakatoa, the ministry said.

"The Husein Sastranegara Airport in Bandung showed indications of being affected. Consequently, we have declared... the airport closed to flights," Dudy Purwagandhi told a press conference Sunday, mentioning the latest airport to be shuttered.

Operations at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, the country's largest and in the capital, Jakarta, were suspended earlier.

Soekarno-Hatta International Airport posted on ‌Instagram that it had ⁠suspended ⁠flight operations until 9:30 a.m. (0230 GMT) due to volcanic ash.

New volcano eruptions hit Indonesia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Due to increased activity from the Mount Anak Krakatau eruption, Soekarno-Hatta International Airport has temporarily suspended flight operations from 5:30 a.m. to 9.30 a.m.," the airport said.

The disruption of flight operations has impacted more than 22,000 passengers, the transport ministry said in a statement, adding that 209 flights were affected, particularly to and from Singapore.

Anak Krakatau lies in the middle between Java and Sumatra in Indonesia's vast island chain, which sits on the Pacific "Ring of Fire," where earthquakes and volcanic eruptions are frequent.

Anak Krakatau means "Child of Krakatau." The volcano is the offspring of the famous Krakatau, whose monumental eruption in 1883 triggered a period of global cooling.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

World.title: Saxony-Anhalt: Far-right AfD eyes power in German state vote
World.content:
Skip next section Saxony-Anhalt morning turnout sharply higher than in 2021

09/06/2026 September 6, 2026 Saxony-Anhalt morning turnout sharply higher than in 2021

Voter turnout in Saxony-Anhalt's state election was markedly higher by midday than at the same point five years ago.

By that time, 34.7% of eligible voters had cast their ballots at polling stations, according to the state returning officer. At the same time in the 2021 election, turnout stood at 22.4%.

Final turnout in 2021 was 60.3%, including postal votes.

The sharply higher midday turnout points to strong voter mobilization, but it is too early to say which parties are benefiting,

Nearly 1.7 million people aged 18 and over are eligible to vote in Sunday's election.

The state's 2,130 polling stations remain open until 6 p.m., and postal ballots can also be submitted until then.

The state returning officer said voting had proceeded smoothly during the morning, with no unusually long waiting times reported.

World.title: Ebola: Why children are last to be treated in medical crises
World.content:
In the latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, children are more likely to die than adults. But it's not always due to the disease. Specific medicines for younger people are often harder to come by.

The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been devastating. Since the outbreak began in mid-May, more than 3,000 people have died.

Almost half of people infected with Ebola are expected to die, and the mortality rate is particularly high for young children. According to a commentary by Doctors Without Borders recently published in medical journal The Lancet , the mortality rate for children under the age of 5 is over 60%.

But often, it's because of a lack of medication and information on how to use it with young patients, rather than then disease itself.

"Children must be centered in Ebola treatment and prevention research," the aid organization wrote in early September .

At the heart of the debate is the EBO-PEP study, which began mid-July. The study looks at an experimental antiviral drug called obeldesivir, which is being studied for its ability to protect people exposed to the Bundibugyo Ebola virus, the strain responsible for the current deadly outbreak.

But children weighing less than 30 kilograms (about 66 pounds) and around 12 years old or younger, were not included in the original study. But that could change soon with protocols to include children weighing over 20 kilograms.

Children under the age of 5 are significantly more likely to die from Ebola fever than adults Image: Benediction Murhabazi/AFP

Children weighing less than 20 kilograms — that is, roughly 6 years old or younger — won't be included in the treatment. There is an alternative treatment for them: Another antiviral drug, remdesivir, given intravenously. But as Doctors Without Borders argued, a 10-day course of infusions is difficult to administer during an outbreak, especially for young children.

According to Neal Russell, a pediatric doctor based in London who consults for Doctors Without Borders and who was also the lead author of the Lancet commentary, young children are at particularly high risk from Ebola. This could be due to their weakened immune systems, underlying health conditions, or the fact that treating them for Ebola is especially challenging in an outbreak.

For example, children are often harder to diagnose than adults because early symptoms resemble other illnesses, and young children often find it difficult to describe their symptoms accurately. Other issues include the fact that children cannot always be accompanied into an Ebola treatment center by their parents or caregivers, something that is especially important in their recovery. Younger Ebola patients also require closer monitoring and specially trained staff.

Ebola outbreak in DR Congo outpaces efforts to contain it To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ebola in Berlin

In May, an American doctor was treated at Berlin's Charite hospital after contracting the Bundibugyo Ebola virus while caring for patients. His wife and their four children were also considered at high risk. The medical team in Germany decided to treat the family prophylactically with an experimental antibody drug called MBP134.

"Of course, a careful risk benefit assessment had to be carried out," said Han Ngoc Le, a doctor at the hospital who was involved in the treatments.

The available data about the drug's impact on children was very limited. But at the same time, the children were at high risk of catching Ebola after close contact with their sick father.

In the end, all the family remained healthy and no apparent side effects were seen. It's unclear whether the experimental treatment prevented infection in the children. Such a small sample can't be mapped onto the larger population either.

But the test was valuable nonetheless. "The mere fact that the antibody was so well tolerated even in 1-year-olds and children under 12 is a valuable finding upon which future studies can build," Le said.

Why do such gaps in knowledge exist?

Le explained that, from a medical perspective, children cannot simply be thought of as "small adults."

Their metabolisms function differently, they react differently to medications, their pharmacokinetics — what a body does with a drug — are simply different. The same sort of cautions also apply to pregnant women.

That's why dosages of medication can't simply be transferred from adults to children. It's also why any new medications require separate studies so that specific dosages can be determined and potentially special formulations can be developed. Children might require kid-friendly syrups instead of adult-size tablets, for example.

DR Congo launches Ebola trial for high-risk contacts To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"All of this creates extra costs," said Marc Biot, access coordinator for Europe at Doctors Without Borders, who works to ensure people in need can get affordable, good-quality medical products. He said research institutions and pharmaceutical companies often see investing extra in pediatric studies as a lower priority.

"It is faster and it can be cheaper if you only focus on adults," said Biot — which is why treating children and pregnant women usually only becomes part of the research at a later stage of drug development. "That is our plea — a plea not only to the scientists, to the pharmaceutical companies, but also to those who fund and allow trials to happen — to allow that to happen on the same speed for adults as for children and pregnant women."

Biot said it's sad to see that pressure is needed to make it happen. "Whenever you start a clinical trial, you also should include pregnant woman or children," he argued.

A difficult balance

None of this is new. In 2020, the Global Accelerator for Pediatric Formulations network was founded — supported by the World Health Organization(WHO) — to accelerate the development and availability of child-friendly medicine worldwide.

This isn't an issue limited to Ebola. Russell pointed to the 2024 mpox epidemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where children made up a large proportion of those infected or killed.

Although a vaccine existed for mpox, it wasn't made for children. The WHO advised it be used "off label" for minors, but they tended to get it a lot later than adults anyway. Experts say they've observed similar patterns with other diseases including HIV, tuberculosis, and during the COVID-19 pandemic.

When it comes to the development of medicines and vaccines, the first samples are often made for adult patients Image: Thomas Lohnes/AFP/Getty Images

"When you're doing a research study, which is not in an emergency, [it makes sense] to protect children and pregnant women from any potential harm of an investigational product," said Russell. "But when you're in an emergency, the balance between protecting those people from any potential harm from research, and protecting them from the very fatal disease, changes."

Berlin-based doctor Le believes children and pregnant women should be considered right from the beginning of any new clinical trials. "They shouldn't be excluded from participation just like that," she said. "Instead, sub-studies or parallel studies should be set up from the outset."

Russell calls for a similar approach. He wants to see all people benefit equally from scientific progress during a health crisis — especially in a health emergency, when the most vulnerable should not be the last to benefit from that progress.

"No matter who you are, you should have the same opportunity to have access to these medical products," he said.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Hungary begins hunt for corrupt regime's billions
World.content:
Hungary's new prime minister promised he would recover billions stolen or diverted by the previous administration. A new "super authority" is about to begin that work. Its success or failure will have a big impact.

Asset recovery — it sounds bureaucratic but behind this phrase is one of the most important campaign promises made by Hungary's new government.

Hungary's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, and his Tisza party want to retrieve funds and assets that went — in some dubious ways — to the family of ousted Hungarian leader Viktor Orban or his allies, various oligarchs, or frontmen. The new government wants those funds back for state use, and it also plans to hold the beneficiaries accountable under law.

Billions of euros were stolen or diverted and, if social media is to be believed, many Hungarians want to see the individuals responsible behind bars. Magyar has talked of a sum of around €60 billion ($70 billion), though other estimates suggest the real amount could be three times that much.

Orban, allies lived lives of luxury

Observers say the success or failure of the asset recovery will almost certainly influence the future of Magyar and the Tisza party.

The huge sums of money are linked to images of decadent luxury under Orban. The former Hungarian prime minister's family, party members, and friendly oligarchs lived on luxury estates, flew in luxury jets, vacationed on luxury yachts, and repeatedly won billions worth of public contracts.

Orban-affiliated entrepreneurs, artists, academics, and journalists were also generously supported with public funds for years. Often their main qualification was loyalty to the former prime minister.

Former Prime Minister Viktor Orban has alleged that his successor has 'dismantled the rule of law' since coming to power Image: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Those lifestyles contrasted with the lives led by Hungarians in poverty, the image of neglected public infrastructure, poor conditions in schools and hospitals, and the exodus of many young Hungarians from the country, as well as a huge deficit in the state budget, some 7.5% of Hungary's national income. These contrasts explain why there is such a popular desire for justice.

It's been almost four months since the new Magyar government took office and anti-corruption actions have officially started.

At the end of July, the new government established the National Asset Recovery Authority, or NVVH — a sort of "super institution" with very broad powers and independence.

Hungary hasn't had an authority like this in its modern history. The way state assets were privatized in the 1990s after communist rule was problematic, as it often was elsewhere in the former Soviet bloc. When Orban first came to power in 2010, there was a half-hearted attempt to address the corruption of the previous government under Ferenc Gyurcsany, but it came to nothing.

Hungary new PM lifts lid on Orban-era government luxury To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This time, things are meant to be different.

The NVVH will investigate where public funds flowed and how assets like real estate were used. Although no specific date has been set, the investigations will primarily focus on the Orban government's time in power, so dating back to 2010. The authority is also meant to make sure this cannot happen again, and will look into how public funds and assets are to be used in future.

The NVVH has both policing and prosecutorial powers, so it can investigate cases and bring charges. The authority is accountable to Hungary's parliament.

Controversy around new anti-corruption body

But the creation of the NVVH has not been without controversy.

Late last week, parliament appointed Anna Unger, 46, a political scientist at Eotvos Lorand University in Budapest, to head the new anti-corruption and asset recovery body. Unger is an expert on political systems, democratic institutions, and party financing and was chosen out of almost 100 other applicants in a process with several stages.

Some were surprised at Unger's appointment, as she wasn't really a public figure. Her research has included political corruption but she's not a recognized expert on the topic, nor is she a lawyer. Observers had expected a lawyer or an anti-corruption expert to get the job, somebody like Miklos Ligeti, head of legal affairs at Transparency International Hungary since 2012.

Anna Unger was named head of the new accountability organization in late August Image: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP

Ligeti also applied for the job but is reportedly being considered for a position as a deputy director. Unger will have four deputies with different duties and responsibilities. Katalin Tasnady, a well-known prosecutor with around two decades of criminal law experience, was made the NVVH's deputy chief of investigations.

Government representatives said Unger had presented a comprehensive political vision for the agency's work. During her parliamentary hearing, she said that under Orban, Hungary saw more than just what one might call classic corruption. An almost feudal system had prevailed, she argued. That was why in addition to restitution and asset recovery, the system had to be thoroughly investigated and exposed so that it would never happen again, Unger said.

No justice in next 6 years?

Unger caused the biggest upset when she said it would be folly to expect legally binding verdicts in any major corruption cases during the NVVH's first six-year term.

Robert Puzser, a popular commentator and personality on social media, called Unger's statement "devastating." Voters had given Magyar "unprecedented power to hold the country's plunderers to account," he said on Facebook, and if Hungarians had to wait more than six years, it could cause the collapse of this new government.

The new prime minister himself reacted angrily to critics who said the NVVH should have had a lawyer at its head.

"Nobody promised people they could vote for the leader of the NVVH as if it was a [reality TV] casting show," he wrote on Facebook. Plenty of experts thought Unger was absolutely suitable for the job.

In a podcast on the 24.hu media outlet, political science Gabor Torok surmised that the way that the NVVH had been established indicated that it would be a "strong political institution" that aimed to come to terms with the recent past.

Torok said the public expects the Tisza party to thoroughly reckon with the old system, and the new government will only be able to maintain the public's trust if it doesn't look like the "culprits of the previous order" are getting away with their past crimes, he said.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Marruecos, envalentonado: Mohamed VI se crece gracias al apoyo de Trump (y de Israel)
World.content:
La crisis de Ceuta ha dejado bien clara una cosa: Rabat ha actuado con la tranquilidad que da saberse respaldado por Estados Unidos. En 2020 Donald Trump reconoció la soberanía marroquí sobre el Sáhara Occidental, lo que ha dado alas al país norteafricano para expandir su política exterior y reactivar la cuestión de la soberanía sobre Ceuta y Melilla

Marruecos ha dado pasos diplomáticos de gigante en el tablero internacional, muy por encima de su talla de potencia regional emergente en el norte de África, con la bendición de tres miembros permanentes del Consejo de Seguridad de la ONU —Estados Unidos, Francia y Reino Unido— y la abstención de los dos restantes —Rusia y China—. En el último lustro, este país de poco más de 38 millones de habitantes y un producto interior bruto 10 veces inferior al español se ha convertido, además, en el mayor importador de armas del continente.

El reconocimiento por Donald Trump de la soberanía marroquí sobre el Sáhara Occidental a finales de 2020 marcó un punto de inflexión en la política exterior del país, destaca Bernabé López García, arabista y veterano conocedor de Marruecos: “Por primera vez, una gran potencia como EE UU confirmó la tesis de Rabat saltándose la ONU a la torera. Fue en el tiempo de descuento de la estancia del presidente en la Casa Blanca, lo que dio un aire de improvisación a la decisión, como hecha por la puerta de atrás”, recuerda el profesor honorario de la Universidad Autónoma de Madrid, que explica que, “a cambio de establecer relaciones con Israel, Trump envalentonó a Marruecos, que endureció desde entonces su política exterior presionando a diestro y siniestro, antes de que se aprobara el pasado octubre la resolución del Consejo de Seguridad 2797, obra de la nueva Administración de Trump en su segundo mandato”. Rabat logró el espaldarazo de colocar en el centro del debate de la ONU su plan de autonomía para el Sáhara. “Le sirvió de gran ayuda, una vez conseguidos muchos más apoyos, entre otros los de países clave como Francia, Reino Unido, Alemania o España, la antigua potencia colonial”.

Queda poco para la próxima votación sobre el Sáhara en el Consejo de Seguridad, a finales de octubre. Hasta entonces, hay observadores que se han preguntado, apunta Bernabé López, si lo que está ocurriendo actualmente en Ceuta puede suponer un gesto del sector marroquí más duro del poder para hacerle “un favor al amigo americano que ponga en un aprieto a Pedro Sánchez (como enemigo del republicano), y de paso apoye a los irredentistas (partidarios del Gran Marruecos más allá de sus fronteras reconocidas)”, con vistas a la campaña electoral de las legislativas del 23 de septiembre. Los comicios languidecían ajenos al interés ciudadano antes de que la crisis migratoria de Ceuta actuara como revulsivo de la movilización a las urnas.

El país magrebí parece más sólido hoy en sus relaciones exteriores que en la crisis del islote español Perejil (Laila, para los marroquíes) que marcó en 2002 los primeros años de reinado de Mohamed VI y puso a Marruecos y España al borde de un conflicto armado. Fuerzas de seguridad marroquíes ocuparon un peñasco deshabitado, situado cerca de la costa, hasta que fueron desalojadas por el Ejército español. Incluso se muestra más asertivo que en la crisis de la frontera de Ceuta, en 2021, en la que cerca de 10.000 marroquíes irrumpieron en la ciudad autónoma española ante la laxitud de las fuerzas de seguridad de Rabat. Y, en plena crisis migratoria desde el pasado mes de julio, ha reactivado también la cuestión de la soberanía sobre Ceuta y Melilla —por boca de varios ministros, uno de ellos en presencia del mismo rey Mohamed VI— tras haber avanzado varias casillas en su posición diplomática en el Sáhara.

El rey de Marruecos, Mohamed VI (tercero por la izquierda), mira al presidente de EE UU, Donald Trump (primero por la derecha). Les acompañan Justin Trudeau, entonces primer ministro de Canadá; Mulay Hasán, príncipe heredero de Marruecos, y la primera dama estadounidense, Melania Trump, en el centenario del final de la I Guerra Mundial, en París, en 2018. BENOIT TESSIER ( REUTERS )

Enrocado en la tesis de la autonomía tras la deriva en su favor de Estados Unidos, parece jugar ahora con ventaja. El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, reconoció en 2022 ante Mohamed VI en la capital marroquí que consideraba la propuesta de autogobierno bajo soberanía de Rabat como la solución “más seria, realista y creíble” para el enquistado conflicto del Sáhara, que cumplió 50 años en 2025. En contrapartida, Madrid y Rabat sellaron el “compromiso mutuo de evitar el uso de reclamaciones unilaterales de soberanía y de acciones que puedan ofender a la otra parte”.

Ante la actual convulsión en Ceuta, Bernabé López advierte de que Marruecos no debería estar en condiciones de poder abordar una reclamación sobre las ciudades autónomas sin resolver antes plenamente la cuestión del Sáhara. Pero eso sería “en puridad con el derecho internacional de antes en la mano, ya que ahora todo está patas arriba”. Ceuta y Melilla no son territorios por descolonizar, según la ONU, y Marruecos nunca ha logrado cambiar esa situación, aunque “en los tiempos que corren, eso puede importar poco”.

De la mano de Washington, el país norteafricano se ha rearmado hasta superar las compras militares de Argelia, su mayor rival regional, de acuerdo con el último informe del Instituto Internacional de Investigaciones para la Paz de Estocolmo (Sipri). Estados Unidos suministra el 60% de las adquisiciones de armas, frente al 10% procedente de Francia, que se ha visto desplazada del segundo puesto tras el restablecimiento de relaciones con Israel hace seis años.

El reconocimiento de Washington de la autoridad marroquí sobre el Sáhara conllevó la normalización de unas relaciones ya existentes por debajo del radar con Israel. Avanzaron con brío en materia de seguridad y defensa, en la carambola diplomática de los llamados Acuerdos de Abraham. Como explica Lahcen Haddad, académico marroquí experto en asuntos internacionales, “el paso dado por EE UU supuso un hito significativo. Formó parte de un proceso diplomático iniciado años antes por Rabat para alcanzar una solución mediante la iniciativa de autonomía marroquí”. En su opinión, la importancia de esta decisión radicó en el papel hegemónico de Estados Unidos en las relaciones internacionales y la coherencia de su postura. “Contribuyó a reorientar el debate hacia una solución pragmática y negociada que tenga en cuenta la realidad sobre el terreno”, precisa el también exministro y actual parlamentario.

El ministro de Asuntos Exteriores de Israel, Yair Lapid (izquierda), y el de Marruecos, Nasser Burita, durante su encuentro en 2021 en Beersheva, Israel Israeli Government Press Office (/Anadolu /Getty Images)

En cuanto a la reanudación de las relaciones con Israel, considera que se enmarcaron en el mismo contexto diplomático, y en los “vínculos históricos que unen a Marruecos con su comunidad judía y la diáspora en Israel [cerca de un millón de habitantes de origen marroquí]”. Además de los acuerdos en materia de seguridad y defensa, Haddad resalta la expansión de cooperación en ámbitos como la tecnología y la ciberseguridad.
