In an age of alcoholic beverages with preservatives and other ingredients that are difficult to describe, let alone pronounce the names of, Van Kleef is still doing things the old-fashioned way.

“All of our recipes have been preserved,” Kruyt said. “We have an archive full of them that began in the 1840s. Everything you’re tasting is real in the sense that there’s no artificial flavouring or colourings.”

The distillery continues to attract international visitors and aficionados of liqueurs. Kruyt said a few of them are household names, but she demurred when asked for the details.

“What happens at Van Kleef, stays at Van Kleef,” she said. “So any celebrities out there, you can come here and we won’t talk about you.”

World.title: The Many Lives of Anne Frank: a fascinating work
World.content:
The Many Lives of Anne Frank is a biography, of the German Jewish teenager herself, of her famous diary and, also, of her legacy. Ruth Franklin’s innovative approach to the most famous work of the Holocaust is fascinating, thought-provoking and well worth the read.

The Diary of Anne Frank has been assigned to thousands of students and has sold millions of copies. The annex where the teenager hid with her family during the Second World War is visited by a million tourists a year, whose queue snakes along the canal in Amsterdam for blocks.

Published in 2025, the first half of the book is a classic biography. We follow the Frank family from Germany to exile in the Netherlands and then to further banishment above a warehouse on the Prinsengracht. Franklin brings the story to life, with minute details (it was raining on the evening the Franks walked across the Dutch capital to their hiding place) and wider context (the ongoing round-up of Jews by the occupying Nazis.)

The biography does not end, as most biographies do, with the subject’s death. The young girl died somewhere in March or April of 1945 at Bergen-Belsen concentration camp, possibly just weeks before it was liberated by the British army.

Her legacy lives on, in her diary published, following edits from her father, shortly after the war. Anne herself also edited the work, inspired by a 1944 appeal from the Dutch minister for education diaries and letters documenting the German occupation. The teen aspired to get her thoughts and feelings into print.

The second half of the book follows the legacy of the diary, how it came into being and how it became a phenomenon, vaulting Anne Frank to an epic level of fame.

Franklin delves into the details of the book’s publication journey, raising questions about what it means for something to be “authentic.”

Anne’s father Otto sends a translated (and edited) version to relatives in Switzerland, who encourage him to publish the work. A composite of Anne’s two versions, plus her father’s edits is submitted to a publisher, who suggests certain cuts as to not offend more conservative readers. A longer, critical edition was published in 1986 and, based on that, the English-language version was published in 1989.

The first German-language version edits a passage Anne wrote taking a dig at the country. She writes “Only civilized languages are permitted [in the Annex], therefore no German,” which is changed to “all civilised languages may be spoken.” The occupants made an effort to speak to one another in Dutch, rather than in their native German, as a form of resistance.

The chapters are all titled with descriptors of the various versions of Anne. The final one is called “Pawn” and addresses her legacy. Otto intended for the diary to “promote peace and tolerance,” Franklin writes, but he couldn’t control his daughter’s celebrity.

The adaptation of the diary in a play in the United States is complicated by differing artistic versions of the work, the iconic image of Anne is used by those protesting South African apartheid and later, Israel’s war on Gaza. Franklin’s chronicle leaves the reader with many questions about how to contextualise the diary of a teenage girl.

A prize-winning literary critic, Franklin is a former editor at The New Republic. Her first biography, Shirley Jackson: A Rather Haunted Life, won multiple awards. The Many Lives of Anne Frank was a finalist for the 2025 Los Angeles Times Book Prizes.

The Many Lives of Anne Frank is deeply researched, well-written and stimulating.

You can get your copy at the American Book Center.

World.title: Amsterdam travel app leaked users’ personal data for months
World.content:
Polarsteps, an Amsterdam-founded travel app used by more than 23 million people, left users’ photos, locations and home addresses reachable by anyone through an unsecured data feed – including trips put on private mode – and had known about the flaw for months, an investigation by Follow the Money (FTM) has found.

The investigation found that anyone could connect to the free app’s data feed and pull users’ names, 230 million photos and videos, and 1 billion GPS locations from nearly 2 million trips – enough to plot journeys on a map and follow many of them close to real time.

More than a million of those trips had been shared only with followers. Even accounts set fully to private gave away who a user followed, who followed them and which device they logged in from. And once FTM held the link to someone’s trip, removing it as a follower changed nothing.

Home addresses were among the most sensitive details exposed. FTM pinned down dozens from the exact location saved inside users’ photos – a shot of packed suitcases taken at home, for example, and worked out many more from the spots people returned to each night.

That photo-location data appeared nowhere in Polarsteps’ privacy policy, and was missing from the file the company released when FTM asked to see its own records.

A year’s warning

The problem was first flagged last year by a French cybersecurity researcher who said Polarsteps told him it already knew what was happening. He took his findings to FTM, which said the data stayed exposed for at least six months.

Marc Schuilenburg, a professor of digital surveillance at Erasmus University, called the company negligent, and warned that leaked location data can be used to stalk, harass or threaten people.

The leak was not from a hack – no passwords were taken and no accounts entered. Anyone with basic technical skill could connect to Polarsteps’ servers and scrape the data, with none of the request limits, CAPTCHAs or login walls.

Company response

Polarsteps, which has grown from 1 million users in 2019, said no passwords or accounts were compromised and that it is in contact with the AP.

Chief executive Clare Jones, appointed in 2024, said the company should have caught the problem itself and was working out what went wrong. It has since tightened its systems, and noted that much of the exposed data had been made public by users’ own choice.

The company’s own website warns travellers that sharing location details in real time “can make you a target.” FTM said a second part of its investigation, on dozens of military personnel it tracked to bases and missions at home and abroad, would follow on Saturday.

World.title: Prosecutors hold 32 over Overasselt attack, including two minors
World.content:
Public prosecutors are detaining 32 people on suspicion of murder or manslaughter in connection with the killing of a security guard in Overasselt on Tuesday.

Thirty-four people were initially arrested in the area surrounding the Gelderland village but two were released as there was insufficient evidence to hold them. CCTV footage shows dozens of masked men getting out of a truck outside the property, some heavily armed, before one shoots a man sitting in a car.

They also opened fire on police shortly afterwards, injuring two. Of those arrested, two are minors aged 16 and 17, the rest are men from France, Netherlands, Algeria, Libya, Belgium and Ukraine – all aged between 18 and 32.

Footage emerged online after the attack purportedly by a drugs gang, threatening the resident of the property that was attacked and saying that he had stolen a large quantity of goods from them.

That man, known as Jan G. Jr, has been barred from entering the council around Overasselt for at least two weeks and will not be allowed back to live in the property for at least a year.

He has been linked to the drugs trade before and the house was shot at last year with an AK-47 by a young man from Amsterdam, said to be a drug addict who was paid to carry out the attack. He never named who paid him.

World.title: Public officials among those abusing Jetten online, AD finds
World.content:
A council official, a police employee and a member of the Dutch air force are among thousands of people posting homophobic abuse under prime minister Rob Jetten’s social media messages on X, an investigation by the Algemeen Dagblad (AD) has found.

The paper analysed 45,860 replies to 323 posts sent from the prime minister’s official account during his first six months in office. One in 20 – 2,293 replies – was homophobic, it said.

The abuse appeared under routine posts, from a congratulatory message for Queen Máxima to a post about Amsterdam Pride, and did not depend on the topics Jetten was writing about.

AD identified two recurring forms of abuse. The first was crude slurs and the second, far more common, was a single insinuating question posted in Dutch hundreds of times: “Did you tell them you’re gay?”

Hard to prosecute

Most of the accounts did not belong to anonymous trolls, AD said. The large majority left a single homophobic reply and never returned, and the 10 most persistent accounts together produced less than 6% of the total.

Only a handful of repeat posters could be traced, among them the council, police and air force employees. Marloes van Noorloos, a professor of criminal law at Leiden University, told the paper that the insinuating questions were hard to prosecute as hate speech or criminal insult, because it depends largely on wording and context.

Civil servants, she said, could face disciplinary action under the rules governing public employees.

Jetten’s response

Jetten is the Netherlands’ first openly gay prime minister, and has said he files a police report every week over the abuse he receives about his sexuality. At the WorldPride conference last month he said big social media companies were “barely moderating content for hate speech”.

X’s own rules prohibit attacking users over their sexual orientation, but the company has taken little action, according to AD.

Dutch acceptance of homosexuality has stalled after years of progress. Jetten has said the Netherlands needs to get back on track and return to the top 10 countries for LGBTQI+ rights, from where it fell to number 13 after 2018.

World.title: Farmers face livestock cuts as nitrogen plan falls short
World.content:
Dutch farmers are still facing a compulsory cut in the number of animals they can keep as livestock, after the government’s environmental assessment agency found the cabinet’s nitrogen plan would fall just short of its own 2035 target.

The agency, PBL, assessed the €20 billion nitrogen plan at the cabinet’s request and called it an important step that could bring the farming emissions target within reach.

But it found the measures worked out so far leave a gap, and that an across-the-board cut of 5% to 10% in farmers’ livestock rights, the permits that cap how many animals a farm may hold, is still needed.

The coalition has always said that a blanket cut is a last resort, to be used only if the targets are missed in 2035. Agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen called it an “emergency brake” on Friday and “a no-go for the cabinet.”

Farmers must reduce ammonia emissions by 42% to 46% by 2035, against 2019 levels, under the package agreed in June. PBL expects the herd to shrink further regardless as farms adapt to those rules, with some businesses forced to close.

The agency was more positive about the plan’s benefits for the environment, but warned the nitrogen problem will not just disappear. On more than half the area of the most sensitive protected sites, deposition is still expected to breach the critical threshold in 2035.

Nature groups called the plans the minimum needed to start repairing decades of damage. The farmers’ party BBB and the farm lobby LTO said the extra cut was unacceptable, though LTO is staying at the table to negotiate the rest of the package.

World.title: Dutch soil scientist wins Ig Nobel for burying 1,000 underpants
World.content:
A Dutch scientist has won the Ig Nobel prize for conducting a study that involved burying around 1,000 pairs of underpants and digging them up two months later.

Marcel van der Heijden, a soil scientist at the University of Zurich, shared this year’s Ig Nobel for soil science with three colleagues. The annual prizes, a parody counterpart to the Nobels, reward research that “first makes people laugh and then makes them think.”

Volunteers buried identical cotton underpants across more than 25 countries, then dug them up after two months and recorded what was left. The more the fabric had rotted, the healthier and more biologically active the soil.

“Our results show that how soil is managed can significantly affect both soil life and soil quality,” van der Heijden said in a statement, adding that healthy soil was crucial for fertility and for the wider ecosystem.

This year’s ceremony was held in Zurich, the first time it has taken place outside the US after more than three decades in the country.

Organisers said they could not in good conscience ask winners or visiting journalists to travel to the US this year, a decision widely assumed to be down to American immigration policy. Next year’s event will be in Antwerp.

Dutch researchers are Ig Nobel regulars. According to broadcaster NOS, they have won 22 times since the first ceremony in 1991, including last year’s award for showing that a drink can improve people’s foreign-language skills.

World.title: Poland’s oldest operating electric train, 63-year-old “Granny”, returns to the tracks after a refurb

Poland’s oldest operational multiple-unit electric train, a 63-year-old vehicle nicknamed Babcia (meaning “Granny”), is returning to service after refurbishment. The train, whose official name is EN57-038, rolled off the production lines on 9 May 1963 at a factory in the city of Wrocław belonging to Pafawag, a state locomotive manufacturer. For decades, it served in the southern Małopolska province, transporting passengers in cities including Kraków, Tarnów, Nowy Sącz and Sucha Beskidzka. In 2003, it was transferred to Masovia, the province around Poland’s capital, Warsaw, where it has operated ever since. “Masovian Railways continually invests in modern rolling stock, making our fleet among the most modern in Poland,” said Czesław Sulima, the operations director for the regional rail operator. “However, we fully understand the importance of tradition and sentiment.” “Babcia has become a permanent fixture in Polish railway history,” he added. “We are delighted that after a major overhaul, this unique vehicle will once again serve passengers and delight lovers of old-time travel, combining history with modernity.” Babcia has previously undergone periodic modernisation and maintenance, most recently in 2022, when she regained her original yellow and blue livery associated with the historic Pafawag factory. The latest work included upgrades to the train’s monitoring system and toilet, which now operates in “closed circulation” (a polite way of saying that waste is no longer dropped directly onto the track). State rail operator PKP has for years been promising to phase out the few remaining old “open” toilets. Now that Babcia has been refurbished, she will return to service early on Saturday morning, running a 10 km route on weekends between the town of Tłuszcz and village of Mostówka, just northeast of Warsaw. Babcia is one of the EN57 class of electric multiple unit trains produced by Pafawag between 1961 and 1993. A total of 1,429 were manufactured, with many still in use – though none as old as EN57-038. The history of the Wrocław factory itself dates back to the 1830s (when the city was part of Germany and called Breslau), making it one of the oldest manufacturers of rolling stock in Europe. After World War Two, when Wrocław became part of Poland following border changes, the factory came under the ownership of the new communist state. In the 1990s, after the fall of communism, it was privatised, being acquired in 1997 by German company ADtranz, which was in 2001 itself taken over by Canada’s Bombardier Transportation, which was then acquired in 2021 by France’s Alstom. Train travel has been booming in Poland in recent years. In the first half of 2026, a record 44.7 million passengers travelled with PKP Intercity, the main long-distance operator, more than 10% up on the previous year’s record and some 45% higher than three years earlier. While the country is seeking to expand its high-speed rail network and increase train speeds up to 320 km/h (199mph), there has also been a growing interest in older trains. That prompted PKP to launch a special “unhurried” service earlier this year, allowing passengers to travel along scenic routes in restored 1980s trains. World.title: Poland to begin using sewage water to cool power plants
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland will begin using reclaimed sewage water to cool power plants from the start of next year. The measures are intended to reduce the use of fresh water and make the power system more resilient to increasingly frequent droughts. The change comes after some of Poland’s power plants were partially shut down this summer amid a series of heatwaves and lack of rain that led to record-low water levels in many rivers. 💧⚡ Otwieramy sektor energetyczny na wodę odzyskaną. Od 1 stycznia 2027 r. polskie elektrownie i elektrociepłownie będą mogły wykorzystywać wodę odzyskaną ze ścieków komunalnych w systemach chłodzenia. Nowe rozwiązania przedstawiliśmy dziś wspólnie z ministrem energii… pic.twitter.com/qRDOgjcDwb — Dariusz Klimczak (@DariuszKlimczak) September 3, 2026 “This may seem to many like a minor change, but it is of fundamental importance for many power-generating units in Poland,” said energy minister Miłosz Motyka. “Thanks to this, we will be even more resilient and even better prepared for crises of all kinds.” The legislation was first proposed by a group of MPs from The Left (Lewica) and the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), two members of the current ruling coalition, in May, and was then approved by parliament in July. Last week, President Karol Nawrocki signed it into law. The law, which will come into force at the start of 2027, introduces a definition of water recovered from municipal sewage, which, in turn, will allow its use in the cooling circuits of power stations and combined heat and power plants. Power stations require large amounts of water to help cool and condense steam, which drives the turbines, back into liquid form so that it can be reheated into steam once more. Orlen Termika, a subsidiary of state energy giant Orlen, has announced that it plans to invest more than 1 billion zloty (€230 million) over the next four years to maximise the benefits of the change by connecting sewage treatment plants with three of its power and heat plants around Warsaw. According to Andrzej Gajewski, the CEO of Orlen Termika, one of the plants, Żeran, will be able to save up to 80% of previous water use. Another, Siekierki, will save up to 20%. The company also plans to install heat pumps to extract heat from sewage, which can then be used to help supply heat to residents of Warsaw before the water is then used to cool down the plants. Sewage is relatively warm, typically between 10°C and 20°C, making it a good source of recoverable heat. “From the point of view of security of supply for Warsaw’s residents and from the point of view of efficiency – that is, the price of heating – this is the best and most advantageous solution,” emphasised Gajewski. Poland’s power grid operator has, for the second time in three days and third time this summer, invoked emergency measures to ensure supply amid a heatwave. Before this summer, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced https://t.co/fIDR4SimgG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 6, 2026 Poland has experienced increasingly hot temperatures in recent years. This summer, the country broke its all-time record, as temperatures reached more than 40°C. That, along with low amounts of rainfall, has seen rivers reach record lows. As a result, Poland’s power grid operator has this summer been forced three times to invoke emergency measures to ensure supply. Previously, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced. Around 1.1 gigawatts (GW) of capacity, just over 1% of Poland’s total, was taken offline. World.title: Prime minister’s “right-hand man” elected as Polish constitutional court judge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has succeeded in having Maciej Berek, whom he recently described as his “right-hand man”, elected by parliament as a Constitutional Tribunal (TK) judge, staving off a rebellion from some members of his own coalition. Critics argued that the nomination violated the government’s pledge to “depoliticise” the TK, including by banning recently active politicians from sitting on it. Berek served as a government minister from 2023, when Tusk came to power, until last month, when he stepped down in order to run for the TK. However, it is far from clear what will happen next. Opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has this year refused to swear in four TK judges chosen by parliament, and he has made clear that he also opposes Berek’s candidacy. ✅Sejm dokonał wyboru Macieja Berka na stanowisko sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. pic.twitter.com/ek0ak9C33v — Sejm RP🇵🇱 (@KancelariaSejmu) September 4, 2026 In mid-August, Berek announced that he was leaving the government, where he had served as minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy. Shortly afterwards, Tusk confirmed that Berek would be nominated to fill an upcoming vacancy on the TK. The prime minister argued that, during his time in government, Berek had undertaken a technocratic role that was “apolitical and nonpartisan”. He said that Berek’s extensive experience in constitutional law and the legislative process made him an ideal candidate. However, some MPs from Tusk’s junior coalition partners publicly opposed the nomination. They noted that the government’s parliamentary majority had, in 2024, approved a law banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. The law never went into force as it was effectively blocked by a combination of then-President Andrzej Duda and the TK itself, which were both aligned with the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party from 2015 to 2023 and now the largest opposition group. Polish NGOs have urged Tusk's "right-hand man" to withdraw his Constitutional Tribunal candidacy, warning his political ties could undermine efforts to restore the court’s independence. The nomination has also exposed tensions within the ruling coalitionhttps://t.co/jQn0MyuS7G — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 21, 2026 Ahead of today’s vote in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, it remained unclear if Berek’s candidacy would be approved. In the end, he obtained the necessary majority, receiving the support of 226 MPs among the 437 who voted in the 460-seat chamber. Within the ruling coalition, only four MPs voted against Berek’s candidacy, including one from Tusk’s own centrist Civic Coalition (KO), Klaudia Jachira. Another opponent was Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is the leader of The Left (Lewica), one of Tusk’s junior coalition partners, and the speaker of the Sejm. Eleven MPs from the ruling coalition did not take part in the vote. The entire right-wing and far-right opposition voted against Berek’s candidacy. Berek is now meant to join the TK after the next vacancy on its 15-person bench opens up on 18 September, when the nine-year term of an existing judge, Justyn Piskorski, ends. However, under Polish law, a new TK judge must first swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki has used this requirement to refuse to swear in four of the judges chosen by the ruling majority in the Sejm this year. He has, however, sworn in three others. Nawrocki argued that there were legal doubts over the appointment of the quartet whose oaths he refused to receive. However, the government says that the president does not have the right to assess their candidacies and that the swearing-in is merely a formality. The crisis around Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has deepened further after the tribunal ruled that the president is not obliged to swear in new TK judges appointed by parliament. President Nawrocki last month refused to swear in four new judges https://t.co/ycnweW9pSR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 13, 2026 The four judges instead organised their own swearing-in ceremony in the Sejm before a notary, after which they forwarded their oaths to the president and attempted to take their seats on the TK. However, the tribunal’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, refused to allow them to serve, citing their failure to swear an oath before the president. Święczkowski previously served as a deputy justice minister in the former PiS government and is still seen as loyal to the party. In May, the European Court of Human Rights issued an interim order requiring that the four judges be allowed to take up their positions. However, Święczkowski has ignored it, arguing that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 It appears likely that Nawrocki will refuse to swear in Berek. “I think the last thing the TK needs is another politician, especially a politician who is a close collaborator of Prime Minister Donald Tusk,” said Nawrocki on Thursday. On Friday morning, ahead of the Sejm vote, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, addressed the chamber to outline the president’s opposition to Berek’s candidacy. He said that, as well as Berek’s political association with the government, there are doubts over whether he even meets the formal requirements to sit on the tribunal, in particular the need to have practised the law for at least 10 years. Berek says he does meet that requirement. Adding to the confusion is the fact that Tusk’s government does not regard the current TK as legitimate because of the presence of judges, including Piskorski, who were unlawfully appointed when PiS and Duda were in office. It ignores all TK rulings. Tusk has emphasised that one of the reasons he wants to appoint Berek to the TK is to help “fix” the tribunal. Berek’s nomination means that there are now eight TK judges chosen by the ruling coalition, giving them a majority on the court. However, with Nawrocki and Święczkowski refusing to accept four of them, and likely to reject Berek too, some kind of drastic action would be required to allow them to begin to serve. The proportion of Poles who negatively assess the justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law. State pollster @CBOS_Info found 61% now hold a negative view, up from 55% in 2022 and 51% in 2017 https://t.co/P3fbTTbS5C — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. President Karol Nawrocki has launched a programme allowing Polish companies looking to expand into international markets to apply to join his foreign visits. “Seats on the presidential plane will soon be available to Polish businesses,” Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, announced in a video published on X. “I want Polish companies, including small and medium-sized ones, to be able to establish new contacts, develop existing business relationships and successfully conquer foreign markets alongside the president.” Już niedługo miejsca w prezydenckim samolocie będą dostępne także dla polskiego biznesu. Chcę, żeby polskie firmy, również te małe i średnie, mogły u boku prezydenta nawiązywać nowe kontakty, rozwijać już istniejące relacje biznesowe i z sukcesem podbijać zagraniczne rynki.… pic.twitter.com/kO6L1t1m4D — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) September 3, 2026 To launch the programme, Nawrocki’s office is already accepting applications from business representatives interested in joining the president on his trip to New York later this month to attend the United Nations General Assembly. A one-day Polish-American Economic Summit is also planned during the visit, linked to Poland’s participation in this year’s G20 summit, which is being hosted by the United States. When deciding which businesses to invite on the trip, the presidential chancellery says it would seek “well-established companies with the potential to grow in the US market and seeking new partners and opportunities for collaboration” Those selected will be invited to travel on the presidential flight from Warsaw to New York and back, and will also receive local transportation. However, other costs, such as accommodation, meals and any necessary visas, will have to be paid by the businesses themselves. Nawrocki’s office says that the new programme was launched in response to long-standing calls from businesses for presidential foreign visits to be used to promote the international expansion of Polish companies. Opportunities to join presidential visits will be offered regularly, with details of new application rounds published on the prezydent.pl website. In recent years, a growing number of Polish companies have expanded abroad, helped by the country’s strong economic growth over the past three decades. Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, has announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as it seeks to expand its operations across Europe https://t.co/N1wE1aYL5m — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 12, 2026 Parcel delivery giant InPost, for example, has invested heavily in the United Kingdom, France and Spain, while convenience store chain Żabka now operates more than 100 outlets in Romania. Polish mobile payments system BLIK has, meanwhile, expanded into Slovakia, while state energy group Orlen has sought to grow its presence in other European markets. Polish companies are less likely to expand beyond Europe, but there are some exceptions. Earlier this year, Polish infrared sensor maker Vigo Photonics acquired a US rival to reduce the impact of tariffs. Some Polish firms have also been looking to expand their presence in Africa. Polish firm Vigo Photonics has acquired US rival InfraRed Associates for $8.4m. Poland has summoned Russia’s ambassador in response to recent hostile actions against Germany. “[We] expressed our strong condemnation of state terrorism perpetrated by Russia – because what is a problem for one ally is a problem for the entire alliance,” said Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “Putin’s Russia remains one of the most serious security threats – not just for Europe, but for the entire world order,” he added. “Its goal is to permanently destroy the European security architecture.” 💬 Nie ma zgody na podpalenia, ataki na kolej, morderstwa i inne prowokacje. Polska też wezwała ambasadora Rosji po to, aby wyrazić nasze stanowcze potępienie dla terroryzmu państwowego autorstwa Federacji Rosyjskiej. | wicepremier, minister spraw zagranicznych @sikorskiradek… pic.twitter.com/LChAjwsX8H — Ministerstwo Spraw Zagranicznych RP 🇵🇱 (@MSZ_RP) September 3, 2026 On Tuesday, the German government announced that it held Russia responsible for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport last month. In response, it ordered the closure of Russia’s consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural centre in Berlin. This week also saw attempts to sabotage Germany’s electricity network in two locations. While they are still being investigated, on Wednesday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggested that they may also be part of “Russia’s escalatory actions throughout the region”. On Thursday, the spokesman for Poland’s foreign ministry, Maciej Wewiór, confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that Russia’s ambassador to Warsaw, Georgy Mikhno, had been summoned to the ministry. Wewiór said that Poland wanted to convey “our firm opposition to the escalation of Russia’s aggressive actions” as well as to show solidarity with Germany. A number of other European leaders have also this week expressed solidarity with Germany, including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. Poland has itself been a major target for Russia. Earlier this year, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland was the “primary focus” of Russian sabotage. It has also suffered cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns, and “weaponised migration” on its eastern border. In response, Poland has successively closed down all of Russia’s consulates in the country, with Moscow responding by doing the same with Polish consulates operating on its territory. This week, after a fire broke out at a drone factory in Poland, Tusk said that there is “no doubt” it was caused deliberately and suggested it was also likely carried out on behalf of Russia. World.title: Poland moves to allow local communities to ban short-term rentals
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals – the type of privately owned accommodation offered through services such as Airbnb and Booking.com. Such services have boomed in Poland in recent years, like in other parts of the world. But that has prompted a backlash from many communities, which argue that short-term rentals can cause disruption, reduce the availability of housing, and drive up prices. However, the proposed measures have already caused divisions within the ruling coalition and must still be approved by parliament, where the government has a majority, and by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of bills. ❗ Rada Ministrów przyjęła autopoprawkę do projektu ustawy dotyczącego najmu krótkoterminowego. Nowe rozwiązania dadzą mieszkańcom i samorządom konkretne narzędzia do reagowania tam, gdzie najem krótkoterminowy powoduje problemy z bezpieczeństwem i porządkiem publicznym. ➡️… pic.twitter.com/7KvW2O4AKW — Ministerstwo Sportu i Turystyki (@SPORT_GOV_PL) September 2, 2026 Speaking ahead of a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk confirmed that, following a “difficult process” of discussion, his coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, had agreed on the measures. They would grant “greater rights for residents, communities, housing cooperatives and local authorities regarding the situation in the short-term rental market”, said Tusk. “Wherever order, safety and basic comfort of life are threatened, decisions can be made to exclude these types of businesses.” The new rules would allow homeowner associations (wspólnoty mieszkaniowe) and housing cooperatives (spółdzielnie mieszkaniowe) to prohibit short-term rentals. If a majority of members voted to adopt such a ban, operators of short-term rental properties would have six months to end operations. Municipal councils (rady gmin), at the request of the mayor, would also be given the power to designate specific areas within their territory in which short-term rentals would be banned or restricted (for example, to a certain number of days a year). There would also be greater powers for residents and housing groups to initiate official inspections of properties if they believe there are violations of public safety and order rules. If a property violated such regulations three times within six months, it would be banned from operating for a year. Tusk noted that, if the bill becomes law, it would not fully go into force until 2028, in order to give enough time for businesses and communities to adapt to the new rules. If Poland does introduce the new measures, its cities could follow the example of many of their European counterparts, such as Barcelona, Paris and London, which have introduced various restrictions on short-term rentals. The European Union has also moved to more tightly regulate the sector. EU to help tourism hotspots crack down on Airbnb-style holiday rentals https://t.co/0Y5nzfZZYF — Financial Times (@FT) August 30, 2026 The measures have been subject to intense debate within the ruling coalition. When the legislation was first submitted to parliament in July, some parts that had previously been included, such as provisions allowing municipalities to ban short-term rentals in certain areas, were removed. That prompted a backlash from two junior coalition partners in particular, The Left (Lewica) and the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), prompting further discussions over the summer, resulting in the bill now being toughened again. The Left celebrated the government’s decision to restore tougher elements of the bill, saying it would help avoid “situations where short-term rentals turn into a nightmare, stripping residents of their peace”. The leader of Poland 2050, Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, declared that they had “scored another goal against the lobbyists” by toughening the legislation. Previously, her party had accused the government of watering down the original bill due to industry lobbying. Znowu wbiliśmy lobbystom gola. Właśnie spłynęła nowa wersja rządowej ustawy o Airbnb. Jest decyzyjność wspólnot, spółdzielni i samorządów. Patohotele strzeżcie się – idziemy po was. Czasem warto być „kłótnicą” rządu 😉@PL_2050 — Katarzyna Pełczyńska (@Kpelczynska) August 31, 2026 It also appears that the bill could obtain support from the opposition. In July, after the government initially removed parts of the legislation, the largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), called for them to be restored, saying that power should be put in the hands of local communities. If the bill is approved by parliament, it also requires the signature of Nawrocki, who was elected last year with the support of PiS, before becoming law. He has vetoed a record number of government bills, but has signed an even larger number. It remains unclear what his position on short-term rentals is. ‼️ To mieszkańcy najlepiej wiedzą, co służy ich wspólnocie. Dlatego wspólnota powinna mieć prawo powiedzieć NIE, jeśli chodzi o najem krótkoterminowy. 👉 Udostępnij! pic.twitter.com/dWURZ9awAY — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) July 27, 2026 Poland has seen a boom in tourism in recent years. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-largest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation. Its increase of 7% was behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta (9.9%). However, the growth in tourism has also prompted tensions. In 2024, Kraków, which is Poland’s second-largest city and its main tourist destination, appointed a new “night mayor”, who is responsible for reconciling the needs of the city’s residents, business owners and tourists. Previously, in 2020, the city formed a partnership with Airbnb to promote responsible and sustainable tourism. The following year, it launched a “tourist patrol scheme” to inform visitors of the “rules and norms they should follow”. In 2024, Kraków also appealed to the government to allow it to introduce a new tax on tourists. It warned that “overtourism has led to tensions and social discontent in many places in Europe…because residents increasingly feel like tourists in their own city”. World.title: NfP podcast: How small towns became a testing ground for Poland’s far right
World.content: In our new podcast, Notes from Poland’s editor-in-chief Daniel Tilles speaks with deputy editor-in-chief Alicja Ptak about her research into how four contentious issues – migration, women’s rights, Jewish heritage and LGBT+ rights – have played out in 19 smaller towns and cities in Poland. They discuss how national far-right talking points are being imported into smaller towns, how these issues are covered and contested at the local level, and what this all means ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections. There is now “no doubt” that a fire this week at a drone factory in Poland was caused deliberately, says Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who also suggested it was carried out on behalf of Russia. Speaking ahead of a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Tusk noted that there had been “some very disturbing incidents and events in Poland and Germany over the past few [days]”. “This is a continuation of Russia’s escalatory actions throughout the region,” he continued. “Unfortunately, these are not the first cases and, even worse, they certainly won’t be the last.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Najbliższe tygodnie i miesiące będą krytyczne nie tylko jeśli chodzi o zdarzenia na froncie i w ogóle całą wojnę rosyjsko-ukraińską, ale te tygodnie i miesiące będą także bardzo dużym wyzwaniem dla wszystkich państw w tej części Europy, ze względu na… pic.twitter.com/ZcjVMjhWc0 — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 2, 2026 On Sunday, a fire broke out at a production facility in the Polish city of Lublin belonging to JFG Composites, a company that produces components for the aerospace industry, including for military helicopters. Then, in the early hours of Monday morning, another fire occurred at a plant in Skarżysko-Kamienna, south-central Poland, belonging to WB Electronics, a Polish firm that is the largest producer of drones in the European Union. It supplies the armed forces of Ukraine and Poland, among others. By Monday afternoon, Polish prosecutors and the security services had confirmed that they were investigating the Skarżysko-Kamienna fire as a potential “crime of a terrorist nature” carried out with the involvement of “foreign intelligence”. On Tuesday, improvised explosive devices were found at one electricity substation in Germany near the border with Poland while another substation in the west of the country was attacked. That came on the same day that Germany announced it held Russia responsible for a drone attack on Leipzig airport last month. Polish prosecutors have launched an investigation into whether a fire last night at a facility belonging to WB Electronics, the EU's largest drone maker, was a “crime of a terrorist nature” committed with the “participation of foreign intelligence” https://t.co/rBKmy2A13V — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026 In his remarks on Wednesday, Tusk said that “there is no doubt” that the incident in Skarżysko-Kamienna “was deliberate arson, meaning an act of sabotage”. “In the case of Lublin, we do not have such evidence but, considering the nature of the production, it cannot be ruled out that deliberate arson occurred there as well,” he added. “I am in constant contact with the leaders of the countries in our region, and everyone realises that the coming weeks and months will be critical, not only in terms of events on the front and the entire Russian-Ukrainian war,” continued the prime minister. “These weeks and months will also pose a very, very significant challenge for all countries in this part of Europe, precisely because of Russia’s plans to escalate tensions and destabilise.” On Tuesday, a deputy interior minister, Czesław Mroczek, told broadcaster RMF that surveillance cameras had recorded a masked person entering the WB Electronics plant in Skarżysko-Kamienna. He said it was “obvious” that Russian involvement was suspected, pointing to previous similar cases in which agents working on behalf of Russia have carried out acts of sabotage in Poland. A report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published earlier this year found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russia’s growing campaign of sabotage in Europe. Last year, Poland confirmed that Russia was behind the fire that in 2024 destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre. The Polish authorities are also seeking to detain two men believed to have sabotaged a rail line last year on Russian orders. Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism. However, in contrast to Tusk’s remarks on Wednesday, Kierwiński said that the fires in Lublin and Skarżysko-Kamienna are “two separate incidents and likely unrelated” to one another. “Regarding the Lublin incident, with the information currently available, I’m not so convinced that we were dealing with sabotage,” he explained. “In the case of Skarżysko[-Kamienna], all signs point to an act of terror and sabotage.” Minister @MSWiA_GOV_PL @MKierwinski: Jeżeli chodzi o kwestię pożaru hali w Lublinie, z dostępnymi obecnie informacjami nie mam takiego twardego przekonania, że mieliśmy do czynienia z sabotażem.https://t.co/cspYL5Bn0w — Radio Lublin (@RadioLublin) September 1, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
