World.title: Live: Piastri eyes off 'usually chaotic' Monza start after grid penalty
World.content:
— reporting by ABC and Reuters

What a few days it has been for Pierre Gasly.

On Friday he lost his third place finish from the Monaco Grand Prix on June 7, then last night he drove his Alpine to pole position. the first of his F1 career.

Let's start with losing his Monaco podium.

Gasly lost the podium to Isack Hadjar for the second time after penalties from the Monaco Grand Prix were reinstated following a successful appeal by two Formula 1 teams.

As a result, Gasly dropped from third to seventh place in the June 7 race after a pair of five-second penalties were applied. Initially, the penalties for speeding infractions had been rescinded one week after the race.

McLaren and Red Bull appealed to the FIA's International Court of Appeal, with a hearing held in Paris on Aug. 25. The decision to reinstate the original finish order was announced Friday.

Red Bull's Hadjar, in turn, and McLaren's Oscar Piastri were elevated to third and fourth, respectively, ahead of the Racing Bulls duo of Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad.

"The team expresses its disappointment and frustration with the outcome reached by the FIA International Court of Appeal relating to the result of the 2026 Monaco Grand Prix," Alpine said in a statement.

"While we disagree with the decision, and still fully maintain that (Gasly's) Car 10 did not exceed the Pit Lane speed limit at any point during the race, the team acknowledges the decision of the judging panel from the recent hearing in Paris.

"While the result is not what we had hoped for, as we feel that we have been unjustly punished, the team is firmly focused on continuing to improve its performance on track and remains in a close and very competitive Championship fight. This outcome will not deter the team's efforts and motivation in achieving its objectives by the end of the season."

Now, let's talk about the pole position

Galsy loves Monza. It is the scene of his only win in F1, a stunning upset in 2020 driving for AlphaTauri (now Racing Bulls).

Alpine has been running in the midfield this season, but my word they found some pace in Monza on Saturday.

From the start of qualifying both Alpine drivers, Gasly and Franco Colapinto, were in the top 10, but Gasly was really threatening pole.

On his final flying lap, the Frenchman put it all together. None of his sector times were the overall fastest in the session, but he was the driver who nailed a lap with three excellent sectors to secure a stunning result.

World.title: US delegation lands in Kyiv amid Russia-Ukraine capitals ceasefire
World.content:
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have arrived in Kyiv as part of a push to revive peace talks in Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Russia, Ukraine to halt strikes on capitals during peace talks Vladimir Putin and Volodymyr Zelenskyy have agreed to halt strikes on their respective capitals.

The visit by the emissaries follows a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday.

Mr Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy agreed to pause strikes on each other's capitals while the talks took place.

Mr Zelenskyy said on Sunday that Kyiv was ready for a "constructive" discussion with US representatives.

"We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer. Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A just and sustainable postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are prepared," he said in a post on Telegram.

No breakthroughs in Moscow talks

Vladimir Putin greets Steve Witkoff prior to talks in Moscow on Saturday. (AP: Mikhail Metzel/Sputnik)

Saturday's meeting in Moscow lasted more than 3 hours behind closed doors and ended without announcements of any breakthroughs.

Mr Putin's foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov described them afterwards as constructive, frank and useful but did not discuss specific outcomes.

While Moscow offered its "comprehensive assessment" of the battlefield situation in Ukraine, Mr Ushakov said the talks were not purely focused on the war in Ukraine.

"Economic issues and potentially large, mutually beneficial joint projects for Russia and America were discussed in considerable detail," he said.

Prior to these meetings, Washington's push to end the fighting had lost momentum, with the United States focused for the past six months on the Iran war.

The last known visit to Moscow by Mr Witkoff and Mr Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, was in January when they also held talks with Mr Putin at the Kremlin.

Russia and Ukraine continue to exchange fire

Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomes Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in Kyiv. (Reuters: Valentyn Ogirenko)

Mr Putin and Mr Zelenskyy had agreed to pause strikes on each other's capitals while the talks took place.

Still, the two traded fire overnight into Sunday in other regions, officials said.

Russian attacks across multiple Ukrainian regions killed one person and injured at least 10 others overnight into Sunday, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.

In Zaporizhzhia, drone strikes killed a 74-year-old man and wounded three people, while a drone damaged an apartment building, injuring seven people, in the Khmelnytskyi region.

Ukraine's air force said on Sunday that it had intercepted 82 drones out of the 108 launched by Russia overnight, along with six missiles.

In Russia, a man was killed and a woman seriously wounded when a Ukrainian drone struck a vehicle, local authorities in the Belgorod border region said.

The Russian Defense Ministry said on Sunday that its air defences overnight shot down 258 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions, occupied Crimea and the waters of the Black and Azov seas.

The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250-kilometre front line. Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, and the recurring wail of air-raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv.

ABC/Wires

World.title: 'People were screaming': Qantas passengers tell of engine spitting fire
World.content:
People screaming and widespread panic are how passengers have described the moment they heard loud bangs and saw fire spitting from an engine on a Sydney-bound Qantas flight.

On Saturday afternoon, Flight QF122 had just left Queenstown in New Zealand when it had to be diverted to Christchurch in what the airline said was a "suspected engine issue".

Kriti Sethi was on her way home after her holidays, and was sitting towards the back of the plane where she "could see the fire" coming from the left-hand side.

"It happened around five times, so we hear bang, bang, bang and there was five times fire coming out," she told the ABC from Sydney Airport after spending the night in Christchurch.

"And then the people were screaming; people were like, 'Oh my God.' It was quite scary."

Kriti Sethi says she was sitting in the back of the plane and could see the fire. (Supplied)

Despite the cabin crew initially blaming the landing gear, Ms Sethi said that, because of her seat's location, she could see everything.

"So we were like, 'No, it's actually fire coming out of the engine, it's not landing gear'."

Adding to the panic and fear was the turbulence.

"So the plane was shaking as well. So it was fire and then went straight into shaking; it was just so scary," she said.

Announcements from captain

Sari-Elle Kraemer, who was sitting on the right-hand side of the plane, said there was a lot of nervous energy on board, especially after the lights went off.

The flight was forced to divert to Christchurch. (Supplied: Kriti Sethi)

While she could not see the fire, she could hear other passengers talking about it and did not know what to think.

"I've never experienced something like that," Ms Kraemer said.

"Just the noise and the fact that people could see fire on the plane was scary, but obviously the pilots are trained to deal with that, and I felt it was under control after a few minutes."

Throughout the ordeal, passengers were kept informed of what was happening.

Ms Sethi said the flight's captain told passengers in one announcement that the plane had experienced a chemical failure with the engines, forcing the aircraft to make an emergency landing in Christchurch.

Fire engines and emergency services were on hand at the tarmac.

Sari-Elle Kraemer says she has "never experienced something like that". (ABC News)

Both women have commended the professionalism of the cabin crew, praising their handling of the incident, and were grateful for the safe landing.

"The cabin crew were amazing, and the captain was amazing,' Ms Sethi said.

"Once we landed, everyone was clapping."

She was still nervous on her trip home, but again the captain "made an announcement, saying 'That we understand what happened yesterday. It was a traumatic experience for you guys'."

Incident under investigation

A spokesperson for Qantas said the plane had been grounded in Christchurch as engineers carry out an inspection and examination.

It will remain there until it is cleared to resume flying, with an investigation underway into what caused the fire.

Engine flames prompt diversion of Qantas flight The Sydney-bound Boeing aircraft left Queenstown in New Zealand after 3pm before it had to be diverted to Christchurch.

In a second incident in two days, another Qantas plane has been grounded temporarily and is under inspection after it was forced to return to Sydney Airport this morning.

Flight QF121 was en route to Queenstown when an incident took place halfway into the trip.

"A flight deck alert indicated a potential issue with the aircraft's anti-skid system," the airline told the ABC.

A recovery flight is being organised for Monday, with passengers forced to stay in Sydney overnight.

'Aircraft is designed for these sorts of things'

International aviation consultant Neil Hansford said that while it remained unclear what caused the issue, an engine blade might have detached.

"And obviously when it's a piece of metal going at that many revs, it's hit a fuel line and the fuel's ignited," he said.

"So the captain's able to shut the engine down, use the fire suppression system and put the fire out.

"The aircraft is designed for these sorts of things, so if an engine loses power on take-off, it's designed to fly on safely and continue to climb.

"These are all controllable circumstances, and you don't necessarily want them, but at least with the training of Qantas pilots, they totally know how to handle it; they're tested in the simulator."

World.title: Dozens of bushfires burn as Qld swelters through above-average temps
World.content:
A large bushfire has caused major disruptions on the Warrego Highway west of Brisbane, as dozens of fires burn in Queensland.

A Prepare to Leave warning was issued about 3:45pm for the blaze burning at Plainland in the Lockyer Valley, forcing the highway to close in both directions between Brisbane and Toowoomba.

The warning has since been downgraded to a Stay Informed advisory, and the highway fully reopened about 5:30pm.

The fire is expected to continue to burn for several days.

The Warrego Highway was closed earlier on Sunday and has since reopened. (ABC News)

There are 78 bushfires across south-east Queensland.

A 24-hour fire ban was imposed yesterday for Ipswich and the Lockyer Valley, set to end at midnight tonight.

Queensland Fire Department deputy chief officer Joel Gordon said hot, dry weather had created challenging firefighting conditions.

"We're currently watching three fires that have been burning for a little while … one up at Sandy Creek … we've also been monitoring [the] fire that started yesterday at Plainland, another one just a little bit further down at Prenzlau."

Homes under threat

Lockyer Valley Regional Council Mayor Tanya Milligan said up to 20 homes could have been at risk.

"They're the homes that the QPS [Queensland Police Service] went and doorknocked," she said.

"A lot of people voluntarily evacuated and left; some decided not to.

"We had some pain-in-the-backside northerly winds, which created some havoc and just made it really unpredictable. We had 26 appliances on site … we had two water bombers. The fire also … jumped across the highway."

Parts of the state sweltered through some of the hottest September temperatures in seven years today, with temperatures five to 10 degrees above average for the month in parts of the south-east.

Senior meteorologist Steven Hadley said the mercury in inland areas reached 34 to 36 degrees Celsius.

"That's the hottest we've seen in September since 2019," he said.

"We're getting into spring now so the sun's getting higher in the sky, [and] more intense, so it's able to heat the ground and air up more readily than it was in August."

World.title: Dockers AFLW star turns ruck coach after injury to assist victory
World.content:
Injured AFLW powerhouse Mim Strom was forced to play ruck coach on the bench as the Dockers steamrolled a Monique Conti-less Richmond by 25 points on the road.

Two-time All-Australian ruck Strom was in agony at Princes Park after a tackle from Tigers midfielder Emelia Yassir in the first quarter of Sunday's clash.

Recruit Eden Zanker was first cab off the rank in the ruck, while Gabby O'Sullivan kicked three goals to help lift the Dockers to a 9.6 (60) to 5.5 (35) win in Indigenous Round.

Later on Sunday, Aishling Moloney finished with four goals as Geelong posted a 13.5 (83) to 7.9 (51) result to pile the misery on a winless Essendon at Kardinia Park.

Lisa Webb's Dockers (2-2) can finish the fourth week of the 12-fixture competition in the top eight, but are bracing to lose Strom for part of their finals push.

Before Sunday, Strom had played 78 consecutive matches since making her debut in 2020.

"She's been on the bench with a big smile, so she's hard to get a read on, but I'll get a medical update," coach Webb told Seven Plus at three-quarter time.

"She's been a ruck coach on the side. She's been a warrior for us, and we'll look after her."

Gabby O'Sullivan (pictured) kicked three goals as Fremantle recorded a 25-point road win over Richmond. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Richmond, which, like Fremantle, has not reached finals since 2024, drop from sixth and could finish as low as 13th with a 2-2 record.

The Tigers are unsure of how serious Conti's injury is, with the 2023 league best-and-fairest managing Achilles soreness.

The five-time All-Australian midfielder was a late withdrawal alongside Fina Dethlefsen, with recruit Georgia Stubs and Kate Dempsey returning to the side.

Youngster Isabel Bacon (24 disposals, six clearances) led the game in Conti's absence, and Olivia Wolmarans kicked two goals.

Geelong's Mikayla Bowen (left) picked up a game-high 40 disposals in her side's 32-point win over Essendon. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

The Dockers took the early advantage after three lead changes in the opening quarter, pipping the Tigers by five points thanks to a goal from O'Sullivan.

Strom's absence did little to sap Fremantle's momentum, with O'Sullivan piling on back-to-back goals as the hosts were kept scoreless in the second term.

It was much the same after half-time, with the Dockers maintaining a perfect record against the Tigers across four meetings since season six in 2022.

At Kardinia Park, scores were level at 1.1 (7) for much of the first quarter before Chantal Mason gave away a free kick for a high tackle on Maggie Johnstone in Essendon's forward-50.

Johnstone converted after the quarter-time siren for a six-point lead, but the Bombers' ascendancy did not last long after Moloney came to life.

The star Irishwoman kicked four of Geelong's six goals in the second term, while the visitors managed just two to trail by 18 points.

Geelong improved its record to 3-1 to tighten its grip on a top-four spot, leaving Essendon languishing in 16th.

Mikayla Bowen had a monster 40 disposals, while Cats star Georgie Prespakis matched older sister and Essendon veteran Maddy with 27 disposals and five clearances.

AAP

World.title: Burnouts and drag races as Red CentreNATS takes over Alice Springs
World.content:
Sitting in the passenger seat as her dad lined up in his classic Ford Falcon XC 393 Stroker to drag race at the 12th annual Red CentreNATS, Montana Taylor looked jubilant, and proud.

The teen and her dad, Ben, had travelled from South Australia to be a part of the festival that celebrates all things horsepower.

"I love it so much, I'm so glad I get to come and experience this," she said, with a massive grin.

Ben and Montana Taylor travelled from South Australia to be at the Red CentreNATS. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

She said she could not wait to drive her dad's car.

"Maybe one day," Mr Taylor said.

The Red CentreNATS is held over four days. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

The event has been part of the Alice Springs calendar for 12 years. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

The Taylors are among the 700 registered entrants into this year's Red CentreNATS — more than half of whom come from interstate, boosting the local economy by about $5 million each year.

The weekend's program was huge, featuring street cruising, show and shines of the incredible array of vintage and new muscle cars, drag races, burnout competitions and a street parade that stopped the town.

The event drew about 700 entrants this year. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Labours of love

A pale blue 1984 Holden Kingswood ute shone bright against the red-brown of the dirt dragway.

It was right at home — it had been in Alice Springs its whole life, according to owner Paul Totani.

Paul Totani enters his Kingswood in the Red CentreNATS every year. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Mr Totani, whose family has been in town since the 1960s, is a licensed aircraft engineer and pilot. But on Saturday he swapped the sky for the dirt, tearing down the drag strip, dust flying.

"It's a family heirloom. It will go to the kids later on, but we get it out once a year for Red CentreNATS," he said.

People of all ages attended this year's Red CentreNATS. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Drag races were a popular event. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

At the show and shine car display, dozens of automobiles sparkled in the sun and inside the Alice Springs Convention Centre.

Proud owners stood beside their lovingly cared-for cars, excited to share their stories.

Heather and Laurie, pictured at the show and shine display, love their car. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Spectators also enjoyed the action from the stands (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Parading the past

Sitting on the back of utes, in deckchairs and on car roof-racks, Alice Springs turned out in force and lined the streets for the annual Red CentreNATS street parade.

It was a perfect day for the parade in Alice Springs. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Australian and Northern Territory pride was on show. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Hundreds of cars rolled around the town's largest roundabout at the base of the MacDonnell Ranges, which glistened in the afternoon sun.

Plenty of old utes were on display. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

These kids watched the parade from a good vantage point. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

It was a family affair for many locals watching the parade. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

One of the spectators was Alice Springs local Lisa Morgan, who said events like the Red CentreNATS helped Alice Springs to shine.

She has volunteered for the event for years.

"Everyone bands together for the excitement, and the rumbles," she said.

World.title: Canadian woman dies in moped crash on Magnetic Island
World.content:
A woman has died after the moped she was riding collided with a car on Magnetic Island in north Queensland.

Emergency services were called to Horseshoe Bay just before 12pm.

A 74-year-old woman, a Canadian national, died at the scene.

The driver of the car was not physically injured.

A Queensland Police Service spokesperson could not confirm whether the woman was a tourist visiting the island.

Horseshoe Bay resident Simone Wall told the ABC multiple bystanders tried to save the woman.

"Everyone, including residents, tourists and lifeguards, worked tirelessly trying to save her," Ms Wall said.

"They never gave up. CPR was commenced immediately and when the lifeguards arrived the defibrillator was applied.

"Our deepest condolences go to her family."

The forensic crash unit is investigating and anyone with information or dash cam footage is urged to contact police.

World.title: Osaka apologises to children after struggling with Achilles issue at US Open
World.content:
Naomi Osaka continued to impress with her style and staying power at the US Open on Saturday as she shrugged off a late Achilles problem to beat Belgian Elise Mertens 6-3, 3-6, 7-5 and reach the fourth round.

For her latest eye-catching walk-on look, the four-time major champion blended boardroom and locker-room aesthetics in a grey checked blazer-hoodie and wide-leg pants, putting a tailored twist on traditional pre-match attire.

She looked on course for a business-like win after the first set but was dragged into a battle in the third, where she had to fight through the Achilles niggle to advance.

"I wouldn't say it's a huge injury," Osaka told reporters. "I'd say it's this ongoing problem that I've had since the grass season.

"I don't know why it hasn't gone away. I feel I've done a lot of things in order to make it better, but maybe the time off wasn't enough. I'm not really sure what the reason is, but the medical timeout was to address that.

"You know, she massaged my leg and stuff, so that seemed to help, and gave me Tylenol."

The 28-year-old, a two-time champion at Flushing Meadows, reeled off three games in succession to take a 4-1 lead in the first set under the lights of Louis Armstrong Stadium, clinching it with a battling hold thanks to a string of booming serves.

Naomi Osaka was pushed hard by Elise Mertens (right) but eventually prevailed in a three-setter. (Getty Images: Dustin Satloff)

Osaka pushed the 23rd seed hard at the start of the next set with some heavy hitting from the baseline before pouncing with a break in the third game, only to surrender the lead by dropping the next two games.

"Honestly, I can't believe I won this match," Osaka said on court after sealing victory, thanking the crowd for the energy it provided.

"There was a certain point where I put my heart on the court and kept trying in every point. Thank you so much, but honestly, I'm shocked I won. I'm not going to lie."

After levelling the match to force a decider, Mertens capitalised on several unforced errors by a frustrated Osaka to gain the upper hand, but there would be another momentum shift in the match after a medical timeout for the Japanese player.

"I didn't play amazing and it was getting me down, sorry about my behaviour, for the little kids watching," said Osaka, who threw her racket to the floor at one point.

"This is my favourite tournament. I wanted to play well in front of you. I'm just that glad I have the opportunity to play another match.

"I thought I was going to be OK, but clearly I was shaky."

After recovering a break late on, Osaka fired a huge ace to take a 6-5 lead and revved up her forehand in the following game to complete the win and earn a meeting with Elena Rybakina in the next round.

Reuters

World.title: You need Uncle Samistan
World.content:
“Trump’s patriotic re-naming of parts of the world is intriguing,” thinks George Manojlovic of Mangerton. “I’m waiting for something more imaginative than Gulf of America or Lake America. American Mayan Yucatán rolls off the tongue, as does Unclesamoa and Unclesamistan. How about Yankee Chewing Guam or Southern Fried Türkiye? Londonald has a familiar ring to it, too.”

The Bee Gees’ Easter Show gig (C8), has notoriety, according to Andrew Cohen of Glebe: “I remember when a handsome young man about 17, brought my 15-year-old sister home to Pymble about 6pm from the Easter Show with his two young brothers in the back of his yellow FC Holden. He politely apologised to my scary fuming father, ‘My brothers and I had commitments’. Dad: ‘I know who you are Mr Gibb. You’re one of those singers on Bandstand. How dare you bring my daughter home after dark. Get back in your car. Don’t go near her again.’ Maurice and Robin saw me watching from a window and their eyes were messaging me their alarm. My sister remains none too pleased about this.”

Marjie Williamson’s pill-popping enquiry (C8) has flooded our mailbox to the extent that it’s challenging to find material on any other subject. It led Nola Scott of Wagga Wagga to say, “I’m right-handed, so I open tablets in a foil pack from the left, just as I write from the left. I don’t think I could do it going backwards.” Michael Johnston of Corlette starts “each of my four foil sheets of tablets in a random spot and congratulate myself when they all finish on the same day. Being right-handed I open them with my left hand as an anti-dementia strategy.”

All very instructive, but maybe it’s worth heeding Col Burns of Lugarno: “I may be ambidextrous or just disorganised, but if I noticed that I was selecting tablets other than at random, I’d assume that those tablets were treatment for my OCD.”

“Lyndall Dawson succinctly and incisively describes the genius of Cathy Wilcox (C8),” says Robyn Cashman of Fernhill. “The suggestion of a book of her work is welcome. It would make a great addition to every school’s modern history reading list. So much food for thought.”

World.title: Part of North Sydney Pool roof blows off just one month after opening
World.content:
NationalNSWSydney councils Part of North Sydney Pool roof blows off just one month after opening Rachel Rasker September 6, 2026 — 8:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A portion of the roof of North Sydney Olympic Pool blew off on Saturday, almost a month to the day since the embattled $122 million project opened its doors on August 7. Photos circulated online showing what appeared to be roof flashing trailing along the street on Saturday afternoon, after powerful winds that reached more than 80km/h pummelled Sydney. North Sydney Pool’s flashing appeared to have blown off on Saturday. Facebook: North Sydney Living/Madaj Bre Residents expressed disappointment at the damage, and questioned how much it would add to the troubled pool’s repair bill. North Sydney residents already face a 52 per cent jump in rates over three years to help fund the project. “I think it’s horrible because this is not the first time that’s happened,” said resident Gregory Barros, referring to the power supply issue that forced the pool to shut its doors a week after opening.



He said someone “needs to be accountable for the hundred million” spent on the beleaguered project, which had an initial estimated cost of $58 million. “Think about if someone was there. It would have been a very big issue,” Barros said. Pool staff confirmed no one was hurt in the incident. North Sydney pool on Saturday. Facebook: North Sydney Living/Madaj Bre “North Sydney experienced significant wind conditions on Saturday, along with many other areas across Sydney. The strong winds resulted in minor damage to a section of roofing at North Sydney Olympic Pool,” a spokesperson for North Sydney Council said in a statement. “The area was made safe and contractors attended the site promptly to undertake repairs. Pool operations were not affected.”





The council was also mired in a separate legal battle with Brewster Hjorth over costs and delays caused by the roof, which was pulled down in 2023 and later replaced. Brewster Hjorth Pty Limited, the corporate trustee behind the architectural practice, has since entered liquidation. While the damaged section had been removed by Sunday, the roof’s blue underlay was exposed to the elements. North Sydney Pool was back open on Sunday, with a section of the roof’s edge missing. Rachel Rasker “It’s a great pool and it’s a shame they have repairs already, when it’s only been open a couple of weeks,” said Matt, a regular swimmer and local who declined to provide his surname. North Sydney Living posted photos on their Facebook page on Sunday, and questioned whether another closure was likely. “No word yet from pool management or council about the extent of the damage or potential disruption to opening times,” the post read.

World.title: Secret hotel meetings and emergency visas: Inside the daring escape of Iran’s female footballers
World.content:
NationalMiddle East at war Secret hotel meetings and emergency visas: Inside the daring escape of Iran’s female footballers Tara Brown and Anne Worthington September 6, 2026 — 8:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The two female footballers from Iran who courageously took on Tehran before seeking asylum in Australia have broken their silence, saying they have no regrets about standing up to the Islamic Republic’s brutal regime. Speaking exclusively to 60 Minutes six months after they and their teammates refused to sing Iran’s national anthem at the Asian Cup on the Gold Coast, Atefeh Ramezanisadeh and Fatemeh Pasandideh – who go by Ati and Pasand – have recently been granted Australian citizenship. Atefeh Ramezanisadeh and Fatemeh Pasandideh (Ati and Pasand) have recently been granted Australian citizenship. 60 Minutes Now finally safe, the duo have shared the inside story of how they triumphed over tyranny. Arriving in Australia in late February – just weeks after Iranian authorities slaughtered tens of thousands during widespread anti-government protests – the team, known as The Lionesses, had been explicitly warned against any acts of disloyalty.



Yet with the world watching as they took the field in Queensland, Ati, Pasand and their teammates made the extraordinary decision to stand in solidarity with those killed and remain silent as their national song played. “We just wanted to stand with our people,” Pasand said. “I was scared at times, but I just tried to do what was right, and to say that no one should be killed just for protesting.” Members of the Iranian women’s soccer team disembark in Sydney on their way back to Iran. Ben Symons Ati said her decision to not sing was done knowing full well the act of defiance could mean a matter of life and death. “I wanted to sing the anthem with pride and from my heart but because of the situation in Iran, I really couldn’t do it. At that moment, the only thing that gave me peace and a clear conscience was not singing it.”



The backlash was immediate. Iran’s state broadcaster released a video branding the women traitors and demanding they be punished. Pasand said she knew that was no empty threat and feared the reality back home would be “even worse” than the threats made by the broadcaster. Related Article Exclusive

Middle East at war Tears, terse interactions as officials swoop in to escort Iranians home Watching closely from Canberra was Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke. War had erupted in Iran days after the team’s arrival in Australia, already sparking safety concerns within the federal government. But Burke said it was Tehran’s furious reaction to the protest that proved to be the “volcanic moment”, leaving no doubt about the urgent need to protect the Iranian players. “It was at that point that I knew we couldn’t end up in a situation where these women played all their games, got to the airport, left, and we’d never found a way of checking if they wanted to stay,” Burke told 60 Minutes. But finding a way to get a message to the women was no easy feat, with Iranian minders watching the players’ every move.



Burke said the opportunity came on March 8, as the women came from the field after their third and final match against the Philippines. “There were the tiniest interactions with some of our officials where we just said, ‘If you want to seek protection from Australia, we’re open to have that conversation with you’. And the seed was planted.” Australian officials were able to further discuss possibilities to stay with some of the players in a secret midnight meeting in the foyer of their Gold Coast hotel. Iranian footballer Atefeh Ramezanisadeh fled her national team to remain in Australia. 60 Minutes Ati said the enormity of the decision to leave their loved ones in Iran and begin a new life in a strange country or return home and face the consequences was an agonising choice.



“We were under so much stress. We didn’t know if we were doing the right thing. We were terrified and anxious – it was a mix of feelings,” she said. “And the night we made the decision, none of us slept until 5am.” At lunchtime the next day, Ati, Pasand and three other players managed to indicate to Australian Federal Police officers waiting in the hotel lobby that they had made up their mind. The players’ escape from team officials was co-ordinated by the AFP, who took the women to a safe house where, later that evening, Burke granted emergency humanitarian visas to the five Iranian women. Pasand recalls feeling “in complete shock” at the time and worried about whether she had made the right decision.



“The team was like my family and I felt like I was leaving them. I was worried about what would happen to them and to me,” she said. Two other women would also seek asylum in the days that followed, but one by one those who had opted to stay changed their minds until only Ati and Pasand remained. Burke said enormous pressure was being placed on the players’ families by the Iranian authorities, something he said Australia had no control over. “We couldn’t keep their families safe,” he said. “And the pressure that I could never do anything about was the pressure that they might receive over the phone. You can’t imagine what that would be like. Where there’s an outcome that is so good for you that carries such grave risk for your family and for the people you love.” Ati says her family was also visited by Iranian authorities and given internet access so they could contact her and request she come home. Despite knowing she might never see her family again, she stood firm.



“The fear grew, the stress got worse and we felt more alone than ever. I kept questioning if staying was right but in the end I am glad I stood by my decision,” Ati said. Six months on, Ati and Pasand said they are doing their best to start new lives in Australia and are enjoying newfound freedoms they once could only dream of. The pair are training with Brisbane-based club Wynnum Wolves and have ambitions to one day play professional football again. Atefeh Ramezanisadeh and Fatemeh Pasandideh training with the Brisbane-based club Wynnum Wolves. 60 Minutes But their thoughts are never far away from the family they left behind and their fellow Lionesses who returned to Iran.



“I miss my teammates and I hope they’re doing well,” Pasand says. As the war rages on in their homeland they can only hope to one day return to a free Iran. But Pasand remains optimistic that change in her homeland will happen. “The only thing I believe is that brutality will never last forever.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: AFLW round four: Few knew there was a double-header on. That’s a real problem
World.content:
Sunday at Ikon Park showcased an action-packed day of footy with a double-header that saw Fremantle triumph over Richmond, and Carlton continue their winning streak with a resounding victory over Collingwood.

It’s a shame more people weren’t there to see it.

Blues and Pies during Sunday’s double-header. Getty Images

A crowd of 1931 fans showed up to watch the Richmond game at 12.30 at Ikon Park for the second week of Indigenous Round. The Carlton versus Collingwood clash at 3pm had an attendance of 3892 (an accumulative figure that counts fans who came for the first game, but might not have stayed for the second).

This is obviously a nuanced conversation.

Mother’s Day has traditionally been a dead fixture for AFL men’s with significantly lower attendance records, so it makes sense the women’s league would experience a similar decrease for Father’s Day.

It’s also important to note we’re in the middle of the men’s finals season – a time when many fans could be experiencing footy fatigue or aren’t paying attention to the women’s league.

But walking around Ikon Park, you couldn’t help feel this weekend was a missed opportunity. Most of the stands were empty, and the green space outside the suburban stadium was fairly barren.

Fremantle triumphed over Richmond by 25 points in the first double-header on Sunday. Getty Images

A double-header typically means you want to encourage fans to stay at the stadium for both games, which means the following need to be on offer: music, entertainment, activation stands and numerous food options and stalls.

There was none of that on Sunday, except a few merch stands and one gourmet burger stand.

Longtime AFLW fan Amy Stephens has only missed two Collingwood games since 2018 and was cheering for the Pies from the boundary line on Sunday.

However, the supporter said she had no idea there was a double-header on today, citing the lack of advertising around the event.

Stephens said only realised there was a double-header when she checked the fine print on her Ticketmaster account, but she’d already left home and missed the game.

“I think there needs to be more advertising for AFLW in general, let alone a double-header,” she said.

Stephens said it would be good to have activities or entertainment between the two games, to “break up the day” and encourage people to stay.

She also wanted to see a bigger advertising push on social media and on television, so fans could actually know a double-header was on.

Several other fans this masthead spoke said they had no idea a double-header was on today.

Sunday’s attendance at Ikon Park is made more bleak by the fact double-headers – when advertised and publicised properly – do really well. Footy fans have voted with their feet over the first three rounds, with AFLW attendances up by more than 50 per cent compared with the same stage last season. The growth has been driven largely by five double-headers, with the men’s game, which have drawn crowds as big 20,000, in tier one stadiums.

Carlton coach Matthew Buck reiterated his support for the double-header concept after the Blues won by 39 points – their fourth consecutive win this season.

When asked if he was hoping for more  around the double-header, Buck didn’t specify his thoughts, but said he thought there was “a great vibe within the crowd”.

“I’m all for it [the double-headers],” he said. “I think we could take those to Marvel as well, and fill Marvel up with them, it’d be fantastic.

“But what we know is when we play at Ikon Park and our Carlton fans turn up, that it’s a great place to be. And I think Freo, Richmond might have felt a little bit of that towards the end of their game.”

Double-header are proven to work.

But if the AFL want to meet their attendance benchmarks and fill stadiums for W games, they need to make sure fans actually know when the games are on.

World.title: A school separated boys and girls until year 10. It has delivered record VCE scores
World.content:
When Brad Fry arrived as the new principal at Tintern Grammar in 2015, the school was just emerging from a profound period of change. The school that began as a co-educational school had become girls-only before opening a separate campus for boys and then becoming co-educational again. Principal Brad Fry with students at the school’s farm. Simon Schluter But this time, there was a difference, with students at the Ringwood East school taught in single-gender classes between prep and year 9, and coming together for lunch and extracurricular activities such as orchestra, drama productions and time spent on the school’s farm. Fry says the two-stream system is one contributor to Tintern Grammar’s academic success. It has been named The Age’s 2026 Schools that Excel award winner for the eastern Melbourne region.



The annual series celebrates schools that have achieved outstanding advancement in their VCE results over the past decade. “I think the model we have is one of the key things that gets them ready for VCE,” Fry says. “We can instil a lot of really positive attitudes and dispositions by virtue of the fact that they’ve been parallel.” Related Article Consent crisis ‘Girls feel betrayed’: Dani survived sexual assault by a boy at 14. She says girls’ education is now at stake In 2016, Tintern Grammar recorded a median study score of 32, but during the depths of the COVID-19 pandemic, that dipped to 30. In the past few years, its results have shot up, with the school attaining a median study score of 33 in 2023, and then achieving its best-ever median study scores of 34 in 2024 and 2025.



The percentage of students achieving study scores of 40 and above is also on the rise, climbing from 11.1 per cent in 2016 to a 10-year-high of 18.6 per cent last year. A total of 11 students achieved a study score of 40 or above in maths methods last year, there were 10 scores of 40-plus in general maths, seven in physical education and four in business management. This was the best result Tintern has achieved in each of these subjects in the past decade. One student recorded a perfect score of 50 in English, but keep in mind these figures are from students who permitted their VCE results to be published, so the school’s true total is likely even higher. For Fry, a former science and maths teacher, the parallel learning model works because girls and boys learn differently.



“I think we can say that, in a general sense, young men don’t do things like sit still as well as girls do,” he observes. “They like to learn by doing things.” Year 12 student Olivia Cardamone joined Tintern in year 9 from an all-girls school. The 17-year-old says the parallel learning model gave her a chance to settle in and build confidence in an environment in which she was comfortable before transitioning to co-educational classes. “It was an easy move because we already knew each other from being around the school,” she says.



“And it was really great in classes like English because until year 9, we’d always had the female perspective in discussions. But afterwards, we got the male perspective, too, so it broadened how we interpreted things.” Sebastian Humphrys, joint school captain with Cardamone, says the model had served him well. “It let me develop leadership skills and confidence, and then the gradual merge to co-ed classes was more comfortable,” says the 18-year-old aspiring teacher. Students Sebastian Humphrys and Olivia Cardamone with some of the school’s merino sheep. Simon Schluter Vice school captain Isabella Di Felice, 18, found the model allowed her to develop whom she was in a supportive environment, and to try new things.



“And now that it’s co-ed, we mix really well and have friendship groups made up of boys and girls.” Another secret to the school’s success is its well-established careers program, which Cheuk Yui Lam, 18, says gave him invaluable work experience in the hospitality industry. This, he says, allowed him to hone the communication and people skills he hopes to call on as a secondary teacher. Fry considers the program a collaboration between staff and senior students at the school which marks its 150th anniversary next year. He says it is a chance to ensure students don’t just focus on subjects that “get marked up” when the ATAR is calculated. “If students aren’t studying subjects that they are passionate about, then they are not going to do well,” he says.



Fry is proud of students’ achievements and the dedication of his 119 staff but says ATAR results are not what makes the school tick. “We don’t even talk about results, apart from in the staff room when they come out,” he says. Editor's pick Science A Cinderella story: Why most women are wearing the wrong size shoes “The analogy I use is you don’t run onto the football field thinking about what the score will be at the end because if you do that, you’re not concentrating on the things that create the score.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Schools that Excel 2026: Find out your school’s VCE results over the past decade
World.content:
Welcome to the eighth edition of Schools that Excel, an annual series in which The Age celebrates schools that achieve outstanding improvement in their VCE results. The Age has gathered VCE results data from the past 10 years for every secondary school in the state offering year 12 subjects and turned it into an easy-to-use dashboard to show how each school fared over time, its top subjects, and more. Enter the name of your school in the interactive below to see the results: The Schools that Excel interactive brings together detailed results from Victorian government, independent and Catholic schools.



Loading What can I learn from this interactive tool? The interactive tool lets you gauge a school’s VCE performance over a 10-year period, so you can see whether it has improved or maintained its results. When VCE results are released in December, only the current year’s figures are provided. That information is useful, but doesn’t tell you about how representative the results are of the school’s typical performance. By threading together data from the past decade, a much clearer picture emerges. Ava Du’Pratt (front), Evie Parisis (back)Thomas Murton and Nithara Anooj (front). Former student Dylan Gekas tutors VCE students at Overnewton Anglican Community College. Joe Armao



But not all schools cater to students who are aiming for a place at university, and the Schools that Excel dashboard reflects this – you can also see how students enrolled in VET programs fared. Kardinia International College students Sam Carr and Zahli Williamson with principal Catherine Lockhart. Eddie Jim What does the dashboard show? The information about each school is divided into several panels. Here is a guide to interpreting the data: Average student performance shows the median VCE subject study score for the school since 2016, which is a good indicator of typical student achievement. Study scores are out of 50, and 30 is the average. The horizontal line at 30 on the graph is the yardstick that shows how the typical student at this school fares against the statewide average.



The interactive does not show median ATARs because this data is not available for the past decade for each school. High achievers shows the percentage of the school’s VCE subject scores that were among the best in the state. These are scores of 40 or above, which put students within the top 10 per cent of all those who completed that VCE subject. This panel also shows the subjects in which students obtained the best results. Tintern Grammar School students Sebastian Humphrys and Olivia Cardamone with some of the school’s merino sheep. Simon Schluter Completion rates shows the enrolment numbers in VCE and VET over the past five years, as well as the satisfactory completion rates among year 12s. Unfortunately, data was not released on VET completion rates in 2021, which is highlighted in the interactive. VCE VM and VPC provides data on the new VCE Vocational Major and the Victorian Pathways Certificate programs, which were implemented in schools to replace the Victorian Certificate of Applied Learning (VCAL) from 2023. The data shows whether the vocational major or pathways certificate were offered at a school and how many year 12 students completed either stream. And while VCAL has been phased out, the interactive displays enrolment and completion data for it from 2020-2022.



In addition, changes to VCAL – due to the VCE Vocational Major and the Victorian Pathways Certificate being phased in from 2023 – also mean that there were far fewer VCAL enrolments in 2023. School awards shows five high-gain schools that The Age judged as having shown the best improvement in their VCE results over the past decade. One school was selected from Melbourne’s south, east, north and west, as well as rural/regional Victoria. Starting in 2025, we also started recognising one school in Victoria that has shown improvement in its vocational education completion rates over the past five years. In previous years, we included a Student pathways section that shows whether a school’s graduates from the previous two years went on to further study at university or TAFE, or whether they took on an apprenticeship or joined the workforce. This data was from the Department of Education’s annual On Track survey. This survey was not carried out with 2024 graduates in 2025, so this section is blank in this year’s Schools that Excel interactive. However, the results for participating schools from the survey of students who graduated in 2023 can be found here in our Victorian Schools Guide. Gleneagles Secondary College Principal Jo Sayer and former student Jonah Heta, who now works at the school. Eddie Jim



Which schools are featured in the dashboard? The interactive dashboard features data on more than 500 Victorian schools that offered year 12 subjects in 2025. Principal of Sandringham College Amy Porter with some of her students. Simon Schluter It also includes schools classified as “small” by the VCAA, for having enrolments below a certain threshold. A dialogue box will pop up in the interactive if you enter the name of a small school and flag that its performance may not be comparable with larger schools, and that it may not be possible to observe a trend in results over the 10-year time frame. If a school has few students, it means the median and its percentage of study scores of 40 or above can fluctuate greatly year-on-year depending on the cohort.



Which schools do not feature in the interactive? Schools for which there is insufficient data, schools that exclusively offer the International Baccalaureate, and adult education institutions do not show up in the interactive. There might also be gaps in the data for years in which student enrolments did not reach a certain threshold. What other VCE and VET data is available at The Age? Earlier this year, The Age launched our Victorian Schools Guide, an interactive dashboard that displays comprehensive VCE and vocational data.



Most of the information that is available in the Schools that Excel interactive can be found in the Victorian Schools Guide, along with more detailed data on school performance and enrolments. Mill Park Secondary College principal Tim Natoli and Mustafa Khraim, Shub Bath, Scarlett Yaziji and Yangu Pan. Ruby Alexander The Victorian Schools Guide is a section of The Age website that also features some of our education team’s most recent reporting and analysis on VCE teaching, school performance and trends. We plan to add new sections and additional data sets to the Victorian Schools Guide in coming months to help guide you in your school choices, so it is worth bookmarking it in your browser. Type the name of your school in the search box below to check it out:



How were the Schools that Excel awards decided? We used Department of Health boundaries to categorise schools as metropolitan or regional and divided the metropolitan region into west, north, east and south Melbourne. Schools in each region were chosen based on their records of improvement in median VCE study scores, while the winner for the new vocational education category was chosen based on improvement in VET completion rates. Schools that Excel winners 2026 Eastern Melbourne: Tintern Grammar School

Tintern Grammar School Southern Melbourne: Sandringham College

Sandringham College Western Melbourne: Overnewton Anglican Community College

Overnewton Anglican Community College Northern Melbourne: Mill Park Secondary College

Mill Park Secondary College Regional and Rural Victoria: Kardinia International College

World.title: The Swans’ famous finals win that reclaimed their club
World.content:
Four Points SportAFLAFL 2026 The Swans’ famous finals win that reclaimed their club Michael Gleeson September 6, 2026 — 7:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading Key points The Swans reshaped an image of themselves in just two hours.

When Jack Ginnivan said what he said, it felt like he was dead right.

Oh, Errol!: What could have been goal of the year.

The ovation for Matthew Nicks showed the Crows board what the fans thought.

Sydney’s image reshape The Swans did, if not the impossible, then the highly unlikely. In some ways, winning the game was their least surprising achievement. Somehow, they made themselves likeable. Admirable even. That outcome seemed more implausible for the past three weeks than the prospect of them winning a final against the reigning premiers. The shamed club reshaped an image of themselves in two hours on the SCG. Even long-term fans had spoken of finding it hard to support the club, or to reconcile what they felt for them, after the embarrassment of the Pullman Hotel saga. So the real consequence of Saturday’s win was not the upending of the finals series – and they certainly did that – it was the reclaiming of an image of them as a club.



Playing with pride: Sydney’s Charlie Curnow. Getty Images After three weeks of ignominy and opprobrium that tainted the club and undermined what it had represented they performed in such a manner on the field, doing the thing they exist for, that it moved you to want them to win. You found yourself barracking for them. Maybe that is just the enjoyment of watching an underdog win. Maybe it is the simple sympathy for the players and coaches who were collateral damage from what happened at the Pullman that left the whole club gasping for air. Another perspective AFL 2026 From the dark hours of Pullman shame, Swans produce one of their finest wins This is not a comment that implies winning excuses behaviour or is a salve for any hurt. It is a recognition that those not suspended responded in a way to repay or reclaim fans and members.



It is recognition that the club said when they punished their players that they were prepared for the fact the players’ behaviour which prompted the suspensions might have torpedoed the season. And yet, the players and coaches left to play out the year said ‘no it hasn’t, we’re better than that and we will show you’. So the Swans, five players down, three of them bona fide elites of the competition, lose their captain early in the game and still thoroughly outplay the best side of the last two years. The Swans will hope that the two hours on the SCG were as influential to mould the idea of what Sydney stands for as the early morning hours in the Pullman. The fact is, this was one of the great finals wins by any club. Full stop. That’s the point. As a contest, it was absorbing. As a game, it was exhilarating. But that element alone didn’t make it great.





Logan McDonald decided now was the time to play his best-ever game, indeed his best ever three games in a row. James Rowbottom offered a singlemindedness and aggression that compensated for any missing midfielder. The Swans were great because of Errol Gulden. The man whose name sounds like a London law firm, he played with a speed and class superior to anyone on the field. The Swans’ midfield might now be called Errol Gulden and associates. It was a great final because Brisbane got back to three goals down and could have and should have had the greater depth of class to prevail, and didn’t. Pausing for thought: Brisbane coach Chris Fagan. AFL Photos Chris Fagan could not resist thinking his players, like the rest of us, had agreed with Andrew Pridham that the Swans had torpedoed their season.



“Somewhere back in the deep recesses of their mind, I just wonder whether they really thought it was going to be as hard as what it was,” Fagan said. “Did you really think that Sydney were going to be that good, or did you think it was going to be maybe a walk in the park? Because that’s how it had been painted by all and sundry that’s following football. And probably quite rightly so.” Loading Jack’s oopsy Jack Ginnivan after Thursday night’s win delighted in the fact Hawthorn were now on the “right side of the (finals) draw”. That is, they had either Adelaide, the Bulldogs or Sydney.



And when he said it, it felt like he was dead right. Everyone had discounted the idea of Sydney winning, or being any form of threat in the finals. Now it is far less clear which side of the draw is right. Simply pumped: Hawthorn’s Jack Ginnivan. via Getty Images Oh, Errol … goal of the year contender Errol Gulden can’t win goal of the year. But he should. He kicked it on Saturday afternoon. Izak Rankine offered up a similarly disallowed challenger hours later, but Gulden’s was still better. Nights earlier Jordan Clarke might have taken mark of the year. Also not allowed.



Gulden’s was special. Sam Draper had just kicked a goal for the Lions 30 minutes into the third quarter. Strangely, with only a couple of minutes of playing time left, he ran off to the interchange. The Lions had if not a sniff, then a whiff. They were 34 points down but with a flush of momentum. The next bounce and Gulden takes it away lifts the ball out of the grasp of Hugh McCluggage and runs by the rest of the centre back. He takes a bounce, runs through centre half forward drawing and handballing over a Lions defender, got a handball back, ran to his left baulking another Lions defender and snapped the ball at goal on his left. All at full pace. It had striking similarity to Noah Anderson’s goal of the year last year, but this had far greater consequence. Later on Saturday Rankine’s crumb and snap on his right foot from the right point post while he was facing the crowd had to bend in a way it shouldn’t have.



Neither can win goal of the year because, like mark of the year, the eligibility period doesn’t include finals. Which is silly really because firstly, it deserves to at least be considered, and secondly and yes, it’s a bit pedantic but rename it goal of the season not year if you are not going to include finals. Nicks of time for win Football boards get twitchy. The idea that Matthew Nicks was coaching for his job was silly given his team were minor premiers last year, lost their most dynamic player to suspension for the whole finals series, and he’d made finals again this year. Silly perhaps, but that doesn’t mean it was not true. The board, any football board, would wonder if they had the right coach to take them further if they went out of the finals again. Geelong famously did with Mark Thompson as did Richmond and Damien Hardwick. Chris Fagan’s Lions went out in straight sets twice in his first three finals series. He was one win and five losses in his first six finals over three years. They stuck with him. He turned out alright.



Nicks took over a team before it had bottomed out and he drove them up the ladder. As is the odd thing in coaching he started with a three-year contract when they were poor but when they won the minor premiership he got the shortest of his contract extensions, just one year. The ovation for him when he was on screen and could not suppress his smile in the last quarter showed the board what the fans thought. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: You need Uncle Samistan
World.content:
“Trump’s patriotic re-naming of parts of the world is intriguing,” thinks George Manojlovic of Mangerton. “I’m waiting for something more imaginative than Gulf of America or Lake America. American Mayan Yucatán rolls off the tongue, as does Unclesamoa and Unclesamistan. How about Yankee Chewing Guam or Southern Fried Türkiye? Londonald has a familiar ring to it, too.”

The Bee Gees’ Easter Show gig (C8), has notoriety, according to Andrew Cohen of Glebe: “I remember when a handsome young man about 17, brought my 15-year-old sister home to Pymble about 6pm from the Easter Show with his two young brothers in the back of his yellow FC Holden. He politely apologised to my scary fuming father, ‘My brothers and I had commitments’. Dad: ‘I know who you are Mr Gibb. You’re one of those singers on Bandstand. How dare you bring my daughter home after dark. Get back in your car. Don’t go near her again.’ Maurice and Robin saw me watching from a window and their eyes were messaging me their alarm. My sister remains none too pleased about this.”

Marjie Williamson’s pill-popping enquiry (C8) has flooded our mailbox to the extent that it’s challenging to find material on any other subject. It led Nola Scott of Wagga Wagga to say, “I’m right-handed, so I open tablets in a foil pack from the left, just as I write from the left. I don’t think I could do it going backwards.” Michael Johnston of Corlette starts “each of my four foil sheets of tablets in a random spot and congratulate myself when they all finish on the same day. Being right-handed I open them with my left hand as an anti-dementia strategy.”

All very instructive, but maybe it’s worth heeding Col Burns of Lugarno: “I may be ambidextrous or just disorganised, but if I noticed that I was selecting tablets other than at random, I’d assume that those tablets were treatment for my OCD.”

“Lyndall Dawson succinctly and incisively describes the genius of Cathy Wilcox (C8),” says Robyn Cashman of Fernhill. “The suggestion of a book of her work is welcome. It would make a great addition to every school’s modern history reading list. So much food for thought.”

World.title: Part of North Sydney Pool roof blows off just one month after opening
World.content:
NationalNSWSydney councils Part of North Sydney Pool roof blows off just one month after opening Rachel Rasker September 6, 2026 — 8:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A portion of the roof of North Sydney Olympic Pool blew off on Saturday, almost a month to the day since the embattled $122 million project opened its doors on August 7. Photos circulated online showing what appeared to be roof flashing trailing along the street on Saturday afternoon, after powerful winds that reached more than 80km/h pummelled Sydney. North Sydney Pool’s flashing appeared to have blown off on Saturday. Facebook: North Sydney Living/Madaj Bre Residents expressed disappointment at the damage, and questioned how much it would add to the troubled pool’s repair bill. North Sydney residents already face a 52 per cent jump in rates over three years to help fund the project. “I think it’s horrible because this is not the first time that’s happened,” said resident Gregory Barros, referring to the power supply issue that forced the pool to shut its doors a week after opening.



He said someone “needs to be accountable for the hundred million” spent on the beleaguered project, which had an initial estimated cost of $58 million. “Think about if someone was there. It would have been a very big issue,” Barros said. Pool staff confirmed no one was hurt in the incident. North Sydney pool on Saturday. Facebook: North Sydney Living/Madaj Bre “North Sydney experienced significant wind conditions on Saturday, along with many other areas across Sydney. The strong winds resulted in minor damage to a section of roofing at North Sydney Olympic Pool,” a spokesperson for North Sydney Council said in a statement. “The area was made safe and contractors attended the site promptly to undertake repairs. Pool operations were not affected.”





The council was also mired in a separate legal battle with Brewster Hjorth over costs and delays caused by the roof, which was pulled down in 2023 and later replaced. Brewster Hjorth Pty Limited, the corporate trustee behind the architectural practice, has since entered liquidation. While the damaged section had been removed by Sunday, the roof’s blue underlay was exposed to the elements. North Sydney Pool was back open on Sunday, with a section of the roof’s edge missing. Rachel Rasker “It’s a great pool and it’s a shame they have repairs already, when it’s only been open a couple of weeks,” said Matt, a regular swimmer and local who declined to provide his surname. North Sydney Living posted photos on their Facebook page on Sunday, and questioned whether another closure was likely. “No word yet from pool management or council about the extent of the damage or potential disruption to opening times,” the post read.
