World.title: Secret hotel meetings and emergency visas: Inside the daring escape of Iran’s female footballers
World.content:
NationalMiddle East at war Secret hotel meetings and emergency visas: Inside the daring escape of Iran’s female footballers Tara Brown and Anne Worthington September 6, 2026 — 8:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The two female footballers from Iran who courageously took on Tehran before seeking asylum in Australia have broken their silence, saying they have no regrets about standing up to the Islamic Republic’s brutal regime. Speaking exclusively to 60 Minutes six months after they and their teammates refused to sing Iran’s national anthem at the Asian Cup on the Gold Coast, Atefeh Ramezanisadeh and Fatemeh Pasandideh – who go by Ati and Pasand – have recently been granted Australian citizenship. Atefeh Ramezanisadeh and Fatemeh Pasandideh (Ati and Pasand) have recently been granted Australian citizenship. 60 Minutes Now finally safe, the duo have shared the inside story of how they triumphed over tyranny. Arriving in Australia in late February – just weeks after Iranian authorities slaughtered tens of thousands during widespread anti-government protests – the team, known as The Lionesses, had been explicitly warned against any acts of disloyalty.



Yet with the world watching as they took the field in Queensland, Ati, Pasand and their teammates made the extraordinary decision to stand in solidarity with those killed and remain silent as their national song played. “We just wanted to stand with our people,” Pasand said. “I was scared at times, but I just tried to do what was right, and to say that no one should be killed just for protesting.” Members of the Iranian women’s soccer team disembark in Sydney on their way back to Iran. Ben Symons Ati said her decision to not sing was done knowing full well the act of defiance could mean a matter of life and death. “I wanted to sing the anthem with pride and from my heart but because of the situation in Iran, I really couldn’t do it. At that moment, the only thing that gave me peace and a clear conscience was not singing it.”



The backlash was immediate. Iran’s state broadcaster released a video branding the women traitors and demanding they be punished. Pasand said she knew that was no empty threat and feared the reality back home would be “even worse” than the threats made by the broadcaster. Related Article Exclusive

Middle East at war Tears, terse interactions as officials swoop in to escort Iranians home Watching closely from Canberra was Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke. War had erupted in Iran days after the team’s arrival in Australia, already sparking safety concerns within the federal government. But Burke said it was Tehran’s furious reaction to the protest that proved to be the “volcanic moment”, leaving no doubt about the urgent need to protect the Iranian players. “It was at that point that I knew we couldn’t end up in a situation where these women played all their games, got to the airport, left, and we’d never found a way of checking if they wanted to stay,” Burke told 60 Minutes. But finding a way to get a message to the women was no easy feat, with Iranian minders watching the players’ every move.



Burke said the opportunity came on March 8, as the women came from the field after their third and final match against the Philippines. “There were the tiniest interactions with some of our officials where we just said, ‘If you want to seek protection from Australia, we’re open to have that conversation with you’. And the seed was planted.” Australian officials were able to further discuss possibilities to stay with some of the players in a secret midnight meeting in the foyer of their Gold Coast hotel. Iranian footballer Atefeh Ramezanisadeh fled her national team to remain in Australia. 60 Minutes Ati said the enormity of the decision to leave their loved ones in Iran and begin a new life in a strange country or return home and face the consequences was an agonising choice.



“We were under so much stress. We didn’t know if we were doing the right thing. We were terrified and anxious – it was a mix of feelings,” she said. “And the night we made the decision, none of us slept until 5am.” At lunchtime the next day, Ati, Pasand and three other players managed to indicate to Australian Federal Police officers waiting in the hotel lobby that they had made up their mind. The players’ escape from team officials was co-ordinated by the AFP, who took the women to a safe house where, later that evening, Burke granted emergency humanitarian visas to the five Iranian women. Pasand recalls feeling “in complete shock” at the time and worried about whether she had made the right decision.



“The team was like my family and I felt like I was leaving them. I was worried about what would happen to them and to me,” she said. Two other women would also seek asylum in the days that followed, but one by one those who had opted to stay changed their minds until only Ati and Pasand remained. Burke said enormous pressure was being placed on the players’ families by the Iranian authorities, something he said Australia had no control over. “We couldn’t keep their families safe,” he said. “And the pressure that I could never do anything about was the pressure that they might receive over the phone. You can’t imagine what that would be like. Where there’s an outcome that is so good for you that carries such grave risk for your family and for the people you love.” Ati says her family was also visited by Iranian authorities and given internet access so they could contact her and request she come home. Despite knowing she might never see her family again, she stood firm.



“The fear grew, the stress got worse and we felt more alone than ever. I kept questioning if staying was right but in the end I am glad I stood by my decision,” Ati said. Six months on, Ati and Pasand said they are doing their best to start new lives in Australia and are enjoying newfound freedoms they once could only dream of. The pair are training with Brisbane-based club Wynnum Wolves and have ambitions to one day play professional football again. Atefeh Ramezanisadeh and Fatemeh Pasandideh training with the Brisbane-based club Wynnum Wolves. 60 Minutes But their thoughts are never far away from the family they left behind and their fellow Lionesses who returned to Iran.



“I miss my teammates and I hope they’re doing well,” Pasand says. As the war rages on in their homeland they can only hope to one day return to a free Iran. But Pasand remains optimistic that change in her homeland will happen. “The only thing I believe is that brutality will never last forever.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: AFLW round four: Few knew there was a double-header on. That’s a real problem
World.content:
Sunday at Ikon Park showcased an action-packed day of footy with a double-header that saw Fremantle triumph over Richmond, and Carlton continue their winning streak with a resounding victory over Collingwood.

It’s a shame more people weren’t there to see it.

Blues and Pies during Sunday’s double-header. Getty Images

A crowd of 1931 fans showed up to watch the Richmond game at 12.30 at Ikon Park for the second week of Indigenous Round. The Carlton versus Collingwood clash at 3pm had an attendance of 3892 (an accumulative figure that counts fans who came for the first game, but might not have stayed for the second).

This is obviously a nuanced conversation.

Mother’s Day has traditionally been a dead fixture for AFL men’s with significantly lower attendance records, so it makes sense the women’s league would experience a similar decrease for Father’s Day.

It’s also important to note we’re in the middle of the men’s finals season – a time when many fans could be experiencing footy fatigue or aren’t paying attention to the women’s league.

But walking around Ikon Park, you couldn’t help feel this weekend was a missed opportunity. Most of the stands were empty, and the green space outside the suburban stadium was fairly barren.

Fremantle triumphed over Richmond by 25 points in the first double-header on Sunday. Getty Images

A double-header typically means you want to encourage fans to stay at the stadium for both games, which means the following need to be on offer: music, entertainment, activation stands and numerous food options and stalls.

There was none of that on Sunday, except a few merch stands and one gourmet burger stand.

Longtime AFLW fan Amy Stephens has only missed two Collingwood games since 2018 and was cheering for the Pies from the boundary line on Sunday.

However, the supporter said she had no idea there was a double-header on today, citing the lack of advertising around the event.

Stephens said only realised there was a double-header when she checked the fine print on her Ticketmaster account, but she’d already left home and missed the game.

“I think there needs to be more advertising for AFLW in general, let alone a double-header,” she said.

Stephens said it would be good to have activities or entertainment between the two games, to “break up the day” and encourage people to stay.

She also wanted to see a bigger advertising push on social media and on television, so fans could actually know a double-header was on.

Several other fans this masthead spoke said they had no idea a double-header was on today.

Sunday’s attendance at Ikon Park is made more bleak by the fact double-headers – when advertised and publicised properly – do really well. Footy fans have voted with their feet over the first three rounds, with AFLW attendances up by more than 50 per cent compared with the same stage last season. The growth has been driven largely by five double-headers, with the men’s game, which have drawn crowds as big 20,000, in tier one stadiums.

Carlton coach Matthew Buck reiterated his support for the double-header concept after the Blues won by 39 points – their fourth consecutive win this season.

When asked if he was hoping for more  around the double-header, Buck didn’t specify his thoughts, but said he thought there was “a great vibe within the crowd”.

“I’m all for it [the double-headers],” he said. “I think we could take those to Marvel as well, and fill Marvel up with them, it’d be fantastic.

“But what we know is when we play at Ikon Park and our Carlton fans turn up, that it’s a great place to be. And I think Freo, Richmond might have felt a little bit of that towards the end of their game.”

Double-header are proven to work.

But if the AFL want to meet their attendance benchmarks and fill stadiums for W games, they need to make sure fans actually know when the games are on.

World.title: Demand leaders act for our survival
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Demand leaders act for our survival September 6, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Badiucao To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. CLIMATE CHANGE Nick O’Malley (“We broke our covenant with the future” 5/9) highlights our failure to tackle the climate emergency and our likely dire future. Meanwhile, Anthony Albanese justifies opening 36 new fossil fuel developments by stating we can’t shut down fossil fuels overnight.

Only a blind idealist would argue for an immediate shutdown of fossil fuels and that is not what climate groups have argued for. The ALP’s failure to tax fossil fuel exports and stop the industry’s expansion is clear indication its aim is really to get out of fossil fuels as slowly as possible while keeping mining company support. The policies of the LNP are worse, and those of One Nation diabolical.

We require urgent and significant changes that only government can implement, and yet it’s not happening. However, the solution is in our hands. About 80 per cent of Australians believe more action is needed to tackle climate change. If a large proportion of them put active pressure on their MPs, government would be forced to act.

Unfortunately, too many have been seduced by the fossil fuel industry’s focus on limiting their “individual carbon footprint”. Individuals can’t fix this. We get the government we deserve and the solutions to tackling climate change can be achieved if enough of us pressure them to act – for us.

Peter Cook, Essendon Choice is simple for survival

It boggles my mind that there is even a discussion about the reality of climate change. Scientists have been warning us for decades that a failure to act will be deadly. Just look around at the global deaths, devastations and disasters currently in the news, yet many still refuse to believe it.

It boils down to one question: which do we want more? A short-term, head-in-the-sand approach of doing nothing and hoping all will be OK? Or, embracing reality and taking steps to (hopefully) enable a liveable future for our children and grandchildren?

Joyce Butcher, Williamstown



Earth’s delicate balance

In an otherwise excellent article (5/9) Nick O’Malley inadvertently highlights the very reason we may not extricate ourselves from the environmental mess that we have created.

In saying, ″⁣ the world we are left with will be permanently damaged by (fossil fuels) at immeasurable cost to human life ... let alone to the natural world”, he highlights the “us” and “them” thinking that does not yet accept that living things are inextricably linked, we are just one species in this delicate balance. In my opinion, until we change that mindset, extinction of our species is on the cards.

Keven Doman, Grovedale Murdoch is a businessman, not a sun king

Gabriel Sherman’s article (″⁣How Murdoch the Sun King sold out the planet″⁣, 5/9) would fail almost any test of rational thinking and reasoning. He asserts that Rupert Murdoch has done more than any other living person to cause governments not to act to cut emissions.

Murdoch might be interested to know the evidence Sherman used to claim he somehow controls the decisions of the ruling elites in the world’s biggest emitters China, Russia, India, or even the US.

The Obama and Biden administrations won office despite any opposition from Fox News commentators, and I am not convinced Donald Trump takes advice from anyone, no matter how well-informed or sympathetic to the Republican cause.

As for Sherman’s criticism of Murdoch for being beholden to the ideology of profit, and giving customers what they want to read or hear, surely, that is just good business sense for any company operating in a competitive market?

Would Sherman have Nine’s outlets not seek to give readers and viewers what they want: surely, a recipe for going out of business ? Even the taxpayer-funded ABC cancels programs that consistently fail to attract viewers, no matter how “worthy” the program might have been.

William Vickers, Melbourne THE FORUM Dump trams for buses

In contrast to your correspondent (Letters, 6/9), I do not think it is a good idea to go back to the old tram system. Trams are a pain in the backside at the best of times, and a disaster at others.

Who thought it was a good idea to block a tram with 50 or 100 people inside because a car wants to turn right? Who thought it was a good idea to create a lethally dangerous situation for pushbike riders in the tiniest bit of rain?

Electric buses are the answer to today’s problems: they are flexible in their tracks and on their routes, they can go wherever they are needed, so let’s design a network of them where they are needed today. And if that changes tomorrow, we can easily change that. And all that at a fraction of the price for trams or trains, be they above or below ground.

Dieter Liebrich, Swanpool Alight at your peril

The saga of Melbourne’s inaccessible tram stops provides adequate plot material for a full series of Utopia (″⁣Dozens of tram stops have been upgraded, but wheelchair users still can’t board″⁣, 6/9).

After decades of deferring upgrades ahead of the 2022 deadline of the Disability Discrimination Act, new non-compliant stops are now pretending to be relocated existing stops.

Along with constraining the lives of disabled people, this limits anyone with a pram or shopping jeep. But communities anticipating upgrades should remain vigilant, as some “level access” platform configurations may not be safe.

The northern stops on Route 96 directs 60 km/h arterial traffic over the platform via stunt ramps with no provision for cyclist safety, leaving a narrow footpath shared by waiting tram patrons, passing pedestrians, mobility scooters, and kids riding (legally) to adjacent primary schools.

Frequently, trucks and cars pass stationary trams as people alight. Superficial consultation prior to these works avoided any informed scrutiny by refusing to share design details.

Rod Duncan, Brunswick East



Starry-eyed council

My Maroondah Council 2026-27 budget and rates pamphlet includes a list of 15 projects identified for delivery over the next 12 months. Five of these are described as either a vision, a strategy or a project, and two involved ″⁣well-being″⁣ ″⁣transformation″⁣ and ″⁣liveability″⁣. Only one mentioned new footpaths.

I just endured several years of noise, dust and traffic disruptions due to the creation of new stations at Ringwood and East Ringwood, and the admittedly very welcome loss of several level crossings. Now, my journey to and from my pharmacy and shops in Heathmont involves two U-turns because of roadworks on Canterbury and Bedford roads, the latter seeming to have permanently narrowed the road.

Would it be possible for the mayor to descend from his idealistic cloud and fill the potholes in the roads which aren’t currently being dug up?

Maggie Peck, Ringwood Social housing

How heartening to see the United Nations criticise the Victorian government’s decision to demolish 44 public housing towers, warning that the policy could violate the international human right to housing.

What is deeply disturbing is the way this government has pursued the demolitions – seemingly with the mindset of a property developer rather than a government with a responsibility to protect its most vulnerable citizens.

There was no meaningful prior consultation with the people whose lives would be turned upside down. These towers are not simply concrete structures to be demolished and replaced. They are homes. They provide security, stability, and community to people who often have very few other options.

For three years, since this policy was first announced, advocates for public housing have fought against it, but there has been no widespread community uproar.

How can we accept the demolition of existing homes during a housing crisis? The irony is particularly stark when, across Melbourne, expensive new build-to-rent apartments are being promoted while some of our most vulnerable citizens are being told that their homes are no longer good enough.

The Victorian government should be providing more secure, affordable public housing – not destroying it.

Sue McNamara, Rye Build-to-rent furphy

I am glad The Age has investigated the build-to-rent model (“Not buying it”, 5/9) before it takes further root in our housing market. It seems to primarily benefit developers over renters – with generous state absentee land tax exemptions

BTR apartments are not a way of increasing housing affordability in Australia, given rents are typically significantly higher than suburban medians (up to 70 per cent). They also don’t seem a sustainable rental option, as long-term rental contracts in European countries are because rents here are not capped.

I also wonder about commitment to basic maintenance of buildings. From your report, early adopters are planning to move out, apartments are slow to rent due to the higher costs – and they end up being packed with foreign students.

BTR is another lurk for developers to exploit government subsidies, fast-tracked approvals and land tax reductions. Yet again, young Australians are denied genuinely affordable housing.

Caroline Leslie, Hawthorn Anti-boy nonsense

As a teacher, I am tired of politicians using schools as fodder for the latest culture war. Federal Opposition Leader Angus Taylor suggesting teachers are “pushing agendas”, while Nationals leader Matt Canavan labelling Respectful Relationships “anti-boy” and pointing to his own son having to “endure” these lessons, is particularly disappointing coming from two national leaders.

Around one in five Australian women have experienced sexual violence, while a recent Monash University survey of more than 2600 teachers found 78 per cent had witnessed or experienced sexism or misogyny in schools.

Yet, while teachers are dealing with the very real influence of Andrew Tate-style misogyny among young people, the Nationals’ leader suggests teaching boys about respect, consent and gender equality might somehow be driving them towards it. Quite the intellectual somersault.

Respectful Relationships is not an attack on boys. Teaching empathy, consent, healthy relationships and positive masculinity gives our boys tools to navigate an increasingly ugly online world. Given the violence women and girls continue to experience in Australia, surely, the evidence points to more thoughtful education in this space, not less.

Debate education policy, absolutely. But our political leaders should bring evidence, not outrage.

Jessica Bowey, Haven Loaded reference

Re “Eye of the Trump storm” (Spectrum, 5/9). This profile of Kim Sajet is largely a study of Trump’s assault on America’s cultural institutions, but makes a passing reference to NGV protests over its Jewish donors that sits uneasily.

The article states protesters objected to the gallery’s “high-profile Jewish donors” – but this blurs an important distinction. The demonstrations targeted John and Pauline Gandel’s public support for the Israeli government’s actions, not their Jewish identity. Conflating criticism of a state’s policies with hostility towards a faith or ethnicity does a disservice to readers and to social cohesion.

It also makes honest conversation about both the Israel-Palestine conflict and antisemitism harder, not easier.

Adnan Mansour, Armadale



New world order

The UN has voted to adopt a new map that more accurately reflects the size of nations on earth. The vote was 164 in favour, one against, six abstained. The only nation to vote against was the US.

Its reasons not to support the resolution were that it was an ″⁣ideological agenda″⁣ and was a distraction from the ″⁣genuine problems of international peace, prosperity or good relations″⁣. Someone obviously forgot to let the president know that that is America’s position.

Tom Stafford, Wheelers Hill Wildcard irrelevance

The real test of the success of the AFL’s Wildcard concept introduced for the 2026 finals series is not the numbers who attended the games or the consequent television ratings, but the competitive outcomes for the clubs involved.

In the 10 years to 2025 since the AFL introduced the pre-finals bye, at least one of the teams finishing in seventh or eighth position has progressed to the semi-finals on eight occasions. Several went even further.

Famously, the Western Bulldogs won the premiership from seventh place in 2016. Greater Western Sydney in 2023 qualified for a preliminary final from seventh. Last year, Hawthorn progressed to a preliminary final from eighth position.

This year, with the introduction of a so-called Wildcard Round pitting the clubs from seventh to 10th against each other, the seventh and eighth-placed clubs, no longer with a bye to prepare for a finals campaign, were obviously disadvantaged.

We now have the outcome. Not one of the four clubs involved in Wildcard progressed beyond the elimination round. For seventh and eighth, Wildcard was a detour to irrelevance.

By expanding the finals to more than half the teams in the competition, an absurdity in itself, the AFL has diminished the prospects for the real wildcard – a charge at the premiership from the bottom reaches of the eight.

Ian Munro, Albert Park AND ANOTHER THING World map

I think it’s a very good idea for the UN to adopt a new world map to correct colonial bias (6/9), particularly since it seems to be the Robinson projection (no relation though, pity). It still has distortions particularly at the poles. The Antarctic is shown to be enormous and stretched.

Wayne Robinson, Kingsley, WA I think America voted against the new world map because it made it look smaller. There is a positive in the new map for Greenland because it, too, looks smaller, and therefore less attractive to Trump. But beware Australia, we have now become a bigger target for his attention.

Tim Crawford, Boat Harbour Beach, Tas



Victoria

Jess Wilson says abortion laws will not change under a Liberal-National party. But what if the puppet master (One Nation) is pulling the LNP strings?

Marie Nash, Balwyn Are there more potholes in Victoria this year? (“Victoria’s deepening pothole crisis”, 6/9). They have lost count, I think. But probably.

Murray Horne, Cressy Furthermore

Rather than quibbling about the tax on tobacco products, governments should spend more on the simple message that smoking kills and makes your breath stink.

Juliet Flesch, Kew Do we want young people to be able to buy houses or not?

Malcolm McDonald, Burwood Keep it simple stupid. Ban the application of algorithms.

Elisabeth Schiller, Glen Iris



As a totally impartial, objective, considered, and thoughtful football follower, nothing pleases me more than seeing interstate football teams lose in the finals.

David Cayzer, Clifton Hill Given the Swans’ emphatic win over the Lions, the club now can dispose of its dropped boys without worrying about the finals or the future. Let the trades begin.

Martin Newington, Aspendale The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: A school separated boys and girls until year 10. It has delivered record VCE scores
World.content:
When Brad Fry arrived as the new principal at Tintern Grammar in 2015, the school was just emerging from a profound period of change. The school that began as a co-educational school had become girls-only before opening a separate campus for boys and then becoming co-educational again. Principal Brad Fry with students at the school’s farm. Simon Schluter But this time, there was a difference, with students at the Ringwood East school taught in single-gender classes between prep and year 9, and coming together for lunch and extracurricular activities such as orchestra, drama productions and time spent on the school’s farm. Fry says the two-stream system is one contributor to Tintern Grammar’s academic success. It has been named The Age’s 2026 Schools that Excel award winner for the eastern Melbourne region.



The annual series celebrates schools that have achieved outstanding advancement in their VCE results over the past decade. “I think the model we have is one of the key things that gets them ready for VCE,” Fry says. “We can instil a lot of really positive attitudes and dispositions by virtue of the fact that they’ve been parallel.” Related Article Consent crisis ‘Girls feel betrayed’: Dani survived sexual assault by a boy at 14. She says girls’ education is now at stake In 2016, Tintern Grammar recorded a median study score of 32, but during the depths of the COVID-19 pandemic, that dipped to 30. In the past few years, its results have shot up, with the school attaining a median study score of 33 in 2023, and then achieving its best-ever median study scores of 34 in 2024 and 2025.



The percentage of students achieving study scores of 40 and above is also on the rise, climbing from 11.1 per cent in 2016 to a 10-year-high of 18.6 per cent last year. A total of 11 students achieved a study score of 40 or above in maths methods last year, there were 10 scores of 40-plus in general maths, seven in physical education and four in business management. This was the best result Tintern has achieved in each of these subjects in the past decade. One student recorded a perfect score of 50 in English, but keep in mind these figures are from students who permitted their VCE results to be published, so the school’s true total is likely even higher. For Fry, a former science and maths teacher, the parallel learning model works because girls and boys learn differently.



“I think we can say that, in a general sense, young men don’t do things like sit still as well as girls do,” he observes. “They like to learn by doing things.” Year 12 student Olivia Cardamone joined Tintern in year 9 from an all-girls school. The 17-year-old says the parallel learning model gave her a chance to settle in and build confidence in an environment in which she was comfortable before transitioning to co-educational classes. “It was an easy move because we already knew each other from being around the school,” she says.



“And it was really great in classes like English because until year 9, we’d always had the female perspective in discussions. But afterwards, we got the male perspective, too, so it broadened how we interpreted things.” Sebastian Humphrys, joint school captain with Cardamone, says the model had served him well. “It let me develop leadership skills and confidence, and then the gradual merge to co-ed classes was more comfortable,” says the 18-year-old aspiring teacher. Students Sebastian Humphrys and Olivia Cardamone with some of the school’s merino sheep. Simon Schluter Vice school captain Isabella Di Felice, 18, found the model allowed her to develop whom she was in a supportive environment, and to try new things.



“And now that it’s co-ed, we mix really well and have friendship groups made up of boys and girls.” Another secret to the school’s success is its well-established careers program, which Cheuk Yui Lam, 18, says gave him invaluable work experience in the hospitality industry. This, he says, allowed him to hone the communication and people skills he hopes to call on as a secondary teacher. Fry considers the program a collaboration between staff and senior students at the school which marks its 150th anniversary next year. He says it is a chance to ensure students don’t just focus on subjects that “get marked up” when the ATAR is calculated. “If students aren’t studying subjects that they are passionate about, then they are not going to do well,” he says.



Fry is proud of students’ achievements and the dedication of his 119 staff but says ATAR results are not what makes the school tick. “We don’t even talk about results, apart from in the staff room when they come out,” he says. Editor's pick Science A Cinderella story: Why most women are wearing the wrong size shoes “The analogy I use is you don’t run onto the football field thinking about what the score will be at the end because if you do that, you’re not concentrating on the things that create the score.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Schools that Excel 2026: Find out your school’s VCE results over the past decade
World.content:
Welcome to the eighth edition of Schools that Excel, an annual series in which The Age celebrates schools that achieve outstanding improvement in their VCE results. The Age has gathered VCE results data from the past 10 years for every secondary school in the state offering year 12 subjects and turned it into an easy-to-use dashboard to show how each school fared over time, its top subjects, and more. Enter the name of your school in the interactive below to see the results: The Schools that Excel interactive brings together detailed results from Victorian government, independent and Catholic schools.



Loading What can I learn from this interactive tool? The interactive tool lets you gauge a school’s VCE performance over a 10-year period, so you can see whether it has improved or maintained its results. When VCE results are released in December, only the current year’s figures are provided. That information is useful, but doesn’t tell you about how representative the results are of the school’s typical performance. By threading together data from the past decade, a much clearer picture emerges. Ava Du’Pratt (front), Evie Parisis (back)Thomas Murton and Nithara Anooj (front). Former student Dylan Gekas tutors VCE students at Overnewton Anglican Community College. Joe Armao



But not all schools cater to students who are aiming for a place at university, and the Schools that Excel dashboard reflects this – you can also see how students enrolled in VET programs fared. Kardinia International College students Sam Carr and Zahli Williamson with principal Catherine Lockhart. Eddie Jim What does the dashboard show? The information about each school is divided into several panels. Here is a guide to interpreting the data: Average student performance shows the median VCE subject study score for the school since 2016, which is a good indicator of typical student achievement. Study scores are out of 50, and 30 is the average. The horizontal line at 30 on the graph is the yardstick that shows how the typical student at this school fares against the statewide average.



The interactive does not show median ATARs because this data is not available for the past decade for each school. High achievers shows the percentage of the school’s VCE subject scores that were among the best in the state. These are scores of 40 or above, which put students within the top 10 per cent of all those who completed that VCE subject. This panel also shows the subjects in which students obtained the best results. Tintern Grammar School students Sebastian Humphrys and Olivia Cardamone with some of the school’s merino sheep. Simon Schluter Completion rates shows the enrolment numbers in VCE and VET over the past five years, as well as the satisfactory completion rates among year 12s. Unfortunately, data was not released on VET completion rates in 2021, which is highlighted in the interactive. VCE VM and VPC provides data on the new VCE Vocational Major and the Victorian Pathways Certificate programs, which were implemented in schools to replace the Victorian Certificate of Applied Learning (VCAL) from 2023. The data shows whether the vocational major or pathways certificate were offered at a school and how many year 12 students completed either stream. And while VCAL has been phased out, the interactive displays enrolment and completion data for it from 2020-2022.



In addition, changes to VCAL – due to the VCE Vocational Major and the Victorian Pathways Certificate being phased in from 2023 – also mean that there were far fewer VCAL enrolments in 2023. School awards shows five high-gain schools that The Age judged as having shown the best improvement in their VCE results over the past decade. One school was selected from Melbourne’s south, east, north and west, as well as rural/regional Victoria. Starting in 2025, we also started recognising one school in Victoria that has shown improvement in its vocational education completion rates over the past five years. In previous years, we included a Student pathways section that shows whether a school’s graduates from the previous two years went on to further study at university or TAFE, or whether they took on an apprenticeship or joined the workforce. This data was from the Department of Education’s annual On Track survey. This survey was not carried out with 2024 graduates in 2025, so this section is blank in this year’s Schools that Excel interactive. However, the results for participating schools from the survey of students who graduated in 2023 can be found here in our Victorian Schools Guide. Gleneagles Secondary College Principal Jo Sayer and former student Jonah Heta, who now works at the school. Eddie Jim



Which schools are featured in the dashboard? The interactive dashboard features data on more than 500 Victorian schools that offered year 12 subjects in 2025. Principal of Sandringham College Amy Porter with some of her students. Simon Schluter It also includes schools classified as “small” by the VCAA, for having enrolments below a certain threshold. A dialogue box will pop up in the interactive if you enter the name of a small school and flag that its performance may not be comparable with larger schools, and that it may not be possible to observe a trend in results over the 10-year time frame. If a school has few students, it means the median and its percentage of study scores of 40 or above can fluctuate greatly year-on-year depending on the cohort.



Which schools do not feature in the interactive? Schools for which there is insufficient data, schools that exclusively offer the International Baccalaureate, and adult education institutions do not show up in the interactive. There might also be gaps in the data for years in which student enrolments did not reach a certain threshold. What other VCE and VET data is available at The Age? Earlier this year, The Age launched our Victorian Schools Guide, an interactive dashboard that displays comprehensive VCE and vocational data.



Most of the information that is available in the Schools that Excel interactive can be found in the Victorian Schools Guide, along with more detailed data on school performance and enrolments. Mill Park Secondary College principal Tim Natoli and Mustafa Khraim, Shub Bath, Scarlett Yaziji and Yangu Pan. Ruby Alexander The Victorian Schools Guide is a section of The Age website that also features some of our education team’s most recent reporting and analysis on VCE teaching, school performance and trends. We plan to add new sections and additional data sets to the Victorian Schools Guide in coming months to help guide you in your school choices, so it is worth bookmarking it in your browser. Type the name of your school in the search box below to check it out:



How were the Schools that Excel awards decided? We used Department of Health boundaries to categorise schools as metropolitan or regional and divided the metropolitan region into west, north, east and south Melbourne. Schools in each region were chosen based on their records of improvement in median VCE study scores, while the winner for the new vocational education category was chosen based on improvement in VET completion rates. Schools that Excel winners 2026 Eastern Melbourne: Tintern Grammar School

Tintern Grammar School Southern Melbourne: Sandringham College

Sandringham College Western Melbourne: Overnewton Anglican Community College

Overnewton Anglican Community College Northern Melbourne: Mill Park Secondary College

Mill Park Secondary College Regional and Rural Victoria: Kardinia International College

World.title: Questions about safety of disabled school transportation after review
World.content:
Questions have been raised about the safety of school transport services for disabled students, after an independent review.

The Ministry of Education commissioned the independent operational review of the Specialised School Transport Assistance (SESTA) scheme, following concerns about new transport contracts.

The review drew on a national survey, interviews and discussions with students, whānau and caregivers, schools, transport providers, drivers, disability organisations and Ministry of Education staff. The survey received more than 800 survey responses.

It identified several recurring issues requiring attention, including problems with communication, supervision arrangements, driver capability and wheelchair transport safety.

"The review heard consistent evidence that successful outcomes depend not only on the commitment of drivers, schools, families and providers, but also on effective oversight, coordination, communication and problem solving across the wider system," the report said.

The independent review panel said maintaining a safe transport system required more than responding to incidents when they occurred.

"It requires ongoing investment in system stewardship, proactive risk management, capability development, monitoring and learning. As expectations of safety, accessibility and responsiveness continue to grow," it said.

"The Panel therefore invites the Ministry to consider whether sufficient capability, capacity and resources currently exist across the SESTA system to maintain and continuously improve a safe, reliable and responsive service. This consideration should not be limited to the Ministry itself but should also include the broader system of support involving providers, schools and those responsible for stewardship, monitoring, safety oversight, training and continuous improvement," it said.

The independent review also found that stakeholders reported differing interpretations of responsibilities, particularly during service changes, incidents, information sharing, student handovers, and the implementation of Safe Travel Plans.

"Lack of clarity can lead to confusion, inconsistent practice and increased safety risks," it said.

The review panel's recommendations include:

Improvements to safety planning

A review of training provided to SESTA drivers

Involving the Children's Commissioner in monitoring SESTA trends.

In a statement, Ministry of Education services and programmes manager Andrea Williams said it accepted the findings, and it had begun work on the recommendations and priority actions.

"Some students and whānau told us their experience of the service did not consistently meet their needs or expectations. Their feedback has helped identify where improvements are needed and has directly shaped the actions we are taking in response," Williams said.

The ministry's focus was now on improving communication, safety planning, driver training and support, supervision, wheelchair transport, service monitoring and information management.

"A project to improve the quality and currency of information in our systems and the processes for sharing this is well advanced," Williams said.

"Work to improve communication is also well underway with the Ministry establishing regional contacts for all schools with SESTA services."

Williams said the ministry had initiated a review of SESTA roles and responsibilities, and would be taking concrete actions to make sure these are understood.

"The review recognises that student Safe Travel Plans are central to effectively managing each student's safety needs. We have now made these mandatory for all students, and we are working on a process to ensure that the information held in these is kept up to date and accurate," she said.

"We will report on our progress, while ongoing feedback from the people who use and deliver SESTA helps shape these improvements.

World.title: Future of Duffy Books in limbo as Ministry of Education considers 'competitive tender process'
World.content:
The Ministry of Education is considering opening its contract with the Duffy Books in Homes programme to competitive tender.

A briefing paper shows it renewed the contract for providing free books to children in poor communities until the end of 2027, but intended to "explore a competitive tender process ahead of any further contract renewals".

The ministry said its contract was with the Alan Duff Charitable Foundation, which funded the Duffy Books programme.

It provided at least 550,000 books to over 550 schools and about 40,000 books to more than 200 early childhood centres.

The programme also ran theatre shows and school assemblies with role models, it said.

"We want to be assured that we are getting the highest possible value for money with this contract. A procurement process will help us determine if there are other suppliers interested and capable of delivering these services," the ministry said.

It said the whole-of-life value of the contract since July 2025 would be $16.6million.

Duffy Books in Homes general manager Linda Vagana said the ministry's funding covered about a third of the organisation's work.

General Manager of Duffy Books in Homes, Linda Vagana. RNZ / Talei Anderson

She said it paid for two free books for each child in participating schools in term two each year, and bridged the gap when schools could not find a partner to fund half the cost of books for their pupils.

Vagana said a competitive tender was unusual but she understood the ministry's funding was tight.

"This is obviously something that's now part of the process," she said.

Vagana said the programme had been running for 32 years and communities needed it. She said it was about more than just dropping books at schools.

"It's also about telling the stories and having kids see themselves in the role models that we send out to all the schools," she said.

World.title: Person in critical condition after incident on Auckland's North Shore
World.content:

Emergency services then rushed them to Auckland City Hospital.

World.title: Warriors fall short of minor premiership, will play Dolphins at Mount Smart
World.content:
The Warriors have fallen just short of what would have been their second-ever minor premiership.

Going into the 27th and final round of the regular season, the Warriors were clear of the Panthers by just one on points differential.

After defeating the Sea Eagles 31-30 in Auckland last night to keep their place on top of the NRL ladder, the Panthers were left needing to beat the Tigers by two or more to finish in first.

They did just that, hammering the 15th-placed Tigers 38-10 in Sydney.

Penrith ran in seven tries including a hat-trick to Kiwi forward Casey McLean.

The result sees the Warriors finish in second, on 42 points with 18 wins and six losses.

However, coach Andrew Webster has maintained his side is chasing a much bigger carrot in 2026.

"There will be no one prouder if we happen to be minor premiers. It's a historical trophy and we'd be proud of it but not at the expense of what we need to do," Webster told media this week.

The Warriors will meet the Redcliffe Dolphins in week one of the finals at Mount Smart at 6.05pm on Saturday night.

World.title: No-confidence motion against Solomon Islands PM withdrawn
World.content:
Prime Minister Matthew Wale Pacific Islands Forum

The motion of no confidence filed against the Prime Minister of Solomon Islands has been withdrawn.

The motion against Prime Minister Matthew Wale, who has only been in the top job for over three months, was set for debate in parliament on Monday, 7 September.

Manasseh Maelanga, who lodged the motion against Wale a week ago, announced Sunday afternoon that he is withdrawing the motion.

Manasseh Maelanga Facebook / O.U.R Party Solomon islands

SBM Online reports Maelanga also signed the required documents for the formal withdrawal of the motion and submitted them to the National Parliament this afternoon.

"I have not taken this decision lightly, the motion was never about professional ambition, personal interest or creating division in our country, it was not a decision I took in isolation," Maelanga said.

In response to the announcement, Prime Minister Wale thanked Maelanga for withdrawing the motion.

"I have been quite concerned since I aware .. the time I landed in Palau.. emotions and public opinion, I think, also a rising level of public anger in terms of how leaders behave in these situations, and this something not good in the public mind."

I welcome the spirit with which he [Maelanga] has acted...and he informed me on Friday afternoon that this is what he would do over the weekend," Wale said.

A week in Solomon Islands politics

The motion came as a shock to Matthew Wale, who was in Palau for the Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting when the news broke.

Mr Wale left Palau early the next day to return home and deal with the domestic political crisis.

On his return to Solomon Islands last week, he faced the resignations of three Cabinet ministers.

Last Thursday, Wale then sacked the Finance Minister, Gordon Darcy Lilo, who also shares a political party with Maelanga.

Lilo told RNZ Pacific that he had no involvement with the motion against the prime minister.

World.title: Pet shop letter fails to keep man out of jail after he bashed brother with a bowl
World.content:
A man who repeatedly struck his brother over the head with a ceramic bowl, leaving him needing 13 stitches, hoped a glowing reference from a pet shop about his care of a rare African grey parrot might help keep him out of jail.

"I know that I could trust him with my flock," the store owner wrote of Anthony Gugich.

The letter of support was among the material put before the court, alongside a Corrections report revealing that Gugich had declined to provide an address for home detention, saying he wanted to "keep his affairs to himself".

This week, Gugich appeared in the Whangārei District Court for sentencing via audio-visual link from Pukekohe District Court before Judge Greg Davis on one charge of injuring with intent to injure.

Judge Davis recently found Gugich guilty at a judge-alone trial for the assault at the family home in Pukekohe.

On August 12, 2025, Gugich arrived at the home to find his belongings on the driveway.

When his brother arrived, the pair argued, and Gugich hit him on the head several times with a ceramic bowl. The brother suffered a serious cut requiring 13 stitches.

Gugich took his case to a judge-alone trial, claiming he was acting in self-defence.

But Judge Davis rejected his defence and, after finding him guilty, warned he would go to prison if he did not find an address at which to serve a sentence of home detention.

Pre-sentence reports were ordered, but Gugich told Corrections he was unwilling to provide an address as he wanted to "keep his affairs to himself", the judge said.

Gugich's lawyer, Kerrie Scott, said he was "taken by surprise" when he read the report, which had left Gugich with limited options.

However, Scott pushed for a reconciliatory approach, submitting that the case could be referred to restorative justice and that community work could be an appropriate sentence.

"I made it pretty clear at the end of the hearing that this was serious, that I wanted electronically monitored options, and he's seen fit not to see it as being that serious community-wise," Judge Davis responded.

"We're having a serious disagreement as to the gravity of this offending here. And sorry, I win these arguments."

Judge Davis said Gugich did not appear remorseful, despite the victim providing a victim impact statement that said he loved his brother and did not want to see him go to jail.

Gugich then addressed the court.

"I have thought about what happened, and I'm very shocked and very sorry about it," he said.

"I have wanted to apologise personally, but the no-contact order prevented me from doing so.

"Since the passing of our mother, we have become closer. Having Craig in my life is something I want very much, as we do get along in a positive way and also we do need each other, especially now."

"I know that I could trust him with my flock," the pet store owner wrote of Anthony Gugich, who cares for a rare African grey parrot. AFP

The letter from the pet shop was given to the court, in which the owner said Gugich owned a rare African grey parrot called Blue, which belonged to his mother, and often brought it in for treats.

"Tony and a selection of other customers buy a toy or treat for their feathered friends as payment for a wing clip," she wrote.

"I also have birds, but not as big as Blue. In the time that I have known Tony, I have found him to be very easy to chat with, and I know that I could trust him with my flock if I needed someone to take care of them."

In sentencing Gugich, Judge Davis did not comment on the letter from the pet shop, but said the assault was significant, given that it involved repeated blows to the head with a weapon and required hospital treatment.

The judge also said the victim had revealed in his statement that there had been no offer of reconciliation and Gugich breached his bail "almost every day" by not keeping his distance from him.

"You broke those conditions nearly every day, he says," Judge Davis said.

"You refused to provide electronic monitoring options to the court, not that I would have adopted them anyway. Your view was this should be dealt with by way of community work. You should keep your affairs to yourself, so to speak.

"However, this offending, in my view, is significantly beyond the scope where community work would be the appropriate sentencing outcome."

He sentenced Gugich to two years and six months' imprisonment.

At that point, Gugich slumped forward and put his head in his hands.

Gugich was also issued a strike under the three-strikes law.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Disabled teen loses deportation appeal, ordered to leave New Zealand
World.content:
A teenager who uses a wheelchair and needs help with daily tasks such as eating, bathing and dressing has been ordered to leave the country or face deportation.

Her resident family will likely have to leave New Zealand with her, after the teen's appeal against deportation on humanitarian grounds failed.

The teen, who has cerebral palsy, spastic quadriplegia, vision impairment and an intellectual disability, arrived in New Zealand from the Philippines in December 2024, having been granted a special visitor visa after a failed first attempt.

She then overstayed her visa by almost a year, making her liable for deportation.

An appeal lodged on her behalf was declined.

The Immigration and Protection Tribunal found last month that the teen, whose name and identifying details are suppressed, had not established that there were exceptional circumstances of a humanitarian nature.

However, given her dependence on family for daily care, the tribunal allowed the family four months to make arrangements for the teen's departure and "potentially their own".

The family also needed time to arrange care for the teen on her return to the Philippines, tribunal member Natalie Small said.

The teen's father arrived in New Zealand in late 2017 on an essential skills work visa, followed by her mother and two siblings in 2020 on work and student visas.

The high-needs teen remained in the Philippines while the family sought ways for her to join them in New Zealand.

In November 2021, the father lodged an application for a resident visa under the Accredited Employers category and included his wife and all three children.

The application was withdrawn a few months later and replaced with one under the "Special" category.

The application included medical evidence disclosing the teen's condition.

Small said the father withdrew the teen from the application in August 2022. In March 2023, the parents and two siblings were granted resident visas and became permanent New Zealand residents in 2025.

Special visitor visa granted on second attempt

An application was lodged on the teen's behalf in January 2024 for a six-month visitor visa but was turned down when Immigration New Zealand found she did not have an acceptable standard of health because she required fulltime care.

The family tried again in May 2024. Four months later, the Minister of Immigration granted her a nine-month special visitor visa.

In evidence presented to the minister, it was noted that the teen's mother had travelled back to the Philippines in 2023 to take care of her daughter.

The pair then travelled to New Zealand in December 2024.

Small said the teen's visitor visa expired on September 7, 2025, meaning she had been unlawfully in New Zealand since then while being cared for by her family.

The tribunal said the evidence suggested the family had been able to make adequate care arrangements for the teen in both NZ and the Philippines. NZ Herald / Supplied

Teen's case 'did not meet statutory test'

In making its decision, the tribunal focused on whether exceptional circumstances of a humanitarian nature would arise from deportation.

Small said the teen's case did not meet the statutory test.

"This is because it has not been demonstrated that the appellant's health needs, or any inability to provide for those health needs, has arisen out of, or as a consequence of her liability for deportation."

Small said the teen appeared to have been adequately cared for in the Philippines after her mother and siblings left in 2020, possibly by the parents' large, extended families who were still there.

"There is nothing exceptional about a person who arrives in New Zealand with a pre-existing medical condition who has had adequate support in their home country," Small said.

She said it appeared that the teen's cerebral palsy had been a constant feature in her life and that of her family, and that she would need ongoing assistance.

"That is true whether she is in New Zealand or in the Philippines."

Small said the evidence suggested the family had been able to make adequate care arrangements for her in both countries.

"In this case, there is no evidence to establish that the appellant cannot access daily support and/or medical support in the Philippines should she require it."

Small said the teen's family, as permanent residents, could leave New Zealand and return at any point.

The fact that her parents were faced with difficult choices was a result of their earlier decisions to move to New Zealand and obtain residence status here.

"They have long known that the appellant will not meet the eligibility requirements for residence and so there is nothing unexpected or uncommon in the requirement that the appellant must go home while they have the ability to remain in New Zealand," Small said.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Dental bills lead surge in requests to Christchurch charity fund
World.content:
Christchurch's Mayor's Welfare Fund has paid more than $200,000 to assist people with dental and electricity payments as the cost of living bites.

Those numbers have nearly doubled from the year prior.

Councillor Yani Johanson, the chair of the advisory fund committee, said the fund has paid out $122,474 for dental work so far in 2026, with a maximum of $2000 given out to any individual.

Dental expenses were previously counted as part of the medical category, but this year the fund had dental as a separate category due to the high number of requests.

"There is a huge need - the tragedy is of course that the more people don't go to the dentist, the longer they leave it, the higher the cost for treatment," Johanson said.

Poor dental health had a huge impact on a person's quality of life, self-esteem and health, he said.

"It's a damning indictment on our society and country that we have such huge need because it has become completely unaffordable for so many people and that's why we are seeing such an increase in demand," Johanson said.

The medical category accounted for $55,702 last year, including dental.

Requests for help with electricity bills had also jumped, with the fund paying out $109,599 so far this year, compared with $58,000 last year and $38,000 in 2024.

"Power prices are just going up and up and up, and people's income is just not meeting the cost of living. So we are seeing a significant increase in requests for help," Johanson said.

The Christchurch City Council's Mayor's Welfare Fund started as the Mayor's Coal and Blanket Fund in 1897 and was renamed in 1973.

In 1992 the Mayor's Welfare Fund Charitable Trust was created to administer the fund.

Johanson said the city has a proud tradition of helping those most in need.

"It's a fund of last resort to help people when there is no other option for funding to meet the basics that are needed to provide for their well-being."

The fund covers specific categories, and applications are assessed by an administrator on a case-by-case basis.

Items covered include electricity and rent arrears, firewood, medical costs, childcare arrears and funeral costs.

In the past year requests for help with child and adult learning assessments were added to the eligible criteria.

The fund gave out $54,876 for adult assessments and $39,936 for child assessments so far in 2026.

In the past year the fund received 702 applications with 447 approved, 98 declined, 129 withdrawn and 28 yet to be decided.

Johanson said the number of applications to the fund had increased hugely, as had the amount of money given out.

The fund is likely to pay $700,000 in grants by the end of this year compared with $371,000 last year.

Councillors had agreed to pay their directors' fees to the fund.

World.title: Swans star 'shattered' after skipper's heartbreaking knee injury
World.content:
Sydney star Tom Papley says he is "shattered" for Swans skipper Callum Mills as Mills braces to miss the club's push for an unlikely AFL premiership.

Mills's feared ACL rupture added a sour note to Sydney's remarkable 53-point qualifying final demolition of reigning premiers Brisbane at the SCG on Saturday.

Scans are expected to confirm the major knee injury for the luckless 29-year-old, who missed the Swans' 2024 grand final loss and has dealt with numerous untimely injuries across his 197-game career.

But Sydney have an opportunity to make amends for previous grand final losses, with a preliminary final at the SCG against either Fremantle or Geelong to come.

Papley admitted it "didn't look great" for Mills following the resilient skipper's first-quarter knee injury.

Mills has earned significant praise for leading the club amid the dramatic fallout from the events at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne last month.

"He is an amazing captain," Papley told the Nine Network of his skipper on Sunday.

"[He's] been amazing over the last few weeks.

"He puts this club on his back and wears his heart on his sleeve. It's just shattering for him.

"I'd love nothing more than to win a premiership and have him by my side, albeit he might not be there [playing].

"He deserves it more than anyone."

Star players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — All-Australian contenders before they were banned from being selected — are among the five serving club-imposed bans.

Important tagger James Jordon and defender Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.

Sydney were given little chance to knock off the Lions, even though they finished the home-and-away season second.

Even club chairman Andrew Pridham conceded the Swans' premiership hopes had been "torpedoed" after suspending the five players.

But all cylinders of the Swans machine fired on Saturday despite those major absences, with Errol Gulden calling the shots in the engine room as Harry Cunningham directed the defence.

Logan McDonald may have led with six goals, but Sydney enjoyed an even contribution from their forward line, with Charlie Curnow and Papley slotting five each.

Tall forward Hayden McLean's three-goal haul is set to further complicate coach Dean Cox's selection conundrum, with Joel Amartey (Achilles) nearing full fitness.

Star winger Justin McInerney is also expected to return from a hamstring strain for the preliminary final.

Errol Gulden (right) marshalled Sydney's engine room in style against Brisbane in the absence of some of his star teammates. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"They should both be available … and that'll be a decision, like we do every week," Cox said of Amartey and McInerney.

Cox said Saturday's win felt like the most complete four-quarter performance in his tenure.

"With the quality of opposition that we were playing and the ability of the match-winners that they have all over the ground," Cox said.

"I was really proud when we've got some of the young kids that come into our football team to be able to execute the roles they had to play at the right time."

AAP

World.title: NRL finals schedule confirmed, Panthers claim minor premiership
World.content:
The Penrith Panthers have a fourth NRL minor premiership in the last seven seasons after battering the Wests Tigers 38-10 at Western Sydney Stadium.

Thomas Jenkins scored a first half double to join Alex Johnston on top of the NRL try-scoring charts for the year with 30 to share the Ken Irvine medal, while Casey McLean nabbed his first career NRL hat-trick.

The Wests Tigers briefly showed some life at the start of the second half, with PNG-bound via Parramatta five-eighth Jarome Luai benched by Benji Marshall after the break.

The lively Latu Fainu ensured the Tigers immediately lifted, amplifying the sense of disappointment fans must have felt at the underwhelming Luai era that had promised so much.

Penrith's victory ensures the Panthers will host the Roosters at Western Sydney Stadium on Sunday in the first week of the finals.

NRL finals schedule week 1 Friday Elimination Final: South Sydney Rabbitohs vs Newcastle Knights at Sydney Football Stadium — 7:50pm AEST Saturday Qualifying final: New Zealand Warriors vs Dolphins at Mount Smart Stadium — 4:05pm AEST

Elimination final: Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks vs North Queensland Cowboys at Sydney Football Stadium — 7:50pm AEST Sunday Qualifying final: Penrith Panthers vs Sydney Roosters at Western Sydney Stadium — 4:05pm AEST

The Rabbitohs and Knights will open the weekend with their elimination final at the Sydney Football Stadium on Friday night (7:50pm AEST).

The second-placed Warriors will take on the Dolphins at Mount Smart Stadium on Saturday afternoon (4:05pm AEST) before the Sharks play the Cowboys at the Sydney Football Stadium that evening at 7:50pm AEST.

The Sharks had hoped to host the match at Shark Park but the 45,500-capacity Moore Park stadium got the nod.

The Cowboys will likely be without star forward Reuben Cotter, who will miss at least week one of the NRL finals after being charged for a high tackle against the Raiders.

The Maroons forward was handed a grade two careless high tackle charge for his contact on Josh Papali'i in the first hit up of the match.

Earlier, Tyrell Sloan scored a 45-metre field goal to secure the Dragons a thrilling 24-22 victory over the Parramatta Eels in Wollongong.

"I guess it's the stuff you dream about," Castleford-bound Sloan told ABC Sport after the match.

"The fans turned up … they stuck with us through a tough year and just to repay them there is the best feeling ever."

Follow the live blog below, keep up to date with all the latest stats in our ScoreCentre, and tune in to our live radio coverage.

World.title: Ex-Eagle says 'conservative and vanilla' AFL club's main focus is money
World.content:
Former West Coast midfielder Sharrod Wellingham says the Eagles have become "conservative and vanilla", with a focus on money rather than on-field success, following another poor AFL season.

West Coast finished 16th with four wins in 2026, which took their total victories to 15 since the beginning of the 2022 campaign.

"I feel like West Coast have become so complacent because they've got a lot of off-field success as a business and they've got a lot of things that they're doing right when it comes to making money," Wellingham said on 102.5 ABC Perth's SportsTalk program.

"I feel like that's where their focus is.

" They're not aggressive, they're not ruthless and the invisible board is definitely a factor. "

Wellingham, who was part of Collingwood's 2010 premiership side under Mick Malthouse before joining the Eagles in 2013, warned West Coast was in danger of going down the same path as other historically successful clubs that have drifted into irrelevance.

"There's the potential for West Coast to develop into an Essendon," he said.

Wellingham played 79 games for West Coast after winning a premiership with Collingwood. (Paul Kane, file photo: Getty Images)

West Coast has made several high profile changes in recent years, with the appointment of Don Pyke as chief executive, Andrew McQualter as coach, and Elizabeth Gaines as chair of the board.

But Wellingham said he didn't feel like much had changed at the club, which had struggled on the field in recent years.

He pointed to the decision to trade away pick three in 2024 to secure the services of now co-captain Liam Baker from Richmond, a decision which ultimately cost the Eagles access to the AFL Rising Star Jagga Smith.

If the Eagles had decided to draft Smith, they would have a midfield boasting Harley Reid, Elijah Hewett, Willem Duursma and Smith.

Jagga Smith was drafted by Carlton. (Getty Images: Russell Freeman)

"It was a terrible decision," Wellingham said.

"There is zero swag that comes out of West Coast ... they're conservative and vanilla.

"I don't know where the change is going to come from. Yes, you want to have good people and be of sound culture, but you've got to have some ruthlessness.

"I feel like there's nothing that sounds like that and feels like that that's coming from the footy club at the moment."

Eagles CEO Don Pyke hinted at the club's determination to return to the AFL summit during West Coast's end of season awards, when he said "September is for finals, not functions".

World.title: Aussie Patterson claims Diamond League Final title with 'insane' win
World.content:
Australia's Eleanor Patterson has continued her outstanding season by winning the women's high jump at the Diamond League Final in Brussels.

Patterson was joined on the podium by fellow Australian and reigning world champion, Nicola Olyslagers, who finished third.

The result gave Australia two victories across the weekend at the King Baudouin Stadium, following Cameron Myers's triumph in the men's 1,500m on the opening night.

Myers wins Diamond League Final Cameron Myers has beaten a star-studded field at the Diamond League Final in Brussels.

Patterson successfully cleared 2.01 metres with her final attempt at the height, edging out Ukrainian Olympic champion and world-record holder, Yaroslava Mahuchikh (1.99m).

Mahuchikh failed with her three attempts at 2.01m.

Olyslagers cleared 1.95m to round out the top-three placings.

Patterson attempted 2.03m, which is the same height as Mahuchikh's 2026 world lead, but could not manage a successful clearance.

She added the Diamond League Final title to her second Commonwealth Games gold, which she won in Glasgow in late July.

Her win came a week after she equalled her personal best (PB) of 2.02m in Germany.

"It's amazing," Patterson said.

"I've only won a Diamond League meet once before in 2023, so to win the final is insane. I knew I was in good shape after jumping 2.02m a few days ago.

"It was chilly, but I just went out to have fun and I'm super happy with how today turned out."

Eleanor Patterson celebrates her win in Brussels. (Getty Images: Tim Clayton)

Patterson said ignoring the performances of her rivals was the key to victory.

"Today, I stayed clinical and stuck to my own process, which really paid off," she said.

Australia's Olympic silver medallist Jessica Hull was third in the women's 1,500m, producing a season-best time of 3:54.73.

"It's nice to run the fastest I have all year in September, I think that shows my training works when you want to peak this time of the year," Hull said.

Poland's Klaudia Kazimierska saluted with a world-leading time and meet record of 3:54.05, which was also a PB.

Kenyan Dorcus Ewoi was second in a PB of 3:54.73, while Hull's Australian teammate Abbey Caldwell (3:57.19) finished seventh.

Meanwhile, Australia's Sarah Billings was fifth in the women's 800m with a time of 1.59.99.

Swiss star Audrey Werro claimed the meet record in winning with 1:54.75.

World.title: Sweeny exits US Open to end Australia's singles chances
World.content:
Dane Sweeny's gallant US Open campaign has come to a frustrating end with a tough third-round loss to 21st-seeded Italian Luciano Darderi.

Sweeny complained of a hip injury during a 6-4, 6-3, 6-3 defeat to the world number 22 that left Australia without a second-week singles hope in New York for the first time in five years.

Alex de Minaur's shock second-round loss to Botic van de Zandschulp meant Sweeny was Australia's last player standing at Flushing Meadows.

"It's been an amazing week, a career-changing week, but I can't help but feel a bit disappointed just with today's performance," Sweeny said.

"I just wasn't really feeling it, just not really feeling the timing and the rhythm as I have been. I just made a lot of cheap errors and that was quite frustrating.

"I was OK to lose a match, but I really wanted to test him more and bring a good level so I could make an absolute fight out of it.

"Win or lose, I wanted to really make him work for the victory at least and I wasn't able to do that."

The world number 123 only gained a last-minute entry to the US Open after two late withdrawals allowed Tennis Australia to grant Sweeny the reciprocal wildcard it initially handed to Alexei Popyrin.

Dane Sweeny reached the last 32 for the first time at a major. (Getty images/USTA: Dustin Satloff)

Despite his disappointment, Sweeny cashed in on his good fortune.

The 25-year-old turned his first US Open main-draw appearance into a watershed run to the last 32 of a major for the first time.

The Queenslander will walk away with a life-changing cheque for $402,500 and a fresh career-high ranking.

"The financial side of things, that will help with coaching and people you travel with," Sweeny said.

Sweeny is provisionally slated to climb to number 109 in the world.

If he can crack the top 100 by season's end, Sweeny will earn direct entry to the Australian Open for the first time.

"That's exciting too. But that will take care of itself," Sweeny said.

"It's hard not to worry about that because we're indoctrinated to want that low number next to our name, but I can just focus on working hard, focus on improving.

"Particularly just staying really kind to myself and trying to enjoy the journey."

American tilt takes a hit

Past US Open finalists Taylor Fritz, Madison Keys and Amanda Anisimova all crashed out in the third round, dealing a stinging blow to home fans.

Men's ninth seed ​Fritz had yet to drop a set in New York and looked well on his way to another routine victory before Argentina's Francisco Cerundolo found his best tennis to flip the script and win 3-6, 4-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4.

It was the earliest exit in four years for the 2024 runner-up, as Cerundolo reached the ​fourth round for the first time.

The American ‌women fared no better as China's Zheng Qinwen fought back from a 5-0 deficit in the decider to beat 2017 runner-up Keys 1-6, 7-6 (7/3), 7-5, collapsing on the court in utter joy as she fights back from a career slump.

Zheng Qinwen celebrates her win over Madison Keys. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

Zheng will next face 2022 champion and former world number one, Iga Świątek, who got past Czech Marie Bouzková 7-6 (7/3), 7-6 (7/3).

Tenth-seeded Anisimova, last ​year's runner-up, was unable to reverse ‌her fortunes in a frustrating year at the majors, with a 6-2, 7-5 defeat by Anastasia Potapova.

Coco Gauff, the 2023 US Open winner, provided the lone bright spot for the Americans when she beat Spain's Cristina Bucșa 6-3, 6-4 in the third round.

AAP/Reuters

World.title: How the Panthers and Warriors can win the NRL minor premiership
World.content:
The NRL minor premiership is still up for grabs heading into the final day of the home-and-away season, with the New Zealand Warriors on top and the Penrith Panthers ready to pounce.

The Warriors moved to outright first with a narrow win in Auckland on Saturday, but the Panthers only need a slender win on Sunday afternoon to reclaim top spot, where they have spent much of the 2026 season.

The Warriors and Panthers will finish in the top two, and in practical terms there is little different between the two spots entering the finals series.

Both sides will host two matches in the finals, including qualifying finals next week.

But the minor premier does get a monetary prize, and confidence heading into finals footy, knowing they finished on top of the pile after 27 gruelling rounds of rugby league.

Here is how the Warriors and Panthers can win the minor premiership, and what happens when first and second are level on points, and point differential.

NRL top two

1st: New Zealand Warriors — 42, points for 728, points against 418, point differential +310

2nd: Penrith Panthers — 40, points for 645, points against 337, point differential +308

How the Warriors can become minor premiers

Panthers fail to beat Wests Tigers

Panthers defeat Tigers by one point

With a nail-biting one-point win over Manly yesterday in Auckland, the New Zealand Warriors put themselves in outright first on the NRL ladder.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

But their fate is out of their hands.

If the Tigers cause an upset and defeat the Panthers this afternoon, then the Warriors will win the minor premiership.

If the Panthers beat the Tigers, they will draw level on points with the Warriors, and then the minor premiership will be decided by point differential.

The Warriors hold a very narrow two-point advantage over the Panthers in the points differential — Warriors +310, Panthers +308.

That means if the Panthers can only manage a one-point win over the Tigers at Western Sydney Stadium, then the Warriors would finish first by having a superior points differential +310-+309.

How the Panthers can become minor premiers

Defeat Wests Tigers by two or more points

The first thing the Panthers must do is beat Wests Tigers.

Then, how much they beat the Tigers by will decide who finishes first and second on the NRL ladder.

The Panthers will finish as minor premiers if they beat the Warriors by two or more points.

If two teams finish on the same points and have the same points differential, the NRL splits the two sides based on a tiebreaker: points for divided by points against, then multiplied by 100 (Points for / points against x 100).

If this tiebreaker is needed, then the Panthers will finish higher as their defence this year has conceded much less than the Warriors, greatly assisting that tiebreaker maths equation.

Who will the Panthers and Warriors face in the first week of finals?

By finishing in the top two, the Warriors and Panthers have earned the right to host two matches in the finals.

Each will host qualifying finals in week one. If they win, they will host a preliminary final in week three.

If the Panthers or Warriors lose in week one, they then host a cut-throat semifinal in week two against a side that was victorious in week one elimination finals played between the teams that finished fifth-eighth.

In week one, whoever finishes first will host the Sydney Roosters (4th) and the team that finishes second will host the Dolphins (3rd).

The NRL will announce dates and times for week one of the final once all matches in round 27 finish.

World.title: Wallabies escape with draw against Pumas after late penalty try
World.content:
The Wallabies have snatched a 28-28 draw with Argentina in Mendoza after they were awarded a penalty try with 10 minutes remaining in the Test.
