How We Test AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Photograph: Simon Hill I test every smart water leak detector by dripping water on top, pooling water slowly beneath, and flooding rapidly to see how effective the water leak detection is and how quickly they alert. I install every app, check different alert options where applicable, and ensure alerts come through on my phone, whether I’m connected to Wi-Fi or the cellular network. I also remove the batteries or unplug each water leak detector to see if it shows as disconnected correctly in the app or sends any alert, then plug it back in or reinsert batteries to see if it recovers. When detectors offer additional features, such as humidity or temperature tracking, I test and compare them with my SwitchBot Hub 3. Our top picks continue to be used over months, so we can be confident that the performance does not degrade.

Tech.title: Why China Is the Bogeyman Data Center Enthusiasts Just Can't Quit
Tech.content:
Welcome to the first edition of Power Play! From now until the midterms, senior writer Molly Taft will be sharing their thoughts every Sunday on this political season’s hottest issue: data centers. We welcome reader comments, and will be answering questions from the comments section in future editions.

Be sure to catch WIRED’s first livestream on data centers this Thursday, September 10, featuring Molly, senior politics correspondent Hugo Lowell, and senior business writer Max Zeff! You can submit questions here.

It’s been a rough summer for data center boosters. Polling is getting even more dismal—as many as 75 percent of Americans now say they would oppose a data center being built in their area, up from 42 percent last year. Politicians from both parties who were previously advocates, like Texas governor Greg Abbott and Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro, are now switching up as the midterms approach, looking to convey to voters that they’re talking a hard line on the hated infrastructure.

But while some Republicans are turning tail on the issue even in the face of President Donald Trump’s vigorous support for data center construction, others are joining prominent tech leaders in doubling down on an old narrative: That China is responsible for all this malaise.

In late August, X announced that it had identified 200 accounts linked to China that were helping to spread anti-data center talking points on the platform, causing a flurry of alarmist headlines and tweets. (“China is secretly fueling America's data center rage,” Axios trumpeted in an article on X’s report, which data center-friendly politicians and right-wing figures amplified using X itself.) Even the president joined in: “China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement,” he wrote in a Truth Social post defending data centers (“let Data Reign!”) made just a few days after the X report.

Tech.title: The Best Gaming Chairs (2026): Are They Worth It?
Tech.content:
The Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro is our favorite office chair, and it's also my favorite gaming chair. As it turns, out a comfortable and reliable design is ideal regardless of the use case. The real “gaming” piece boils down to aesthetics. And now, this chair is available in three different Sega-branded styles, all of which are super comfortable and adjustable. Assembly wasn't too difficult, and the chair isn't too fiddly to get dialed in, though there definitely is a learning curve when it comes to all the different knobs.

Each of the designs is both fun and attractive, and that the chair offers incredible value for the price. The Sonic version has a mesh back, while the Sega Genesis and Sega Dreamcast versions have leather backs. I didn't find the leather-backed version that I tested to be too sweaty. All the little details of the designs pop, and it's hard to find a better gaming chair for the money. I like that I can always lean back and “have a think” when I'm staring at a blank text field or waiting for my Discord friends to get back to the mic. As a 5'1" woman, I do wish this chair got just a little bit lower to the ground, which is a bit ironic considering that Branch sells an optional Tall Cylinder for people above 6 feet tall. I also found the headrest pretty much useless. But again, for the price, and for your health, good luck getting more value. If you're locking in for hours and hours, this chair can help you do it more safely.

Tech.title: 4 Best Alexa Speakers I’ve Tested (2026)
Tech.content:
Comparing the Best Alexa Speakers

Model Speaker Array Screen Specs Camera Specs Other Features Amazon Echo Dot Max One 2.5-inch woofer; one 1-inch tweeter None None Tap controls; smart home hub Amazon Echo Dot (5th Gen) One 1.73-inch speaker None None None Amazon Echo Show 11 One 2.8-inch woofer; two full-range drivers 11-inch display with 1920 x 1200 resolution 13-MP camera with auto-framing Zigbee smart home hub that supports Matter and Thread; spatial audio; Dolby Atmos Amazon Echo Show 8 (3rd Gen) Two 2-inch speakers 8-inch display with 1280 x 800 resolution 13-MP camera with auto-framing Zigbee smart home hub; spatial audio

Honorable Mentions

While I wouldn't call these smart speakers my absolute favorites from Amazon, they have some excellent qualities that make them stand out among the vast lineup of Echo models.

The Echo Studio (2nd Gen) is the best Alexa speaker for sound quality. This is the second version of the Echo Studio to be our audiophile pick. The current version is a similar size to the old Echo (4th gen), but the musical power on this speaker is almost ridiculous. It filled my entire second floor's long great room with music, and I didn't even need to reach the highest level of volume to pull it off. Honestly, I'm almost afraid to use it at full blast. Not only was it loud, but clear and delivered a nice amount of bass, beautifully playing soft tones of Tracy Chapman's “Fast Car” and the piano riffs of “Dark Blue” by Jack's Mannequin with its three 1.5-inch drivers, plus a 3.75-inch woofer. The harmonizing of “What Is This Feeling?” by Ariana Grande and Cynthia Erivo sounded beautiful, too. If you're looking for big sound in an Alexa box, this is it. It's a similar size to the Apple HomePod, but I like the sound much better and it's cheaper, too. You'll also get a built-in smart home hub, spatial audio and Dolby Atmos, tap controls like the Echo Dot Max, and early access to Alexa+ right away.

The Echo Spot (2nd Gen) is the best Alexa speaker for bedside tables. The Echo Spot returned in 2024 after a few years of discontinuation, and it's a great little bedside companion thanks to its half-circle screen that displays the time, plus any alarms you have set are also visible under the main time. You can customize the clock with a couple of different color and face options, and the screen dims nicely when the lights are out to a gentle red that's easy to read without lighting up the room. I like asking for alarms set to my latest playlist or some lo-fi jams, and it's easy to set that up with a voice request. Unlike the Echo Shows, it doesn't have a distracting, constantly moving slideshow that would be annoying for the bedroom, nor does it display ads or have a built-in camera. (Nobody wants a rogue camera in their bedroom.) It does not have fantastic sound, but it's plenty loud for an alarm or casual listening while you get dressed in the morning.

The Echo Dot Kids (5th Gen) is the best Alexa speaker for kids. Do your kids really need their own Alexa speaker? That's up to you. This special edition of the Echo Dot is nearly identical to the fifth-gen Dot above, but it has easy-to-use parental controls that allow you to set time limits, filter explicit content, and review activity. The owl- or dragon-themed sphere comes with a year of Amazon Kids+, which includes thousands of Audible books and other special games and features. After that, you'll be charged $3 per month. Alexa can help your kids spell, play their favorite music, or—via another speaker in your house—remind them of dinner time.

More Alexa (and Alexa-Compatible) Speakers

There are a lot of Echo devices out there, and some third-party speakers that are Amazon Alexa–compatible. Here's every Alexa smart speaker we've tried and what we thought of it. Some of these speakers didn't raise in price like the models above, which might make them more appealing than before if you're looking to spend less.

Amazon Echo Dot (5th Gen) With Clock for $60: I like this version of the older Echo Dot that adds an LED clock to the front of the speaker, and was thrilled to see it in stock again last year. The LED clock can also display information like the weather when you ask Alexa questions. It's once again temporarily out of stock as of this writing, and has had spotty availability (it's out of stock right now, but Amazon says it's temporary). Still, it's a good find when it's available.

Amazon Echo Hub for $180: The Amazon Echo Hub is similar to an Echo Show, but without the speaker. Instead it's a thin device that feels a bit like a tablet, designed to be mounted on the wall (or placed on a separately purchased stand, which is how I used it) and used to control your smart home devices. It's a great choice for anyone who wants something focused on smart home control only. You can still ask Alexa questions and even play music, but the thin speakers aren't worth playing music from. But you can tell your Echo Hub to play music on a different set of speakers, and even set up default speakers to work with it. It's a great companion device if you already have a smart home setup.

Amazon Echo Pop for $40: The Echo Pop is a perfectly fine little speaker, and the cutest one in Amazon's lineup. Does it have great sound? No. It's fine enough for background tunes or if you're limited to a dorm room, but you'll get much better sound for a similar size from the Echo Dot (but you'll pay a little more, and you won't get as cute of colors)!

Amazon Echo Show 5 (3rd Gen) for $100: This smart display is another just-fine option, but it's too small to be a great display, and the included camera makes it a no for a bedside table; better to go with the above Echo Spot or an Echo Dot. This model did raise in price by $10.

Amazon Echo Show 8 (4th Gen) for $200: I usually love an Echo Show 8, but this model didn't have the same sound quality as the older model. If you're going to get one of Amazon's new displays, you're better off getting the Echo Show 11 ($220) for the same experience with a slightly larger screen (while it's a 3-inch difference, it doesn't feel that big) and better sound. This smart display raised in price by $20.

Amazon Echo Show 15 (2nd Gen) for $350: This smart display is a good display, but it clearly wants to double as a TV and isn't very good at it yet. I'm hoping we see better TV-related performance in the future to make it worth adding to a kitchen or office. It does a great job with widgets, though, thanks to the massive 15.6-inch screen. There's also the larger Echo Show 21 ($500), which is essentially the same thing but larger. Both of these large displays rose in price—the Show 15 went up $50, while the Show 21 went up $100.

JBL Authentics 200 for $380: This JBL smart speaker supports both Google Assistant and Amazon Alexa, letting you switch between them for different tasks without changing your preference in the app. That makes this speaker particularly appealing for folks with a sprawling collection of smart products from both.

Sonos Era 100 for $219: If you're looking for a speaker that can talk to Alexa but isn't necessarily made by Amazon, the Sonos Era 100 is a great option. We just wish we liked the Sonos app better. You can catch our entire guide to the Sonos ecosystem here.

Why Did Amazon's Prices Increase?

Amazon increased many of its prices last month for its products, affecting the Amazon Echo line as well as Kindles, Fire TV streaming sticks, and Eero routers. It's not a huge surprise after other companies have done the same this summer, claiming rising costs and chip shortages. Amazon made a similar claim, with a spokesperson blaming increased storage and memory costs. Still, it's disappointing to see and will lead to a fall sale season with prices that won't be as impressive as earlier this summer.

Amazon's Echo devices saw increases from anywhere between $20 and $100, with the larger price increases being for the Echo Shows. The following Echo speakers all faced a price increase:

What’s Alexa+?

Photograph: Nena Farrell

Amazon has rolled out the new-and-improved Amazon Alexa, named Alexa+, which is built on generative AI and promises a more powerful assistant that can handle more conversational topics and requests. It's available for a free 30-day trial; after that, you either pay a $20 monthly fee or become a Prime member. Being a Prime member is the better deal, likely by design. Neither my colleagues nor I have been impressed enough by Alexa+ to say it's worth paying for on its own. I do like the updated, more conversational voice, and Alexa+ did a good job answering all kinds of questions quickly and thoughtfully. Check out our early access hands-on for everything I thought while testing.

Alexa+ has brought some changes, even for those not using it. It now requires that all voice recordings be sent to Amazon for processing, which wasn't required before. Amazon has changed its features to support this, and now all recordings with regular Alexa go to Amazon, too. There used to be a “Do Not Send Voice Recordings” privacy feature you could select to have voice requests processed locally, but it was discontinued on March 28, 2025, per an email Amazon sent to current users.

FAQs What’s the Difference Between an Echo and an Echo Show? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron A regular Echo is a smart speaker, or a speaker with microphones in it so it can hear you speak to it and respond. An Echo Show is a smart display, which has a screen and a camera to let you make video calls, stream content, and see your questions answered on a screen. Both have similar capabilities when it comes to smart home control, answering questions, and playing music, but Echo Shows have extra abilities thanks to the screen. All Echo Shows have a camera and come with a physical camera cover for privacy. When’s the Best Time to Buy an Echo? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron The best time to buy any Amazon speaker is during a major sale event like Black Friday or Amazon Prime Day, when there are often steep discounts. You'll often see the cheaper speakers for around 50 percent off, and the larger speakers see some nice sale prices too. How and Where Should You Set Up Your Alexa? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Alexa speakers get the best use in spaces you're in often. I like setting mine up in my kitchen and living room—usually a display in the kitchen, so I can pull up a recipe or the weather while I make my morning cup of tea, and a speaker in the living room so I can play music and command the lights without a screen to distract from the TV or playing with my son. You can also set one up in the bedroom to use as an alarm clock, but make sure it's a model without a camera for the best privacy. Ultimately, what's most important is that the speaker is somewhere it can hear your commands. Where that will be will vary based on your home, but think about where you'll be when you ask for the weather or to dim the lights, and place your speaker accordingly. You'll set up Alexa speakers using the Alexa app, which allows you to manage multiple Alexa speakers if you own more than one through your Amazon account. Third-party speaker setup methods may vary. Is Alexa Always Listening? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Alexa is always listening, to a certain extent. It's designed to only listen for its wake word and shouldn't be recording or processing any audio unless it hears that word. But Alexa can sometimes mishear a word and think it's the wake word, or it might hear a word similar enough to activate the speaker. If you've owned an Alexa, there have likely been times when the assistant suddenly responds when you weren't speaking to it. Once it hears the wake word (or what it believes to be the wake word), it will start listening to everything in an attempt to hear what you need and respond. Alexa+, the latest version of Alexa, will also remain on for a little bit after you ask a question to listen for follow-up questions, no wake word required. Both Alexa and Alexa+ light up in some fashion (regular speakers will turn the light ring blue, while the displays will have a blue bar appear on the screen) to let you know the assistant is listening. Most Echo devices also have a physical mute button and will display a red light or red bar to let you know when the mute is activated. How Do You Remove Ads and Spam From an Echo Show? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron If you're using an Echo Show device, you've likely noticed there is a ton of default content the device will show you. Sports scores! Local news! A recipe you might be interested in! It makes the device exhausting and annoying to be near. Here's how you can control what you see: Swipe down from the top of your Echo Show to pull up the menu, and select Settings.

In the Settings menu, choose Home Content.

There are more than 40 options you can toggle on and off on this menu, and you should remove as many as you can that you don't use. I usually remove all but weather forecasts and recently played audio. While you're able to turn off interest-based ads from third-party skills (this is under Alexa Privacy in the Settings menu), it won't stop all ads. The only setting that is ad-free is choosing Photo Display mode, which can use either Amazon's included library of photos or your own. The downside is that it turns it into a digital photo frame, so you won't even see a clock or features like widgets. Can I Have My Alexa Requests Locally Processed, or Do They Have to Go to the Cloud? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron There used to be a privacy feature called Do Not Send Voice Recordings that let you have all your voice requests processed locally on your Alexa device instead of being sent to Amazon's cloud storage. That feature was killed in March 2025 to support Alexa+, and even if you continue to use the old Alexa, you don't have access to that feature any longer. How Does WIRED Select Smart Speakers to Test? How Are These Speakers Tested? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron For this guide, we specifically test speakers that are compatible with Amazon Alexa. It's a big limitation and narrows down the options significantly, especially compared to speaker options you'll see in our other guides like the Best Bluetooth Speakers. That's mainly Amazon's own ecosystem of speakers, and while there are third-party options, the best options tend to be of Amazon's own design to work with its own voice assistant. Each speaker gets installed in a tester's home for day-to-day use, to see how the microphone performs, how the speaker sounds with different types of music, how well the smart home control features work with compatible devices such as smart lights and video doorbells, and to test other features as necessary (e.g., streaming features on smart displays). How Does WIRED Get Models? What Does WIRED Do After Testing Them? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron We acquire review units usually as a press sample, though we will also independently purchase samples if need be. All review units in this guide were provided as press samples with no obligation to cover or promises for what that coverage would be. After testing, we keep most of our picks either installed for long-term testing in our homes or in storage to compare against updated models and new speakers that come out. If the sample becomes irrelevant or unnecessary to keep, we donate it locally.

Tech.title: There May Not Be an iPhone 18 This Year
Tech.content:
Every year around this time, Apple announces new iPhones. The products go on sale soon after, usually ranging from a base model to more premium and more expensive Pro models. But this year will likely be different—not just because the company has a brand-new CEO.

Apple’s iPhone event will be held on September 9 at 10 am Pacific (1 pm Eastern), announced last week with the title “Surprise and Shine!” If you tune into the livestream, expect the announcement of an iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and, if all the rumors and widely held analyst expectations are true, the first look at an Apple foldable device.

Based on leaks and the ongoing tech rumor mill and its decent track record for figuring these things out, Apple is expected to prioritize its more expensive, premium devices this year and hold off on announcing its base model iPhone 18. That cheaper model is rumored to launch in the spring of 2027, potentially alongside an iPhone 18e and maybe a second-generation iPhone Air.

Why the drastic change in strategy? It may be due to the ongoing memory shortage, which has made just about everything more expensive. Apple hasn’t been spared. In June, former Apple CEO Tim Cook acknowledged that Apple would raise product prices to keep up with manufacturing costs.

“Our assumption is that they're going to be launching three models in the fall, the premium side of the models of the 18 series,” says Nabila Popal, a senior director of data and analytics at IDC. “Then the mid/budget devices will be launched in the spring.”

Tech.title: This Interactive Tool Visually Compares Your Vaccine vs. Disease Risk
Tech.content:
We live in a time when mixed messages about vaccines are the norm. Often, the Trump administration says one thing, while public health officials say another, leaving at least half of Americans in what the independent health policy organization KFF called the “malleable middle.” They remain uncertain when presented with vaccine myths.

To address the confusion, the free “What’s the Risk?” tool launched in early August. It allows you to visualize the vaccine risks often described as “rare” or “uncommon” right alongside the risks associated with the diseases they were created to prevent.

The interactive tool was designed by the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy and Unbiased Science, a public health communication platform and podcast founded by Jessica Steier, a public health scientist.

More comparisons will be added over time, but right now, you can see the measles and the MMR vaccine and RSV alongside its vaccines and antibody products. Plus, you can compare them to life events, such as deaths caused by drowning, car crashes, falls, bee or wasp stings and lightning strikes.

How to use the vaccine risk tool

First, choose one of the suggested comparisons or build your own by selecting two from the dropdowns.

Life events like drowning and car crashes help put certain risks in perspective. Unbiased Science/CNET Screenshot

But before you scroll down to see the comparison, Steier told CNET in an email that you should read the “Before you compare: a few things to know” list at the top. It explains, for example, that what happens if you get infected versus what happens if you get vaccinated aren’t equally likely. For the former, it depends on many factors, such as where you live and travel and how many people around you are vaccinated.

“They tell you what each side of the comparison is holding constant, and that shapes how you should read everything below it,” Steier said.

Scroll down to view the two side-by-side light gray boxes. Each represents 100,000 people in the population indicated above the boxes in color-coded bands. Comparisons are most reliable when comparing the same population, so when two different age groups are shown, you should treat the results as a rough sense of scale rather than a precise number.

Sources are shown below the squares, along with each risk and the number of those affected per 100,000 of the stated population. Unbiased Science/CNET Screenshot

Plus, these are population averages. Your personal risk will depend on your age, health status and lifestyle circumstances.

All numbers are shown as an annual rate, unless labeled otherwise. Since everyday risks are usually published as lifetime figures, those had to be converted.

Within the light gray boxes, you’ll find colored squares representing each risk. They’re sized to indicate the number of people affected by the stated complication. “A very rare outcome shows up as a tiny speck and a common one as a large block,” said Steier.

Each square has a color meant to illustrate the severity of the outcome. Red indicates serious outcomes, while dark gray indicates those considered mild or temporary.

If you hover over a square or tap on it, you can read the details and see links to the sources for the number shown by the square.

Above the squares, you can switch to a grid view for a different perspective. You can also zoom in to see the risks represented in a population of 50,000.

What the grid view looks like. Unbiased Science/CNET Screenshot

Ultimately, this tool takes numbers that can be difficult to contextualize and helps you visualize them to better understand the relative frequency and severity of vaccines versus their connected diseases.

How sources were chosen

To narrow down the sources for this tool, two rules were applied. “Every figure has to come from a public, citable source, and every figure has to be measured the same way as the one sitting next to it,” said Steier.

For the first rule, the tool’s creators went straight to the source: national surveillance systems and published studies, rather than news articles, fact sheets or advocacy pages that merely cited the original data. The tool links out to these sources, in case you’d like to check their work.

When you hover over a risk, you can see the sources used. Unbiased Science/CNET Screenshot

The makers also matched both the vaccine and disease sides based on age group and population as closely as available data allowed. Where that match isn’t exact, the tool says so.

The goal

A single number or statistic won’t typically tell you everything you need to know when it comes to vaccine or disease risk. According to Steier, to understand a risk, you need three things: how likely the outcome is, how serious it would be if it happened, and what it compares to, including what happens if you do nothing.

“Part of what we’re up against is numbness,” said Steier. “Everyone throws scary numbers around constantly, so we’ve stopped registering them. ‘One in 10,000’ and ‘one in a million’ both just land as ‘rare,’ even though one is a hundred times the other.”

The hope with this tool is that users will better understand what those numbers actually mean and develop a habit of asking “compared to what?”

While not directly comparable due to age differences, it’s still eye-opening to compare vaccine complications with life events. Unbiased Science/CNET Screenshot

The tool’s future

In addition to working on the design and functionality, the team behind “What’s the Risk?” plans to add more vaccines and diseases. Plus, everyday life events, since those help people put an unfamiliar risk on a scale they already understand.

“The addition we’re most excited about is a way to reflect vaccine coverage, because coverage is what drives how likely you are to encounter these diseases in the first place,” Steier said. This could involve pulling in vaccine uptake by ZIP code so people can view their community, or a slider that lets users adjust vaccine coverage to see how disease risk changes.

This expansion would show that many of us live with a low risk of disease because of the number of people around us who are vaccinated.

Steier emphasized that the current version of the tool is merely version 1.0, so if you see anything that can be improved, you can email the team at vaccines@unbiasedscience.com.

Tech.title: Orbitals Review: The Perfect Couples Co-op Game for the Switch 2
Tech.content:
Developer Shapefarm’s debut release is more than just a stellar couch co-op adventure: Orbitals is a celebration of vintage anime that wears its inspirations on its sleeve. It’s Cowboy Bebop, Evangelion and Sailor Moon stuffed into a high-concept sci-fi story, with lovingly crafted animated cutscenes to boot. And while Orbitals never truly breaks away from these visual touchstones to blossom into a stand-alone masterpiece, it’s aping so many nearly perfect hits that the sugary nostalgia will probably be enough to keep you satiated during the game’s short playtime.

The elephant in the room is Hazelight Studios’ string of award-winning hits, like It Takes Two and Split Fiction, which have come to define the couch co-op space over the past 10 years. It’s nearly impossible not to compare similar games to Hazelight’s output, even if that seems unfair to new studios just entering the genre.

But Orbitals holds up against the best of the best — probably in no small part because its development team is helmed by ex-Hazelight talent. Orbitals Game Director Jakob Lundgren previously told Polygon that the game would integrate a lot of the Hazelight DNA, but I actually think it positively iterates on that award-winning formula in many ways.

I spent a lot of time standing around and holding down a single button to help out my partner in It Takes Two and Split Fiction. By contrast, Orbitals ensures both players are always zooming through its challenges together, making meaningful contributions to platforming sections or puzzles without lingering too long in one place.

In Orbitals, players step into the role of young space colonists, Maki and Omura, who have spent their entire lives in a stranded space colony ravaged by a mysterious radiation storm. The only thing keeping the folks on the station alive are high-tech respawn machines, named IMs, but the danger is closing in. In order to save their found family (and potentially help everyone escape the wreckage), Maki and Omura travel into the farthest reaches of space to scavenge what they need to survive.

Studio Massket’s animated cutscenes make Orbitals much more charming than other genre fare. Shapefarm

The ’80s anime style does the heavy lifting for a by-the-numbers narrative

Despite its high-concept sci-fi premise, Orbitals’ story and its characters aren’t anything to write home about — it’s easy to see that they’re loving homages to popular anime series.

The IM respawn machines that bring the main characters back to life time and time again evoke some of Evangelion’s existential horror, though the game doesn’t delve into the implications that much. The spaceships are grimy, industrial and totally Bebop. Main character Maki acts (and looks) a bit like a magical girl, while her partner Omura is intelligent, a bit nerdy and way too prideful, like an endearing mix of Ranma and Spike Spiegel.

It’s regrettable that none of these pieces ever feel like they successfully iterate on those beloved archetypes; the game just copies the best odds and ends from other stories and pastes them piecemeal into this new setting. Orbitals fondly reminisces on the titans of animation yesteryear, and that nostalgia goes far. But most of the game’s narrative beats feel formulaic (and not in a good way). It took me an entire play session to really start engaging with the story; I’m not sure my girlfriend ever fully emotionally engaged with the world at all.

Where It Takes Two and Split Fiction do manage to edge out Orbitals is level design: Hazelight’s best games have players jumping from world to world. Being shrunk down to explore a snow globe is a memorable experience, doubly so when that’s followed up by a perilous journey through an oversize garden. Orbitals mostly offers different flavors of broken-down spaceship to rifle through, and they start blending together once you’ve gallivanted through a handful of wrecks.

That’s not to say that the environmental design in Orbitals lacks charm. The game still offers plenty of gorgeous (and dangerous) vistas to visit throughout outer space, including asteroid field mining settlements, an iced-over power plant, a crackling, lava-filled factory and more. If you end up in an unappealing locale, you can rest assured you’ll be zooming past it soon: Orbitals is short enough that no level overstays its welcome.

The art direction and loving details baked into Orbitals’ DNA are what really hooked my partner and me, and I have no doubt that the little discoveries around every corner will be enjoyable for most players.

If you ever tire of the main story or need a break from the platforming levels, you can divert your attention to the main characters’ lovable purple cat, the little Studio Ghibli-inspired alien dudes scattered throughout the world or some seriously engaging unlockable minigames. (The best minigame is a versus mode akin to Space War, where you try to blow each other up with blasters that have absurd recoil.)

Even when puzzles leave you standing still, Orbitals necessitates a compelling level of coordination between partners. Shapefarm

Puzzles are challenging — and might be frustrating for some

I’m sitting on the fence about whether I should recommend Orbitals to a couple that never quite finished It Takes Two, Split Fiction or any other couch co-op platforming game. Unlike Hazelight’s impressive but lengthy titles, Orbitals is a bite-sized adventure, completable in around three play sessions, making for an easier commitment. But I know other couples that have struggled with the platforming in similar co-op games and drop them when a level gets too frustrating — and Orbitals features some surprisingly difficult coordinated movement challenges.

I personally enjoyed Orbitals’ brand of kinetic puzzling, which felt more active and less handhold-y than many levels in Hazelight games. My least favorite part of couch co-op games is when one player needs to stop engaging with play for the other to progress. If I’m standing on a button, pulling a lever or hanging around doing something similar, I’m probably not having much fun.

Orbitals has only a few instances in where you’ll completely stop to wait for your partner; while some doors and button presses require both players to operate them at the same time, that’s about it.

Even when you’re separated, the game keeps partners constantly engaged with one another. My girlfriend and I used lasers, water guns, jump packs and other cool gadgets to create new platforms for each other, clear out hazards like lava or forge paths in other creative ways. Orbitals forced us to pause and discuss how to time certain maneuvers, which was novel and fun. In the game’s toughest challenge, I had to match my partner’s movement tempo to send platforms back and forth across a side-scrolling screen while a nasty spirit clambered toward us.

I don’t anticipate longtime gamers to struggle with Orbitals, but the level of mechanical challenge feels a little bit higher than other genre fare. The game has many puzzles that require you to execute precision platforming in tandem with your partner, which might be frustrating for novice gamers.

While that could be a blocker for some folks, the game’s handcrafted anime art style makes it approachable, nonetheless. Orbitals is oozing with personality and constantly benefits from the attention to small details like character emotes. (Get ready to spam Omura’s wiggly dance.) And even if you completely bounce off of everything else, Orbitals is worth the upfront payment to experience Studio Massket’s beautiful ’80s-style hand-drawn anime cutscenes.

Orbitals is out now and is exclusively available on the Switch 2 for $40.

Tech.title: We Rated the Weird Tech at IFA 2026 to Find the Wackiest Products
Tech.content:
Thousands of products crowd the halls of IFA, one of the world’s largest consumer technology shows. Most promise to make our lives easier, healthier or more connected. Every year, however, a few exhibitors appear to receive a slightly different assignment.

At IFA 2026 in Berlin, we found an air conditioner that follows you around, a skylight that reads the mood and AI companions waiting to become emotionally complicated. Some of this technology is unexpectedly clever. Some of it solves problems we didn’t know existed.

All of it made us stop walking and ask, “Wait, what is that?”

Govee’s mood-reading skylight

Govee’s giant mood light was on display at IFA. David Watsky/CNET

Govee has long been at the forefront of strange home lighting creations, from literal curtains of light to spread across your garage to table lamps that look more like alien artifacts. Now Govee is showing off one of its oddest products yet: a dome-like ceiling light designed to mimic the sky and be “mood-responsive.”

In this case, mood-responsive means you can use Govee’s AI to talk about your mood or how you’re feeling, and the Govee app will suggest ceiling light color schemes to match. But the light can also create a specific blue wavelength designed to evoke blue skies and natural daylight.

Too weird to work? Not as weird as you may think. I’ve tested Govee’s AI before, and you really can generate lighting patterns based on your mood or random musings. But Govee already has so many lighting scenes in its app that I didn’t find it very practical — though definitely fun. I wonder how well it will work with a full ceiling light.

A gigantic tofu maker

The Nuvell plant protein maker is about the size of an espresso machine. David Watsky/CNET

If your two problems are not eating enough plant protein and having too much counter space, the Nuvell is here. This massive bean cooker and compressor is the size of an espresso machine and churns out blocks of tofu in as little as 30 minutes. It can make other vegan proteins depending on the legume you stick inside.

Plant protein made in the comfort of your kitchen. David Watsky/CNET

I asked the rep on duty whether the Nuvell could make cheese if you poured cow’s milk in. She claimed it could, but didn’t seem too confident.

Too weird to work? While it wasn’t operational at IFA, we assume the Nuvell does what it’s supposed to, since turning soybeans into tofu isn’t rocket science. The real question is whether it’s worth the space on your counter for this one-trick pony of a kitchen appliance.

A toothbrush with a built-in camera

A camera on your toothbrush is definitely a design choice. Dyson

Unless you’re a dentist, you probably don’t want a closer look at your teeth — but one intrepid brand came to IFA bearing a toothbrush that gets personal by using a built-in camera.

The Dyson Camerajet uses a camera with “Gap Optical Targeting.” Fortunately, you don’t have to personally review the 28 images per second the camera can take. Instead, an AI analyzes it for you and targets interdental gaps. From what we can tell, you can then aim the toothbrush’s jet of water at tooth gaps to make sure they get extra clean.

If you do want to play dentist like this, it’ll cost a sweet $500 for the advance.

Too weird to work? I’m calling this one too weird for sure. Price aside, you have to stand with your toothbrush in hand while holding your phone in the other to look at an enormous close-up of your teeth on the screen, then simultaneously brush and use the water flosser at the right angles to hit what look like gaps. The whole thing appears entirely unnecessary if you simply practice good brushing and flossing.

A tiny robot vacuum… for your bed

Yep — a whole robot vacuum, just for the bed. Creatulize

Creatulize came to IFA to show off the smallest robot vacuum in all of Berlin. The X1 Pro is the brand’s second-gen bed robot vacuum, designed to clean your bedding and mattress.

Using precision mode, the vac moves slowly and steadily across a mattress, sucking up dust, mites, hair and whatever else lurks. It can clean a king-size in about 20 minutes and has an easy-to-empty debris canister. Special sensors keep it from tumbling off the bed. When it hits an edge, it stops, turns and keeps on keepin’ on.

That’s one itty-bitty robot vac. David Watsky/CNET

Too weird to work? Mattress vacuums are becoming a thing, based on the idea that dirty mattresses exacerbate allergies. Nobody wants a dusty mattress, but whether or not you need a dedicated vacuum for it is up for debate. We’ll be testing the X1 Pro to find out.

An air conditioner trained to follow you

Midea’s new voice-controlled air conditioner follows you around the room with a stream of cool. David Watsky/CNET

One of the highlights we saw – and felt – was an air conditioner unit that sends custom cool air to you wherever you are. Midea’s new system uses spatial imaging and sensors to track your position in the room and deliver a stream of cool air your way. That means a cooler you and less energy wasted.

Midea’s smart AC works with the brand’s other air-quality appliances, including the humidifier. The two work in harmony through Midea’s smart sync to keep your home’s air at your desired temperature and humidity, no matter what Mother Nature has planned.

It’s also voice-activated, so you can turn it on or off, or activate the “mmWave sensor system” without getting up or even opening your phone.

Too weird to work? While the AC wasn’t officially up and running at IFA, Dyson launched a similar freestanding fan and air purifier that tracks humans in the room and spits fresh, cool air their way. We’re still testing that one in our lab, but would be surprised if the technology doesn’t live up to at least some of its promise.

SwitchBot’s AI shirt pin, the MindClip

SwitchBot’s AI clip sort of… spies on everyone around you. SwitchBot

If you thought AI was already in everything, just wait: SwitchBot is announcing the launch of its AI shirt device, the MindClip, at IFA. It’s made to clip onto your shirt pocket, collar, nearby strap or even belt. Once in place, it, well, essentially listens to everything that happens within a 3-meter radius for up to 20 hours and saves it for you.

The MindClip can recognize people by their voices and summarize conversations or events, ostensibly to help you with planning after a busy day. As far as AI goes, it’s no spying Meta glasses, but it is fairly invasive, especially for strangers you may be chatting with.

Too weird to work? This isn’t the first time we’ve seen an AI pin, although it is the smallest and least distracting version I’ve spotted. The problem is that none of them really took off, and some companies even pivoted to an entirely different product. So yes, it’s too weird to work for now, but maybe the rumored AI capabilities in Apple’s AirPods will be an exception.

The AI-powered companion doll from Lovense

Lovense’s updated AI companion doll also made an appearance at IFA. Lovense

Singaporean intimacy and sex toy company Lovense has brought the latest version of its AI “companion doll” to IFA, aiming to make it more lifelike than ever before. In addition to talking, remembering past facts and adjusting its personality, the silicone doll can blink, smile and look when called by its custom name. Users can also chat with the doll at a distance via a phone app and set up roleplay scenarios, if they prefer.

Too weird to work? Yes, the age of AI sex dolls is here. But it’s such an eclectic — and expensive (between $4,000 and $8,000) — proposition, this one is only for those with very specific tastes and a, ahh, particular relationship with AI. For others, Lovense also debuted several more conventional, AI-free toys.

A Eufy sensor that asks if you fell down

Eufy’s new sensor has a very, very specific purpose in the home. Eufy

When today’s home sensors can do nearly anything from recognizing when dogs bark to knowing when someone is tampering with a mailbox, it may sound strange to make a sensor specifically to say, “Oops, it looks like you fell down!” But that’s just what Anker’s Eufy brand has done.

There’s method behind this madness. The wall sensor uses a combo of algorithms and presence sensing with mmWave technology, no cameras necessary. It’s made to help those aging in place or living in rest homes without creating privacy concerns. The sensor even supports two-way audio, so family members or nurses can check in if they get an alert about a potential fall.

Quick note: As Anker consolidates its brand names, Eufy products are staying with us, but the Eufy name may not be around forever, so keep that in mind when shopping.

Too weird to work? In this case, not at all. I’ve already seen mmWave technology tap into Wi-Fi signals to help those aging in place, although Eufy’s sensor is the first I’ve seen that focuses on falls and enables two-way audio for a quick checkup. It’s a strong use of the technology.

Best DIY Home Security Systems of 2026: Install Them Yourself Dodge installation fees and take security into your own hands with these super smart security kits.

A smartphone for your pet

The Petphone certainly makes a lot of claims about AI pet powers. Petpogo

Ucloudlink has brought the newest version of its award-winning PetPhone to IFA this year, showing a world where cats and dogs have their own smartphone, too. Sort of.

The Petpogo PetPhone is technically a smart pet collar, and we’ve reviewed many of those. But this version comes with two-way audio to talk to your pet with an app and AI features that interpret behavior and motion so pets can theoretically initiate a call themselves, as well as emotion analysis of barks, meows and other actions. It also supports more traditional capabilities like tracking and geofencing, and it alerts pet parents to out-of-routine behaviors.

Too weird to work? No AI features can accurately interpret specific barks or meows into moods and feelings. That’s (currently) nonsense. And trying to get your pet to “call” you with specific behaviors sounds dubious at best. So most of the innovations here are too weird, but the underlying collar functionality looks usable.

These headphones that turn into a Bluetooth speaker

TDM’s Bluetooth speaker headphone hybrid is confusing. TDM

TDM is showing off its unique Neo headphones, with a literal twist. In normal mode, they look like a typical pair of wireless headphones. But twist and collapse the earcups, and they form into a small Bluetooth speaker with up to 8 hours of music playback. The dual-device comes with an aux port, a USB-C charging port and a carrying case.

Too weird to work? When was the last time you saw someone with headphones and thought, “What a pleasant, private music experience that person is having, I wish there was a way for them to share it with all the people nearby?” Nope. No one likes it when you play music out loud in public spaces, especially when the same device could let you listen privately. I’m calling these headphones too weird to work.

A soundwave-creating smart bed

Amada’s acoustic mattress claims many different applications. Amada

Amada brought a fascinating mattress to IFA called the Soundwave Smart Mattress. Yes, it connects to a phone app. And yes, it really does produce sound waves or at least a “vibroacoustic experience” with vibration modes for presleep relaxation, meditation, focus and recharging. I’m not sure how vibration is supposed to help with those things, but CNET health expert Anna Gragert told me vibration therapy does have applications for recovery and disease treatment. The bed is made of polyurethane foam and polyester fabric, with a four-pin power connector.

Too weird to work? Well, Magic Fingers did have their day in hotel rooms across the US, but that day ended pretty fast. I don’t know if a bed with good vibrations is what the average home is looking for, but if you’ve tried it and it works for you, this could be a shakingly good upgrade.

Editor’s note: David Watsky’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by IFA. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own

Tech.title: As a Pet Parent to 3 Asthmatic Cats, I’m Eyeing This New AAFA-Certified Vacuum at IFA 2026
Tech.content:
Anker has made some of our favorite and most innovative robot vacuums over the years, and recently, they’ve also been getting into robot lawn mowers, earning spots on our tested lists. The newest models they’re showing off at IFA Berlin 2026 include a robot vacuum and a robot mower, both with key improvements and features over previous generations.

Anker’s newest robot vacuum — and potentially the last one to keep the Eufy name (more on that below) — is the Omni E35, and it just might be what my three asthmatic cats need because it focuses on sterilization and disinfection. Anker describes it as “baby-grade,” meaning it’s TÜV Rheinland-certified for the “Maternal and Infant Cleaning Robot mark.” It can eliminate bacteria and dust mites, and it has low noise and high efficiency when it comes to cleaning and self-cleaning.

Anker says it’s the first and only robot vacuum to earn the Asthma & Allergy Friendly Certification from the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America. This is especially interesting to me as someone who has the bad luck of having three cats diagnosed with asthma. The vet told me it was incredibly unlikely to occur naturally, so the cause is probably environmental — dust mites, dander, outdoor pollution, fragrances or smoke from the neighbors downstairs. At least a couple of those factors could be addressed by a robot vacuum capable of more thorough fine-dust pickup and sterilization, so I’m interested in seeing it in action and trying it at home.

Anker says the E35 Omni can clean your floors well enough for babies to play on.

It has all the typical flagship features you’d expect from a top-tier model, including 35,000 pascals of suction and the Hydro Jet 2.0 self-cleaning roller mop. It also has a kitchen deep clean mode that uses an algorithm to determine how to tackle tougher stains, by saturating, soaking and then scrubbing.

The Omni E35 will cost $1,300 at MSRP, but pre-sale buyers will receive a discount, bringing the E35 to $1,000. Pre-sale is open now at eufy.com.

Eufy S2 Max

Also new in the robotics space is the Eufy S2 Max, Anker’s first robot mower developed entirely in-house. It has vision-based SLAM navigation and real-time 3D mapping, meaning no boundary wires or RTK beacons are required, which has become increasingly common in the robot mower market. It also has improved computing and full all-wheel drive, letting it handle terrain up to 80% slopes, a dual blade system and edge-to-edge cutting with an extendable trimming arm.

I saw the trimmer arm in action in the constrained demo area and while it wasn’t real grass or a real lawn, it really sold me on the benefits of having the edge trimmer to clean up the spots by fences and bushes. I also watched the mower smoothly navigate up and down the artificial slope Anker set up for the purpose of the demo, while a real-time 3D map showed the locations it was mowing, and still had to mow.

US availability and pricing are still to be determined, but it’ll be available in EU markets in May 2027 for 3,999 euros.

Anker is rebranding

Anker’s Eufy brand includes its lineup of robot vacuums and robot lawn mowers, as well as home security products. At IFA Berlin 2026, the company revealed that after 14 years of operation, it’s bringing all of its sub-brands, including Eufy and Soundcore for the audio products, under the Anker umbrella. In the future, all Anker products, no matter if they’re robot vacuums, robot lawn mowers, security cameras, smart doorbells or headphones, will be sold under the Anker brand.

The change isn’t immediate, and an Anker representative who briefed me prior to IFA said that for a time, consumers in different markets will still see the distinct branding across product categories, but the goal is to consolidate it under Anker. For now, the lineup announced at IFA 2026 will continue to use the Eufy or Soundcore branding. The announcement coincides with the opening of an official Anker Flagship store in Berlin on Sept. 5, the company’s first standalone retail store there.

I cover vacuums and home tech for CNET. While I’m here at IFA Berlin 2026, I’m determined to seek out the most interesting tech that solves your most common cleaning problems. Be sure to check out my other stories on the cool things I’ve found.

Tech.title: I Went Shopping for My Ultimate Smart Home of the Future at IFA 2026
Tech.content:
The IFA 2026 tech conference in Berlin is packed to the gills with gadgets of all kinds, from new foldable phones, innovative alarm clocks and even flying car concepts. But it’s home tech that really dominates the show with brands from all over the world gathering to tell you how you can add smart gadgets to your home in every conceivable way.

Always keen to make my life easier, more colorful and more expensive, I took to the halls of the show to browse for the items I would be most interested in putting in my own home — if I suddenly won the lottery, that is.

Dillon Lopez/CNET

LG OLED EVO AI 83W6

I started with the most important part: the TV. I opted for LG’s new OLED model because it’s massive, its colors looked glorious and it’s exceptionally thin, meaning it won’t look weirdly out of place when I bolt it to my wall.

Does your couch light up? No, nor does mine. But it could. Dillon Lopez/CNET

Govee Smart Lights

My couch currently doesn’t have underlighting like a car from the Fast and the Furious films, but Govee’s smart lights could change all that. I saw (and, indeed, sat upon) a couch with multicolored strips along the underside, giving a glow that could make your living room look like a games arcade. Delightful.

I had to test this multiple times because journalism. Dillon Lopez/CNET

iGulu F1 Smart Home Brewer

I like beer, and I like even more not having to leave my home in order to acquire it, so this smart home brewery setup would be a high priority for me. Simply pour in the ingredients for whatever type of beer you want. (Classic English Bitter? Yes please.) And the brewery setup will do the rest.

I had a taster cup (OK, fine, I had several), and they were delicious.

The fridge can keep water at below freezing but without it actually freezing. Shake the bottle and ice crystals will form. I think it’s magic, maybe. Dillon Lopez/CNET

Xiaomi Mijia Refrigerator Pro Cryo

If I’d made some beer, then I’d of course need to keep it nice and cold, and Xiaomi’s new refrigerator is the one I’d want. It uses various forms of compression and airflow to keep the contents cooler and, therefore, keeps them fresher for longer. That’s great as it means you’ll have longer to use that big of leftover cucumber before it turns into a gloopy mess in the bottom drawer, which will help fight food waste in the home. Nice.

The AI cameras are able to recognize things you might do in your bed. It’s not creepy unless you think about it for even a second. Dillon Lopez/CNET

Xiaomi Smart Bedroom

Xiaomi actually had a lot of stuff on show as it basically makes every kind of tech product you can think of. But it was the way everything came together as an ecosystem that impressed me at the show. In the smart bedroom demo, I sat down on the bed with a book. AI-enabled cameras recognized this and immediately switched on the bedside lamp, adjusted the bed for a comfortable reading position, turned on the AC and drew the curtains closed.

The idea is to have all parts of the home automated like this: Loaded the dishwasher? The robot vacuum will come out to clean up the floor after you’ve been cooking. Open the door of Xiaomi’s car in your driveway? It’ll recognize that you’re leaving and switch off the lights in the home and lock the door.

It’s a wild system, and I can definitely see the appeal. But it also relies on having AI-enabled cameras watching you everywhere in your home. Do I really want that? Absolutely not. But thanks anyway.

It made some adorable squeaking noises as it climbed the sides of the pool, and I loved it. Dillon Lopez/CNET

Roborock Rockaqua P1

In this ideal world, I’d have a salary significant enough for me to afford a home with space enough to build my own pool. And then I’d need a way of keeping it clean without, y’know, having to actually do anything myself. That’s where Roborock’s pool-cleaning robot comes in.

Think of it as a Roomba that can go underwater. It’ll clean dirt and grime from the pool floor and can even climb the walls to keep everything nice and fresh.

I work hard, and nobody can say I don’t. Dillon Lopez/CNET

IFA bumper cars

Classic fairground bumper cars aren’t exactly smart home technology, but they were something I could enjoy at the show, and enjoy I did. But when I thought about it more, I realized they may also be the ultimate urban vehicle: powered only by electricity, runs on overhead power lines so you never need to charge them and are safe enough that you can ram them into another road user and you don’t need to exchange insurance details afterward.

Robot lawnmowers doing a synchronized fan dance isn’t something I knew I needed. Dillon Lopez/CNET

Mova Astra X

Mova’s lawn-mowing robot has a big robotic arm attached to it that is designed to pick up garden debris as the mower automatically circles the grounds of your home to keep things neat. But Mova had a better use for it at the show: a synchronized fan dance set to an electro-metal soundtrack from a live DJ. Count me in.

Cat goes in. Poop goes out. That’s what Neakasa M9 litter box is all about. Dillon Lopez/CNET

Neakasa M9 Litter Box

I love my beautiful fluffy ball of absolute wonderful joy (my cat, Toulouse) more than anything else in the world. But even so, having to go and clear out his daily dumps from the litter box is time that could be spent cuddling him or taking more photos of his paws.

Neakasa’s litter box uses a rotating scoop system that filters out each bit of new nastiness and deposits the mess in a chute for easy removal later. Thanks, technology.

If it says, “pterodactyl spotted on bird feeder,” then you can safely assume the AI has made a mistake. Dillon Lopez/CNET

Birdfy Feeder Metal 2

While “Feeder Metal 2” might sound more like a side-scrolling, beat-em-up game for the Atari games console in the ’80s, Birdfy’s home gadget is much more adorable. Equipped with wide angle cameras, this bird feeder will alert you each time a bird comes for a snack and uses AI to recognize what species you’re seeing.

I love birds. I know I’d thoroughly enjoy just watching the live feed from the cameras and seeing the various garden birds we have in Britain coming to rudely eat the seed I bought them without leaving a thank-you.

The least visually engaging product I saw. Not even a fan dance. Dillon Lopez/CNET

EcoFlow Stream 5000

No smart home setup is complete without a power backup solution, and EcoFlow’s is my personal pick. The Stream 5000 power station can have multiple solar panels plugged into it, and it has a built-in inverter to feed that power directly into your home’s grid. While just one unit will keep your devices working for a short time, you can daisy-chain multiple ones to give you up to several days of home power in case of longer outages.

Editors’ note: Andrew Lanxon’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Xiaomi. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: I Watched a Stain Removing Robot Completley Miss Its Target at IFA
Tech.content:
Ecovacs makes some of the best robot vacuums we’ve tested here at CNET, and for a long time, their unique combo T90 Pro Omni was our top choice for its incredible versatility. The new Ecovacs Deebot X12S OmniCyclone is a bit more iterative than its predecessor, the X12, but it makes key improvements to tackle dust mites and allergies while keeping the water jet that the previous model used to loosen stains. I got to see it in action and…well, let’s just say, there are some parts of the concept that could use some work.

The dust mite removal on the other hand, is something I’m very interested in and I could see a real use for it in my house with three asthmatic cats.

“A dust mite allergy isn’t something you just get over. You clean around it,” said Michelle Jones, associate brand marketing director at Ecovacs Americas. “Most robots skim the top of a carpet. We built the X12S to get down to where the dust actually sits.”

The X12S was tested by the SGS Testing & Control Services Singapore and, in testing, removed an average of 97.44% of dust mite allergens and 95.45% of dust mites from carpet. Ecovacs points out that dust mites live in soft material, especially carpet. Since carpet is underfoot, it traps dust mites and allergens deeper in the pile that a conventional robot vacuum can’t reach.



This might sound niche, but as someone who has three asthmatic cats and occasionally seasonal allergies, I’m interested to see if it lives up to the testing claims. The feature sounds similar to Anker’s new Omni E35, which also claims the ability to remove 99% of dust mites and has Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America certification.

The X12S also has 53 air watts of effective suction, 60% more than the previous-generation X12; Ecovacs claims this gives it handheld-vacuum-level cleaning power, which I’ll be interested to see if that is true in CNET’s lab testing.

You may not want to count on the spray for removing stains

The OZMO Roller 3.0 is self-washing, as is increasingly common among robot vacuums from different manufacturers, so the roller keeps refreshing itself with clean water. Reprising its role from the previous generation is the FocusJet stain spray, which shoots water to loosen and break up older and dried-on stains — this is another feature we’ve seen other manufacturers adopt after Ecovacs showed it off on the X12 earlier this year.

I watched the X12S Omnicyclone steadily mop the test area after the demonstrator squirted a bit of ketchup onto the white tile. The robot didn’t seem to notice the stain at first. It continued its slow and steady mopping pattern, until finally the sensors spotted the ketchup. The sprayers started up and it doused the general area of the stain, but there was just one problem — it didn’t make contact with the stain at all.

The Omnicyclone actually completely overshot the stain with the spray, dousing a good chunk of tile beyond where the ketchup actually was. It was still about to remove the ketchup by going over it with the roller mop, which uses fresh water for each cleaning, but the spray itself didn’t really contribute anything. This may have just been bad luck, so I don’t want to write the system off entirely, but a demo environment like this is really as ideal as it gets for a robot vacuum.

You have a situation here where the X12S has a small, very well-mapped area to clean, great bright lights, and the ideal floor type. The spray really shouldn’t be missing the mark like that. I also noticed that the robot had to get pretty close to the ketchup on one of its passes before it registered and acknowledged it. The fact that it then missed the spray entirely tells me that whatever AI or algorithm the robot is using to calculate the spray force, distance, and quantity is way off.

The good news is that this sounds like it could be a software fix rather than a hardware issue, but it’s not a promising problem to have arise if you’re looking for a reliable cleaner that gets the job done hands-free.

The rest of the cleaning system carries over from the X12, including the 15-millimeter auto-mop lifting and the Mop Roller Smart Cover, which keeps the mop clear of the carpet. It has AIVI 3D 4.0 dual obstacle avoidance, which pairs camera vision with 3D laser sensing to navigate cluttered rooms. There’s also a 3D edge sensor to clean close to walls and baseboards without leaving gaps.

Interestingly, the X12S has a physical privacy shutter, not just software privacy. It covers the AIVI camera so you can be sure that when it’s closed, the lens is blocked.

“A cover you can see is easier to trust, because you can look at it,” Jones said. “As these robots take in more of the home, people will want to ensure they have their privacy.”



This is a first for robot vacuums, at least with the ones I’ve seen, and it’ll be interesting to see if other companies choose to adopt it. Lastly, it comes with the fast-charging system we liked on the X12, which can top up the robot vacuum more quickly between mop-washing dock cycles.

Price and availability

The Deebot X12S OmniCyclone is available in the United States at an MSRP of $1,300. Buyers can order it on Amazon or at ecovacs.com. From Sept. 4 through Sept. 11, an Amazon launch deal brings the price to $1,000.

Editors’ note: Ajay Kumar’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Roborock. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: Apple’s $250M AI iPhone Settlement Is Coming Sooner Than Expected. How to Find Out if You’re Eligible for a Payout
Tech.content:
The legal machinery for class-action settlements grinds slowly, but a court order in Apple’s $250 million case over its iPhone AI features will potentially speed things up by seven months.

Apple settled a false-advertising lawsuit in May, agreeing to pay $250 million to customers who bought some iPhone models during a specified period. The lawsuit alleged that Apple misled customers by promising AI features that didn’t ship when the new devices did. If you purchased an iPhone 16 or iPhone 15 at launch, you may be entitled to receive a portion of the quarter-billion-dollar lawsuit. Payouts between $25 and $95 per eligible device are expected.

Apple lit up its flagship New York City store to resemble Siri’s new color scheme. Bridget Carey/CNET

In an earlier statement to CNET Managing Editor David Lumb, an Apple spokesperson said, “Apple has reached a settlement to resolve claims related to the availability of two additional features. We resolved this matter to stay focused on doing what we do best, delivering the most innovative products and services to our users.”

On July 17, according to an email from Clarkson Law Firm, “The Court has granted preliminary approval of the settlement … This means the Court has reviewed the proposed terms and found them sufficient to move forward to the next phase; it is not a final ruling on the settlement’s fairness.”

The latest Aug. 13 order moves up the final approval date.

Why is there a lawsuit over Apple Intelligence?

When Apple advertised its new iPhone 16 lineup in 2024, it emphasized how the models were optimized for AI features such as an enhanced Siri that could act as an intelligent agent. When the phones did arrive, Apple Intelligence wasn’t yet ready; its first features didn’t arrive until iOS 18.1, five weeks later.

According to the proposed settlement, “Apple allegedly saturated the market with deceptive ads, inducing consumers to purchase iPhones based on the promise of certain enhanced Siri features.”

Some features of Apple Intelligence did ship soon after the introduction of the iPhone 16 and iOS 18, including Visual Intelligence, Live Translation, Writing Tools, Genmoji and Clean Up. But those weren’t the advanced features Apple highlighted. In fact, the type of intelligent interactions Apple advertised are only starting to show up in Siri AI, which is part of iOS 27 that’s expected to be released later this year. The public beta of iOS 27 is available now.

Who is eligible for the $250 million settlement?

People who bought one of the following devices between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, are eligible to receive a settlement payment:

iPhone 16

iPhone 16E

iPhone 16 Plus

iPhone 16 Pro

iPhone 16 Pro Max

iPhone 15 Pro

iPhone 15 Pro Max

The iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max are included because they had the processor and memory to run Apple Intelligence features.

It’s estimated that approximately 36 million customers are eligible for this settlement.

How to claim your portion of the settlement

For now, you need to wait.

As set forth in the settlement, Apple will provide a list of eligible customers and their contact information to a settlement administrator.

After the data has been verified, the company Verita will send email and postal notices to those customers directing them to a settlement website. That site has not yet been created. The deadline for filing your claim will be 90 days after your notice arrives.

When can you expect to receive a settlement payment?

According to the settlement, Apple needed to provide the information about affected customers within five days of the settlement approval. As of late July, preliminary approval has been granted by the court.

After the data is provided and verified, a 45-day notice period begins to inform potential consumers that they’re eligible for a payment.

On Aug. 13, US District Court Judge Noël Wise granted approval to push forward the date from Sept. 29, 2027, to Feb. 24, 2027.

Provided approval is granted, that puts the first checks or deposits arriving sometime within a 60-day window after February next year, depending on court dates and possible extensions.

Tech.title: Welcome to Your Keyboard-Free Future. This Jazzy AI Microphone Is All You Need Now
Tech.content:
For years, tech companies have been telling us that voice will eventually supersede touchscreens as the primary way we interact with our technology, but it’s never quite happened — and I’d come to doubt whether it ever actually will.

At IFA in Berlin, I saw something that made me think again. A team of folks who left design-forward British tech startup Nothing have created an AI microphone that takes us at least one step closer to our voice-controlled future.

About the size of a small lighter, the Relay Q tucks easily and comfortably into your hand to form a bridge between your voice and your computer, between thinking and text. Hold down the tip to capture whisper-level audio, so you can subtly dictate or give voice commands in a quiet office without disturbing people. You can also double-click the top to press Enter or Send.

This design-forward device is a unique entry into the world of standalone AI devices.

What immediately impressed me about the Relay Q is its design and the tactile experience of holding the device. I wasn’t surprised to learn the team members are Nothing alumni, responsible for helping design some of the coolest audio and mobile devices on the market. These are people who know that how the technology looks and feels is an important part of whether people will truly love using it.

The Relay Q is available in dual-color tones — silver and electric blue, which gives Dyson vibes, and baby blue and orange for a jazzier look. The press-to-speak button on the top has a satisfyingly soft yet responsive feel to it as you hold it down to talk.

The Relay Q is wearable, too. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I’m also impressed by the way the tip of the device slides off, turning into a subtle wearable pin that clings to your collar with its built-in magnet, keeping the microphone close to your face. It’s a clever, thoughtful touch that provides flexibility based on how you want to use the product. To activate the mic in wearable mode, you’ll still need to press and hold the top of the main module or use a MagSafe remote (available separately) on the back of your iPhone.

The Relay Q is the gateway device to communicating with Relay’s AI desktop software, which is powered by Google Gemini and runs on macOS only for now (with Windows and Android compatibility coming later). You’ll need to grant the app access to your other apps so that it can carry out any commands you might give it through the Relay Q.

The MagSafe remote is available separately.

In a quick demo, I whisper into the microphone, asking it to draft an email asking someone to be a contributor to CNET. I watch on a screen as Gmail opens and an invite appears. It’s not a bad effort at all, and this is just one of many skills the AI agent can perform. I haven’t had a chance to test any others, but I did take a peek at the personalization options, where you can provide specific instructions about your writing preferences for the AI to reflect in its own writing style.

I’m especially interested in seeing how speech-to-text actually works when I’m putting together a longer draft. I actively enjoy writing — it’s why I do what I do, and I certainly don’t want AI to do it all for me. But now I find myself wondering whether typing always has to be my input method.

I think of old-school field reporters in the days before computers, who had to call the news desk and dictate their copy over the phone, usually off the cuff. There would certainly be a learning curve, but if I could learn how to effectively communicate my thoughts and writing style coherently, it could save me a lot of time. I’d still be writing, just with my voice.

In most circumstances, especially in an office or public setting, I’d be far too self-conscious and worried about disturbing people to do this. I like that the Relay Q is built specifically to capture low-level whispering, so I can mutter away quietly without worrying about people listening in.

The device is currently available to preorder for $150 for early supporters, including a MagSafe remote and 12 months of Relay Unlimited (the company’s software subscription). It sounds like the price might go up before or around the date the device is due to ship, which is currently January 2027.

Stand-alone AI devices are becoming more common, with many companies unveiling concepts and experimental tech right now, but I haven’t seen one quite like this before. I’m curious to see how it fares.

Editors’ note: Katie Collins’ travel costs for the IFA conference were covered in part by Xiaomi. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.
